Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is
an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the
sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so the identity
$1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents
([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and this decomposition is unique up to order
([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of
$A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent
$e$ (the two descriptions agree because $e$ is central).

The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals:
$B_iB_j\subseteq e_iAe_jA=e_ie_jA=0$ for $i\ne j$, and
$e_i\in B_i$ is the identity of $B_i$ since $e_i(e_ia)=e_ia$ and
$(ae_i)e_i=ae_i$. Moreover $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with
units $e_i$: every $a\in A$ is $a=(\sum_ie_i)a=\sum_ie_ia$ with $e_ia\in B_i$,
and if $\sum_ib_i=0$ with $b_i\in B_i$ then multiplying by $e_j$ gives
$b_j=e_jb_j=\sum_ie_jb_i=0$, so the sum is direct. Each $B_i$ is an
indecomposable two-sided ideal: if $B_i=J\oplus J'$ were a direct sum of
nonzero two-sided ideals, the projections of $e_i$ onto $J$ and $J'$ would be
nonzero orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ summing to $e_i$, as is seen by
applying to $e_i$ the $A$-bimodule projections $B_i\to J$ and $B_i\to J'$,
which satisfy $\pi(a x)=a\pi(x)$ and $\pi(xa)=\pi(x)a$; this contradicts
primitivity of $e_i$.

For every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has
$M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules: $\sum_ie_i=1$ acts as the identity on
$M$, so $M=\sum_ie_iM$, and if $\sum_im_i=0$ with $m_i=e_im_i$ then applying
$e_j$ gives $m_j=0$; each $e_iM$ is $A$-stable because $e_i$ is central. A
simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$, and then
$S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block: $S=(\sum_ie_i)S=\sum_ie_iS$ forces
some $e_iS\ne0$, and if $e_iS\ne0\ne e_jS$ with $i\ne j$ then simplicity gives
$e_iS=S=e_jS$, whence $S=e_iS=e_i(e_jS)=(e_ie_j)S=0$, a contradiction. Nothing
here asserts that a block is semisimple or simple, and the construction is
choice-free.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{	imes}$, $d,n\ge0$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda(d,n)$ be the set of weak compositions $\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_d)$ of $n$ (so $\mu_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ and $\sum_i\mu_i=n$; zero parts are allowed and give empty rows). For $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$ let $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]) and let $M^{\mu}:=m_\mu H$ be the right ideal it generates, the **(Hecke) permutation module**; $M^{\mu}$ is free over $R$ with basis $\{m_\mu T_{d(t)}:t	ext{ row-standard }\mu	ext{-tableau}\}$ and is the Hecke analogue of the module induced from the trivial representation of the Young subgroup ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]).

For a weak composition $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$, define $T_0(\lambda,\mu)$ to be the fillings of $[\lambda]$ by $1,\ldots,d$ with exactly $\mu_i$ entries equal to $i$, weakly increasing rows and strictly increasing columns. Put $T_0(\lambda)= igcup_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}T_0(\lambda,\mu)$ and $K_{\lambda\mu}:=|T_0(\lambda,\mu)|$. This explicitly extends the partition-content definition of [[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]] to weak compositions, including internal zero counts; a zero count means that its label is absent. The set is finite, since at most $d^n$ fillings occur for $n>0$, and at $n=0$ its unique member is the empty filling.

Here is the freeness statement in detail: the cosets $S_\mu d$ with $d\in D_\mu$ partition $S_n$, and $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for $u\in S_\mu$, $d\in D_\mu$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), so the standard basis theorem ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]) gives $T_uT_{d(t)}=T_{ud(t)}$ and $m_\mu T_{d(t)}=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}T_{u\,d(t)}$; these are the standard basis elements indexed by the single coset $S_\mu d(t)$, and the cosets are disjoint, whence $M^\mu= igoplus_tR\,m_\mu T_{d(t)}$ is free with the displayed basis as $t$ runs over the row-standard $\mu$-tableaux.

Put $M:= igoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ ([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and define the **q-Schur algebra** $$S(d,n):=\mathrm{End}_H(M),$$ the $R$-algebra of right $H$-module endomorphisms of $M$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]).

Hence $(\varphi,\Lambda^{+}(d,n))$ is a dominance-cellular basis of $S(d,n)$ ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and its cell modules are the **Weyl modules** $W^{\lambda}$, free over $R$ with basis $\{\varphi_T:T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$. Over a field $F$, $W^{\lambda}$ has nonzero simple head $L^{\lambda}$, the $L^{\lambda}$ for $\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$ form a complete set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $S(d,n)$-modules, and the decomposition matrix satisfies $d_{\lambda\lambda}=1$ and $d_{\lambda\mu}

For every $d\ge0$ and partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash d$,
$$h_\mu=\sum_{\lambda\vdash d}K_{\lambda\mu}s_\lambda.$$
Moreover, $K_{\lambda\mu}=0$ unless $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, and
$K_{\mu\mu}=1$. Thus, after ordering the partitions of $d$ by any linear
extension of dominance from smaller to larger, the matrix
$(K_{\lambda\mu})_{\lambda,\mu\vdash d}$ is lower unitriangular over
$\mathbb Z$.

Let $\mathcal C$ be an essentially small abelian category
([[def-abelian-category]]). Its set of isomorphism classes is denoted
$\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)$. The **Grothendieck group** of $\mathcal C$ is

$$ G_0(\mathcal C):=\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]\big/\langle e_Y-e_X-e_Z:\ 0\to X\to Y\to Z\to 0\text{ is short exact in }\mathcal C\rangle. $$

where $\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]$ is the free abelian group on
that set ([[def-free-abelian-group]]) and $[X]$ denotes the image of the
generator for the isomorphism class of $X$. Thus the defining relation is
$[Y]=[X]+[Z]$ for every short exact sequence
([[def-exact-sequence-and-short-exact-sequence-in-an-abelian-category]]).
This is the short-exact-sequence group, distinguished below from split
Grothendieck groups of projectives. No free abelian group on the possibly
class-sized collection of all objects is formed. The sequence
$0\to0\to0\to0$ in particular gives $[0]=0$.

derivations.claim: Multiplication by the central idempotent $\epsilon_B$ is the projection of every right $S$-module onto its $B$-summand: $N=\bigoplus_iN\epsilon_i$ by [F1], so $N\epsilon_B$ is that direct summand and is a submodule, and $N\epsilon_B=N$ exactly when all composition factors of $N$ lie in $B$. The assignment $N\mapsto N\epsilon_B$ is exact, because it is the projection onto a direct summand of the identity functor: for $f:N\to N'$ one has $f(N\epsilon_B)=f(N)\epsilon_B$, $\ker(f|_{N\epsilon_B})=(\ker f)\epsilon_B$ and $\operatorname{im}(f|_{N\epsilon_B})=(\operatorname{im}f)\epsilon_B$, so it preserves kernels and images.

A nonzero finite-dimensional module has a simple quotient: choose a proper submodule of maximal vector-space dimension. If a Weyl module had two nonzero summands, each would have a nonzero head, so its head would not be simple, contrary to [F2]. Thus it is indecomposable. Its block decomposition [F1] has precisely one nonzero summand, the block containing its head $L^\lambda$; hence $W^\lambda\epsilon_B$ is either $W^\lambda$ or $0$.

Apply the exact projection of step 1.1 to the class identity of the hypothesis. Since $M\epsilon_B=M$ by the hypothesis that all composition factors of $M$ lie in $B$, and since $W^{\lambda}\epsilon_B$ is $W^{\lambda}$ or $0$ by step 1.2, the induced identity in $G_0$ reads $$[M]=\sum_{\lambda:\,W^{\lambda}\in B}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}].$$ Subtracting it from the given identity $[M]=\sum_{\lambda}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]$ yields $$\sum_{\lambda:\,W^{\lambda}\notin B}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]=0$$ in $G_0(S\text{-mod})$.

By the linear independence of the Weyl classes [F3], all coefficients in the vanishing combination of step 2.1 are zero: $a_{\lambda}=0$ for every $\lambda$ with $W^{\lambda}\notin B$, which is the contrapositive of the assertion that $a_{\lambda}\ne0$ implies $W^{\lambda}\in B$.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 2.1 and 3.1 allow the subfamily of Weyl labels outside B to be empty: its class sum is 0 and there are no outside coefficients to force. For M=0, F3 linear independence applied to the given class identity forces every coefficient to vanish; the asserted implication then has no nonzero coefficient instance. The full indexing set is nonempty since d,n>=1 in Statement.
steps 2.1 and 3.1: the vanishing combination of classes outside B is the zero case

boundaries.reason: no unit or single-element case is used; the argument is a vanishing-coefficient statement
the algebra S is a fixed finite-dimensional q-Schur algebra; no degenerate range occurs
the argument has no ordered interval or endpoint

The Statement supplies a fixed block of the finite-dimensional Schur algebra. Step 1.1 uses its already determined central idempotent to define an exact projection, and step 2.1 subtracts the projected finite class identity. Step 3.1 applies integer Weyl-basis independence. No roots, bases, representatives or new block are selected; absence of a choice obligation follows from these explicit projection operations, not just from finite family size.

step 3.1 turns the vanishing combination into a_lambda=0 for W^lambda outside B

Let $F$ be a field, $q=1\in F$, and let $H_{F,1}(S_n)$ be the specialization of
the generic type-A Hecke algebra at $v\mapsto1$, so that
$H_{F,1}(S_n)\cong F[S_n]$ with $T_w\mapsto w$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]], step 1.1).
Then the Hecke theory of this page specializes as follows.

1. The Murphy elements $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ specialize to the row
   symmetrizers $\sum_{w\in S_\mu}w$, and the Murphy basis $\{m_{st}\}$ of
   $H_{F,1}(S_n)$ specializes to the Murphy basis of the group algebra
   $F[S_n]$ (the base change $\mathbb Z[S_n]\to F[S_n]$ of the integral Murphy
   basis).
2. For every $\lambda\vdash n$ the specialization of the page's Hecke Specht
   module $S^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) is
   the ordinary Specht module in the Dipper-James convention:
   $S^{\lambda}_{q=1}\cong S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ as $F[S_n]$-modules, with
   the standard polytabloid basis ([[thm-standard-polytabloid-basis]]); the
   specialized cell form is the standard bilinear form on $S^{\lambda}$ whose
   radical defines the James quotient $D^{\lambda}$
   ([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]).
3. The quantum characteristic of $q=1$ is $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ when
   $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$, and $e=\infty$ when
   $\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
   ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); in
   characteristic $p>0$ a partition is $e$-regular exactly when it is
   $p$-regular. Hence $D^{\lambda}_{q=1}\ne0$ exactly for $p$-regular $\lambda$
   ([[thm-specht-radical-quotient-is-nonzero-exactly-for-p-regular-partitions]]),
   and for non-$p$-regular $\lambda$ one has
   $\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}$. Over splitting residue fields this also matches the group-side
   classification and conjugate-sign dictionary of
   [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]] and
   [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]];
   the assertion here holds over every field by the cellular classification below.
   In characteristic $0$ the specialization is split semisimple and all Specht
   modules are irreducible.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), and let $S^{\lambda}$ be the type-A Hecke Specht module of this page in the Dipper-James convention ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) for $\lambda\vdash n$. Then for all partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ the modules $S^{\lambda}$ and $S^{\mu}$ lie in the same block of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Equivalently, for finite $e$, the blocks of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ of size at most $n$ with $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. For $e=\infty$ use $C_\infty(\lambda):=\lambda$; the Hecke algebra is semisimple and its blocks are indexed by partitions of $n$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-core $C_e(\lambda)$ and
$e$-weight $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|$
([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Then
$$n=|\lambda|=|C_e(\lambda)|+e\,w_e(\lambda),$$
so $w_e(\lambda)=(n-|C_e(\lambda)|)/e\in\mathbb N_0$. Equivalently every
sequence of removals of removable border strips of size $e$ from $\lambda$ down
to its $e$-core
([[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]) has exactly
$w_e(\lambda)$ steps, and $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|$ equals both the number
of hooks of the multipartition $Q_e(\lambda)$ and, by the bijection of
[[thm-e-quotient-controls-hooks-divisible-by-e]], the number of hooks of
$\lambda$ of length divisible by $e$.

Throughout the proof, $\lambda\setminus H$ means deletion of the rim strip
corresponding to the node hook $H$, as in
[[thm-e-quotient-controls-hooks-divisible-by-e]].

No choice principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]], [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]), let $n\ge0$ and $d\ge n$, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl modules of $S_F(d,n)$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Then for partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts, $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S_F(d,n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently, for finite $e$, the blocks of $S_F(d,n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. For $e=\infty$ we set $C_\infty(\lambda):=\lambda$; the algebra is semisimple and its blocks are indexed by the partitions of $n$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-abacus configurations as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] and the top-packed set
$X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]. For every $\beta$-set $X$
of $\lambda$ the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ is the same, so the $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)=P(X^{(e)})$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition, and it is
exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing removable
border strips of size $e$ from $[\lambda]$ until none is left
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). In particular every
maximal sequence of such removals gives the same terminal partition
$C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal
partition contains no hook of length $e$. Moreover any two normalised beta-sets
($e\mid|X|$) give the same ordered quotient $Q_e(\lambda)$ and weight.

No choice principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is
an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the
sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so the identity
$1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents
([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and this decomposition is unique up to order
([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of
$A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent
$e$ (the two descriptions agree because $e$ is central).

The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals:
$B_iB_j\subseteq e_iAe_jA=e_ie_jA=0$ for $i\ne j$, and
$e_i\in B_i$ is the identity of $B_i$ since $e_i(e_ia)=e_ia$ and
$(ae_i)e_i=ae_i$. Moreover $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with
units $e_i$: every $a\in A$ is $a=(\sum_ie_i)a=\sum_ie_ia$ with $e_ia\in B_i$,
and if $\sum_ib_i=0$ with $b_i\in B_i$ then multiplying by $e_j$ gives
$b_j=e_jb_j=\sum_ie_jb_i=0$, so the sum is direct. Each $B_i$ is an
indecomposable two-sided ideal: if $B_i=J\oplus J'$ were a direct sum of
nonzero two-sided ideals, the projections of $e_i$ onto $J$ and $J'$ would be
nonzero orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ summing to $e_i$, as is seen by
applying to $e_i$ the $A$-bimodule projections $B_i\to J$ and $B_i\to J'$,
which satisfy $\pi(a x)=a\pi(x)$ and $\pi(xa)=\pi(x)a$; this contradicts
primitivity of $e_i$.

For every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has
$M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules: $\sum_ie_i=1$ acts as the identity on
$M$, so $M=\sum_ie_iM$, and if $\sum_im_i=0$ with $m_i=e_im_i$ then applying
$e_j$ gives $m_j=0$; each $e_iM$ is $A$-stable because $e_i$ is central. A
simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$, and then
$S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block: $S=(\sum_ie_i)S=\sum_ie_iS$ forces
some $e_iS\ne0$, and if $e_iS\ne0\ne e_jS$ with $i\ne j$ then simplicity gives
$e_iS=S=e_jS$, whence $S=e_iS=e_i(e_jS)=(e_ie_j)S=0$, a contradiction. Nothing
here asserts that a block is semisimple or simple, and the construction is
choice-free.

Let $A$ be a unital ring ([[def-ring]]), with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A: za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$. Suppose that
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k=f_1+\cdots+f_\ell$$
where $\{e_1,\dots,e_k\}$ and $\{f_1,\dots,f_\ell\}$ are finite families of
pairwise orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ that are primitive among central
idempotents: each is nonzero and admits no decomposition as a sum of two nonzero
orthogonal central idempotents (zero parts are omitted). Then $k=\ell$ and there
is a bijection $\sigma$ of the index sets with $e_i=f_{\sigma(i)}$ for all $i$;
in particular the decomposition of $1$ into primitive central idempotents is
unique up to order. No choice principle is used, the families being finite.

derivations.claim: Specialisation. Take $q=1\in k^{\times}$ and $e$ the quantum characteristic of $(k,q)$; since $q=1$ and $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$, [F1] gives $e=p$. By [F1] there is an algebra isomorphism $H_{k,1}(S_n)\cong k[S_n]$ carrying the Hecke Specht modules of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$ to the group Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k$, so by [F5] this isomorphism induces a bijection between the blocks of the two algebras that matches $S^{\lambda}$ with $S^{\lambda}_k$; in particular $S^{\lambda}_k$ and $S^{\mu}_k$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if the corresponding Hecke Specht modules lie in the same block of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$.

The core criterion. Applying the Hecke block criterion [F2] with $q=1$ and $e=p$, the Hecke Specht modules of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$ lie in the same block if and only if the labels $\lambda,\mu$ have the same $p$-core. Together with step 1.1 this gives: $S^{\lambda}_k$ and $S^{\mu}_k$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $C_p(\lambda)=C_p(\mu)$.

The parametrisation by cores and weights. By [F2] the blocks of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$, hence by step 1.1 the blocks of $k[S_n]$, are indexed by the $p$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod p$; the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ corresponds to $C_p(\lambda)$. For $n\ge0$ and such a $\gamma$ put $w:=(n-|\gamma|)/p\in\mathbb N_0$; by [F4] this is exactly the $p$-weight $w_p(\lambda)$ of any Specht label with core $\gamma$, and $n=|\gamma|+pw$. Since $w$ is determined by $n$ and $\gamma$, the map $\gamma\mapsto(\gamma,w)$ is a bijection onto the displayed set of pairs, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$.

Steps 2.1 and 3.1 establish both assertions: the same-block criterion by the $p$-core, and the indexing of the blocks by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $n=|\gamma|+pw$ together with the identification of the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ as $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$. [step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

The classification is stated independently, by a Young-module and Brauer-quotient route, as Theorem 1 of O'Donovan's preprint recorded in the sources; that reference is an independent confirmation of the statement and is not used in the proof above. No choice principle is used anywhere in this item.

internal products $s_{n-2,2}*s_{n-2,2}$ at ranks $n=4,\dots,9$
(notation $s_{a,b,c}$ for Schur functions of the padded partitions, and
$s_\bullet$ on the stable row):

$$s_{2,2}*s_{2,2}=s_4+s_{1,1,1,1}+s_{2,2},$$

Consequently the reduced coefficients
([[def-reduced-kronecker-coefficient]]) for the pair $((2),(2))$ are
$\bar g^\gamma_{(2),(2)}=1,1,2,1,1,2,1,1,1,1$ for
$\gamma=\varnothing,(1,1,1),(2),(1),(1,1),(2,1),(2,2),(3),(3,1),(4)$
respectively, and $\bar g^\gamma_{(2),(2)}=0$ for all other $\gamma$; in
particular $\bar g^{(2)}_{(2),(2)}=2$ and $\bar g^{(4)}_{(2),(2)}=1$. The
displayed data also verify directly, for this pair, that the whole product is
$V$-stable at rank $8$ and not at rank $7$: applying $V$ (adding a box to the
first row of every Schur function) to the rank-$8$ expansion reproduces the
rank-$9$ expansion term by term, whereas applying $V$ to the rank-$7$
expansion misses the single term $s_{4,4}$ of the rank-$8$ expansion, the
other nine terms matching term by term. The proved threshold theorem
([[thm-exact-global-stabilization-threshold-for-a-fixed-kronecker-product]])
establishes $V$-stability for every rank from $8$ onward, with exact least
global index $8=|(2)|+|(2)|+2+2$; the displayed finite data independently
verify the six listed products and the failure of the preceding step.

For all partitions $\alpha,\beta$ and every integer
$n\ge\max\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,\,|\beta|+\beta_1\}$:
$$s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]}=\sum_\gamma \bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\,s_{\gamma[n]},$$
an identity in the symmetric function ring, where $s_{\gamma[n]}$ is the
Jacobi–Trudi determinant attached to the integer sequence
$\gamma[n]=(n-|\gamma|,\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\dots)$, equal to $0$ or $\pm1$ times
a Schur function
([[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]],
[[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]), and $*$ is the internal product
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

For an ordinary partition $\delta\vdash n$ the coefficient of $s_\delta$ is
$$g^\delta_{\alpha[n],\beta[n]} =\sum_\gamma \bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\, \langle s_{\gamma[n]},s_\delta\rangle_H,$$
where each Hall factor is $0$ or a sign coming from Jacobi–Trudi
straightening ([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]).
At small admissible ranks the signed terms can cancel or coalesce;
individual coefficients need not yet equal their reduced values. The range
displayed is precisely the set of $n$ for which $\alpha[n]$ and $\beta[n]$
are partitions.

For all partitions $\alpha,\beta$ with missing parts read as zero,
$$\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)=N:=|\alpha|+|\beta|+\alpha_1+\beta_1,$$
with $\operatorname{stab}$ as in
[[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]].

More precisely. At every $n\ge N$ all support labels $\gamma[n]$ of the
finite support of $\bar g^\bullet_{\alpha,\beta}$ are ordinary partitions, the
full product has the fixed nonnegative Schur expansion
$s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]}=\sum_\gamma\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}s_{\gamma[n]}$,
and the family is $V$-stable from $N$ onward. If both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are
nonempty, $N-1$ is admissible and the product at $N$ is not $V$ of the product
at $N-1$: the coefficient of $s_{(\alpha+\beta)[N]}$ is $1$, its first two
parts are equal, and no such Schur basis vector lies in the image of $V$. If
exactly one input is empty, $N$ is already the least ordinary input rank, and
the same image obstruction at $N$ excludes any earlier stabilization index in
the Jacobi–Trudi convention of the Definition. If both inputs are empty,
$N=0$, $s_{(n)}*s_{(n)}=s_{(n)}$ (including $s_{(0)}=1$) and $V^n(1)=s_{(n)}$,
so stabilization begins at zero and no negative-rank product is invoked. No
sharpness for an individual coefficient is claimed.

Let $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ be a partition with $|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_k$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let $n\ge0$ be
an integer. Read $|\varnothing|=0$ and $\alpha_1=0$ when
$\alpha=\varnothing$. Whenever

$$n\;\ge\;|\alpha|+\alpha_1,$$

define the **first-row padding** of $\alpha$ to size $n$ to be
$$\alpha[n]:=\bigl(n-|\alpha|,\ \alpha_1,\ \alpha_2,\ \dots,\ \alpha_k\bigr).$$

The threshold is exact.

**Above the threshold.** Suppose $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$. Then
$n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1\ge0$, so every entry of the displayed sequence is a
nonnegative integer, the entries sum to $(n-|\alpha|)+|\alpha|=n$, and the
sequence is weakly decreasing because $n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1$ and $\alpha$ is
weakly decreasing ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).
If $\alpha$ is nonempty then $\alpha_1\ge1$, hence $n-|\alpha|\ge1$ and the
displayed sequence is a partition of $n$ with positive parts. If
$\alpha=\varnothing$ then the displayed sequence is $(n)$; this is a partition
of $n$ for every $n\ge1$, while for $n=0$ one takes $\varnothing[0]:=\varnothing$,
the unique partition of $0$. Thus the padding is defined and is a partition of
$n$ on the whole displayed range.

**Below the threshold.** If $\alpha$ is nonempty and $n<|\alpha|+\alpha_1$,
then $n-|\alpha|<\alpha_1$; if also $n\ge|\alpha|$ the leading entry is
nonnegative but smaller than the second entry $\alpha_1$, and if $n<|\alpha|$
it is negative. In both cases the displayed sequence is not a partition, so
$\alpha[n]$ is left undefined. The threshold $|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ is therefore
the exact size at which the padded family begins: for nonempty $\alpha$, at
$n=|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ the padding equals $(\alpha_1,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots)$,
which is a partition with a repeated first part when $\alpha$ is nonempty.

**Neutrality of the notation.** This definition records a family of partitions;
it asserts no constancy of any quantity along the family and no stability
property. The same notation is used by the FI-module and
representation-stability developments; no FI-module structure or generation
degree is asserted here.

derivations.claim: *Ranks six, seven and eight.* In the displayed products of [F3]: $s_{4,2}*s_{4,2}$ contains $2s_{4,2}$ (rank $6$), $s_{5,2}*s_{5,2}$ contains $2s_{5,2}$ (rank $7$), and $s_{6,2}*s_{6,2}$ contains $2s_{6,2}$ (rank $8$). Hence the coefficient $g^{(4,2)}_{(4,2),(4,2)}=g^{(5,2)}_{(5,2),(5,2)}=g^{(6,2)}_{(6,2),(6,2)}=2$ equals the reduced value $\bar g^{(2)}_{(2),(2)}=2$ at ranks $6,7,8$.

*Rank five is different.* The rank-five product $s_{3,2}*s_{3,2}$ contains $s_{3,2}$ with coefficient $1$, not $2$, so the coefficient $g^{(3,2)}_{(3,2),(3,2)}=1\ne\bar g^{(2)}_{(2),(2)}$; together with step 1.1 this shows that the least rank from which the coefficient equals the stable value for all later ranks is $6$. For $n\ge6$ this is indeed stable: ranks $6,7,8$ are displayed in step 1.1 and ranks $n\ge8$ follow from [F1] with the padded label $(n-2,2)=\gamma[n]$.

*Comparison with the global threshold.* By [F2] the whole product is $V$-stable exactly from rank $8$ onward, and it is not $V$-stable at rank $7$; the single coefficient of steps 1.1 and 2.1 has already reached its stable value $2$ at rank $6$ and stays there. For every partition $\lambda$, let $s_\lambda\in\Lambda$ be the stable Schur
function defined by bialternants
([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]). For any integers
$r\ge\ell(\lambda)$ and $c\ge\ell(\lambda')$, pad $\lambda$ and $\lambda'$
with zero parts to lengths $r$ and $c$, respectively. Then
$$s_\lambda=\det\bigl(h_{\lambda_i-i+j}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le r}=\det\bigl(e_{\lambda'_i-i+j}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le c},$$
where $h_k,e_k\in\Lambda$ are the stable complete and elementary functions
([[thm-elementary-and-complete-families-freely-generate-the-stable-ring]],
[[def-elementary-symmetric-polynomials]],
[[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]). In these
determinants use $h_0=e_0=1$, set $h_k=e_k=0$ for $k<0$, and take the empty
determinant to be $1$.

Work in $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$. For a
partition $\rho$ write
$m_i(\rho):=\#\{j:\rho_j=i\}$ and
$z_\rho:=\prod_{i\ge1}i^{m_i(\rho)}m_i(\rho)!$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]).

For partitions $\lambda$ and $\rho$ of the same integer, let $N(\lambda,\rho)$
be the number of ways to distribute the cycles of a permutation $w$ of cycle
type $\rho$ among the $\ell(\lambda)$ rows, labelled $1,\dots,\ell(\lambda)$,
so that row $j$ receives cycles whose lengths sum to $\lambda_j$. Cycles of
equal length count as **distinct** here, because they are distinct cycles of
$w$; equivalently,

$$N(\lambda,\rho)=\sum_{(m_i^{(j)})}\ \prod_{i\ge1}\frac{m_i(\rho)!}{\prod_j m_i^{(j)}!},$$

the sum over all matrices $(m_i^{(j)})$ of nonnegative integers with
$\sum_j m_i^{(j)}=m_i(\rho)$ for every $i$ and
$\sum_i i\,m_i^{(j)}=\lambda_j$ for every $j$; each summand is the product
over $i$ of the number of ways to assign the $m_i(\rho)$ labelled cycles of
length $i$ to rows with the prescribed multiplicities $m_i^{(j)}$, so
$N(\lambda,\rho)$ is a nonnegative integer. Then

$$h_\lambda=\sum_{\rho\vdash|\lambda|}N(\lambda,\rho)\,\frac{p_\rho}{z_\rho}\qquad\text{in }\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}.$$

In particular $h_d=\sum_{\rho\vdash d}p_\rho/z_\rho$ for every $d\ge0$.

For every $n\ge0$ and every $\lambda\vdash n$, let $S^\lambda$ be the complex
Specht module of shape $\lambda$
([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]) and $\chi^\lambda$
its character, an irreducible character of $S_n$
([[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]]). Then

$$\operatorname{ch}(\chi^\lambda)=s_\lambda\in\Lambda^n,$$

the stable Schur function of shape $\lambda$
([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]). In particular $\operatorname{ch}$
maps the $\mathbb Z$-basis $\{\chi^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ of $R(S_n)$ to the
$\mathbb Z$-basis $\{s_\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ of $\Lambda^n$, and all values
$\chi^\lambda(\rho)$ are integers.

For all partitions $\lambda,\mu,\nu\vdash n$,
$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=\bigl\langle\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu,\chi^\nu\bigr\rangle=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\chi^\lambda(\sigma)\chi^\mu(\sigma)\chi^\nu(\sigma),$$
where $\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu$ is the pointwise product of class functions and the
sum uses the real-valuedness of the irreducible characters, so that no
conjugation appears on the third factor.

For every $n\ge0$ and every $\lambda\vdash n$, let $S^\lambda$ be the complex
Specht module of shape $\lambda$
([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]) and $\chi^\lambda$
its character, an irreducible character of $S_n$
([[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]]). Then

$$\operatorname{ch}(\chi^\lambda)=s_\lambda\in\Lambda^n,$$

the stable Schur function of shape $\lambda$
([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]). In particular $\operatorname{ch}$
maps the $\mathbb Z$-basis $\{\chi^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ of $R(S_n)$ to the
$\mathbb Z$-basis $\{s_\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ of $\Lambda^n$, and all values
$\chi^\lambda(\rho)$ are integers.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$ and work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be
partitions of $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ be the tensor product of their complex
Specht modules, a finite-dimensional complex $S_n$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). The
**Kronecker coefficient** $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ of a third partition
$\nu\vdash n$ is the multiplicity of $S^\nu$ in this tensor product:

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu):=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}}{\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu},$$

where $\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}$ is the isotypic
component of type $S^\nu$
([[def-isotypic-component-of-a-completely-reducible-representation]]).

**Well-definedness.** The module $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ is
finite-dimensional, and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb C=0$ does not divide the
order of the finite group $S_n$, so complex Maschke's theorem gives complete
reducibility
([[thm-maschkes-theorem-for-finite-groups-over-fields-whose-characteristic-does-not-divide-the-group-order]],
[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],
[[def-completely-reducible-representation]]). The complex Specht modules
$S^\nu$, $\nu\vdash n$, are a complete list of pairwise inequivalent
irreducible $S_n$-modules
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]],
[[cor-distinct-specht-modules-are-inequivalent]]). Consequently a decomposition
into irreducibles has the form
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu S^\nu$
with nonnegative integer multiplicities $m_\nu$, and the isotypic component of
type $S^\nu$ is the direct sum of exactly the $m_\nu$ copies of $S^\nu$
appearing in any such decomposition, by
[[thm-isotypic-decomposition-of-a-completely-reducible-representation-is-unique]]
(Proof step 2.1 identifies each grouped block with the defining isotypic sum).
In particular
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu)_{(S^\nu)}=m_\nu\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu$
and $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu>0$ because $S^\nu$ is irreducible. Hence
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=m_\nu$ is a nonnegative integer, independent of the chosen
decomposition, and $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is by definition the multiplicity of
$S^\nu$ in $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$.

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of
degrees $a$ and $b$ to a module of degree $a+b$, the internal product keeps the
rank: both inputs and the output are $S_n$-modules of the same degree $n$. The
two operations are different constructions on different data; the outer product
is mentioned here only for contrast and is not used in this definition.

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the tensor product, Maschke's theorem,
the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional
complex representation theory of a finite group.

For $\alpha=\beta=(2)$, every rank $n\ge4$ product is $U_nR_{(2),(2)}$, where
$$R_{(2),(2)}=1+s_{(1)}+2s_{(2)}+s_{(1,1)}+s_{(1,1,1)}+2s_{(2,1)}+s_{(2,2)}+s_{(3)}+s_{(3,1)}+s_{(4)}.$$
Its coefficients are the reduced coefficients, and all other reduced coefficients vanish. This finite polynomial and its rank-four cancellation are proved in steps 1.2 and 3.2 above.

For all partitions $\alpha,\beta$ with missing parts read as zero,
$$\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)=N:=|\alpha|+|\beta|+\alpha_1+\beta_1,$$
with $\operatorname{stab}$ as in
[[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]].

More precisely. At every $n\ge N$ all support labels $\gamma[n]$ of the
finite support of $\bar g^\bullet_{\alpha,\beta}$ are ordinary partitions, the
full product has the fixed nonnegative Schur expansion
$s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]}=\sum_\gamma\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}s_{\gamma[n]}$,
and the family is $V$-stable from $N$ onward. If both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are
nonempty, $N-1$ is admissible and the product at $N$ is not $V$ of the product
at $N-1$: the coefficient of $s_{(\alpha+\beta)[N]}$ is $1$, its first two
parts are equal, and no such Schur basis vector lies in the image of $V$. If
exactly one input is empty, $N$ is already the least ordinary input rank, and
the same image obstruction at $N$ excludes any earlier stabilization index in
the Jacobi–Trudi convention of the Definition. If both inputs are empty,
$N=0$, $s_{(n)}*s_{(n)}=s_{(n)}$ (including $s_{(0)}=1$) and $V^n(1)=s_{(n)}$,
so stabilization begins at zero and no negative-rank product is invoked. No
sharpness for an individual coefficient is claimed.

**Padded sequences.** For a partition $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ and an
integer $n$, with missing parts read as zero, the first-row padding is the sequence
$\alpha[n]:=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$, a partition of $n$ exactly
when $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]],
[[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]]). When this sequence is used as
a partition label, omit trailing zero entries; in particular
$\varnothing[0]=\varnothing$ and the missing first part is zero.

**The Jacobi–Trudi completion.** For an arbitrary finite sequence of integers
$\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m)$, define
$$s_\mu:=\det\bigl(h_{\mu_j-j+i}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m},$$
where $h_0=1$ and $h_k=0$ for $k<0$
([[thm-jacobi-trudi-and-dual-jacobi-trudi-identities]]); for the empty sequence
the empty determinant is $1$. Every such determinant is $0$ or $\pm1$ times a
Schur function. Indeed, put $q_j:=\mu_j+m-j$. If $q_j=q_k$ for $j\ne k$, the
$j$-th and $k$-th columns of the matrix agree, so the determinant vanishes.
Otherwise let $\sigma$ be the permutation sorting $q$ into decreasing order
$q_{\sigma(1)}>\cdots>q_{\sigma(m)}$ and set $\nu_j:=q_{\sigma(j)}+j-m$; then
$\nu$ is weakly decreasing and, permuting columns with sign
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ and using
$h_{\nu_j-j+i}=h_{q_{\sigma(j)}+i-m}$, the determinant equals
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\det(h_{\nu_j-j+i})$. If $\min_jq_j<0$ then
$\nu_m<0$ and the last column of this determinant is zero, so the value is
$0$; if $\min_jq_j\ge0$ then $\nu$, after deleting trailing zero entries, is a partition of $|\mu|$
with at most $m$ parts and the Jacobi–Trudi identity gives the value
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)s_\nu$. In particular $s_{\alpha[n]}\in\Lambda^n$
for every $n\ge0$, and $s_{\alpha[n]}=0$ for $n<0$: every term of the
determinant expansion has total degree $n$, so for $n<0$ some factor has
negative index and vanishes.

**The operators $U_n$ and $V$.** The Schur functions form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of
$\Lambda$ ([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]), so there are unique
$\mathbb Z$-linear endomorphisms $U_n$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$) and $V$ of $\Lambda$
determined on the Schur basis by
$$U_n(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda[n]},\qquad V(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda+(1)},$$
where $\lambda+(1)=(\lambda_1+1,\lambda_2,\dots)$. Thus $U_n(\Lambda)\subseteq\Lambda^n$ for $n\ge0$ (and $U_n=0$ for
$n<0$), while $V$ raises degree by one; in particular $V(1)=s_{(1)}$. The operators
are extended linearly, and $V^k$ denotes the $k$-fold iterate of $V$.

**The stabilization index.** The internal product $*$ on $\Lambda$ is the
degree-preserving product of
[[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]] and
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]. For partitions
$\alpha,\beta$, define $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ to be the least
integer $n_0\ge0$ such that
$$s_{\alpha[n_0+k]}*s_{\beta[n_0+k]}=V^k\bigl(s_{\alpha[n_0]}*s_{\beta[n_0]}\bigr) \qquad\text{for all }k>0,$$
following the source. This definition records the source's convention only: it
does not assert that such an $n_0$ exists, nor that a value of $n_0$ satisfying
the display is least for any other property. Existence, least-ness and the
exact value of $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ are proved in
[[thm-exact-global-stabilization-threshold-for-a-fixed-kronecker-product]].

Let $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ be a partition with $|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_k$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let $n\ge0$ be
an integer. Read $|\varnothing|=0$ and $\alpha_1=0$ when
$\alpha=\varnothing$. Whenever

$$n\;\ge\;|\alpha|+\alpha_1,$$

define the **first-row padding** of $\alpha$ to size $n$ to be
$$\alpha[n]:=\bigl(n-|\alpha|,\ \alpha_1,\ \alpha_2,\ \dots,\ \alpha_k\bigr).$$

The threshold is exact.

**Above the threshold.** Suppose $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$. Then
$n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1\ge0$, so every entry of the displayed sequence is a
nonnegative integer, the entries sum to $(n-|\alpha|)+|\alpha|=n$, and the
sequence is weakly decreasing because $n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1$ and $\alpha$ is
weakly decreasing ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).
If $\alpha$ is nonempty then $\alpha_1\ge1$, hence $n-|\alpha|\ge1$ and the
displayed sequence is a partition of $n$ with positive parts. If
$\alpha=\varnothing$ then the displayed sequence is $(n)$; this is a partition
of $n$ for every $n\ge1$, while for $n=0$ one takes $\varnothing[0]:=\varnothing$,
the unique partition of $0$. Thus the padding is defined and is a partition of
$n$ on the whole displayed range.

**Below the threshold.** If $\alpha$ is nonempty and $n<|\alpha|+\alpha_1$,
then $n-|\alpha|<\alpha_1$; if also $n\ge|\alpha|$ the leading entry is
nonnegative but smaller than the second entry $\alpha_1$, and if $n<|\alpha|$
it is negative. In both cases the displayed sequence is not a partition, so
$\alpha[n]$ is left undefined. The threshold $|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ is therefore
the exact size at which the padded family begins: for nonempty $\alpha$, at
$n=|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ the padding equals $(\alpha_1,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots)$,
which is a partition with a repeated first part when $\alpha$ is nonempty.

**Neutrality of the notation.** This definition records a family of partitions;
it asserts no constancy of any quantity along the family and no stability
property. The same notation is used by the FI-module and
representation-stability developments; no FI-module structure or generation
degree is asserted here.

The five tails $\varnothing,(1),(2),(1,1),(1,1,1)$ are already admissible for every $n\ge4$. For the remaining five tails, sorting the $q_j$ of [F4] gives the following values at ranks $4,5,6,7$; each becomes its ordinary padded Schur function once its threshold $|\gamma|+\gamma_1$ is reached: $\begin{array}{c|cccc}\gamma&4&5&6&7\\\hline(2,1)&0&s_{(2,2,1)}&s_{(3,2,1)}&s_{(4,2,1)}\\(2,2)&0&0&s_{(2,2,2)}&s_{(3,2,2)}\\(3)&-s_{(2,2)}&0&s_{(3,3)}&s_{(4,3)}\\(3,1)&-s_{(2,1,1)}&-s_{(2,2,1)}&0&s_{(3,3,1)}\\(4)&-s_{(3,1)}&-s_{(3,2)}&-s_{(3,3)}&0\end{array}$. Multiplying by the coefficients in [F3] and collecting terms yields precisely the four displayed products at ranks $4$ through $7$. At ranks $8,9$ every tail is admissible, and padding the same polynomial yields precisely the two displayed products, including zeros for every unlisted Schur label. This verifies the six products without assuming the source table.

*The reduced coefficients and stable ranks.* By [F3], the ten coefficients of $R_{(2),(2)}$ are exactly the listed reduced coefficients, and all others vanish. For $n\ge8$, [F4] sends each padded label to its rank-$(n+1)$ padding without changing its coefficient. Thus the rank-eight product maps to the rank-nine product term by term, and [F3] proves stability for all later ranks, with exact index $8=2+2+2+2$.

*Failure at rank seven.* The rank-seven expansion has the nine labels $(7),(4,1,1,1),(5,2),(6,1),(5,1,1),(4,2,1),(3,2,2),(4,3),(3,3,1)$, with coefficients $1,1,2,1,1,2,1,1,1$. Increasing their first parts by one gives exactly the rank-eight expansion minus $s_{(4,4)}$. That last term has coefficient one and is outside the image of $V$, since every $V(s_\delta)$ has strictly larger first part than second part. Hence the rank-eight product is not $V$ of the rank-seven product.

*The individual coefficient.* The computed rank-four and rank-five products have coefficient one at their $(n-2,2)$ labels; ranks six and seven have coefficient two, and every $n\ge8$ has the reduced coefficient two by step 2.1. functions of $\Lambda$ ([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]); when
$|\delta|\ne|a|+|b|+|c|$ the coefficient is $0$, the product being homogeneous
of degree $|a|+|b|+|c|$. Since
$s_as_b=\sum_\phi c^\phi_{a,b}s_\phi$ with

derivations.claim: *Degree collapse.* Take a nonzero summand of the expansion in [F1]; by the degree equations of [F1], $|\alpha|+|\beta|-|\gamma|=(|\rho|+|\lambda|+|\theta|)+(|\rho|+|\eta|+|\pi|)-(|\mu|+|\theta|+|\pi|)=2|\rho|+|\lambda|+|\eta|-|\mu|=2|\rho|+|\mu|$, using $|\lambda|=|\eta|=|\mu|$. Since $|\gamma|=|\alpha|+|\beta|$, this gives $2|\rho|+|\mu|=0$, so $\rho=\mu=\varnothing$ and then $|\lambda|=|\eta|=0$, so $\lambda=\eta=\varnothing$.

*Collapse of the sum.* With $\rho=\lambda=\eta=\mu=\varnothing$, the only possibly nonzero summands have $c^\alpha_{\varnothing,\varnothing,\theta}=[s_\alpha]s_\theta=\delta_{\alpha,\theta}$ and $c^\beta_{\varnothing,\varnothing,\pi}=[s_\beta]s_\pi=\delta_{\beta,\pi}$, and $g^\varnothing_{\varnothing,\varnothing}=1$; hence $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}=c^\gamma_{\varnothing,\alpha,\beta}=c^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$ by the symmetry of the threefold coefficient in [F2], which is the first display.

*The top coefficient equals one.* For $\gamma=\alpha+\beta$ we have $c^{\alpha+\beta}_{\alpha,\beta}=1$. If $\beta=\varnothing$, the skew shape is empty and its unique empty tableau proves this; this is also the induction base. Suppose $\beta\ne\varnothing$. Existence: fill row $i$ of the skew shape $(\alpha+\beta)/\alpha$, which has $\beta_i$ cells, with the letter $i$; the rows are constant and hence weakly increasing, the columns are strictly increasing because the letters increase down the rows, and the reading word is $1^{\beta_1}2^{\beta_2}\cdots$, which is lattice because $\beta$ is weakly decreasing. Uniqueness: let $T$ be a Littlewood–Richardson tableau of shape $(\alpha+\beta)/\alpha$ and content $\beta$. The first letter of its reading word is the rightmost cell of the first skew row; the lattice condition on the prefix of length one forces that letter to be $1$, and since the row is weakly increasing every cell of the first row is $1$. The first row is read first and consists of exactly $\beta_1$ cells, so it exhausts the $\beta_1$ letters $1$ of the content. Deleting the first row leaves the shape $(\alpha'+\beta')/\alpha'$ with $\alpha'=(\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\dots)$, $\beta'=(\beta_2,\beta_3,\dots)$, carrying no letter $1$; its reading word, with every letter decreased by one, satisfies the lattice condition: the comparisons among letters $\ge2$ hold because they hold for the corresponding prefixes of the original lattice word, and the comparison with letter $1$ is not required after the shift. Induction on the number of rows now shows that row $i$ consists of $\beta_i$ copies of $i$, so $T$ is the displayed filling and $c^{\alpha+\beta}_{\alpha,\beta}=1$. With [F2] and step 2.1 this gives $\bar g^{\alpha+\beta}_{\alpha,\beta}=c^{\alpha+\beta}_{\alpha,\beta}=1$.

*Empty cases.* If $\alpha=\varnothing$, step 2.1 gives $\bar g^\gamma_{\varnothing,\beta}=c^\gamma_{\varnothing,\beta}=[s_\gamma]s_\beta=\delta_{\gamma,\beta}$ under the top-degree hypothesis. Thus equal size alone does not force $\gamma=\beta$: the value is zero for every other partition of that size. Similarly, if $\beta=\varnothing$ the value is $\delta_{\gamma,\alpha}$. If both inputs are empty then the top-degree hypothesis forces $\gamma=\varnothing$ and the coefficient is one. No choice principle is used.

citations.quote:
**Padded sequences.** For a partition $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ and an
integer $n$, with missing parts read as zero, the first-row padding is the sequence
$\alpha[n]:=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$, a partition of $n$ exactly
when $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]],
[[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]]). When this sequence is used as
a partition label, omit trailing zero entries; in particular
$\varnothing[0]=\varnothing$ and the missing first part is zero.

**The Jacobi–Trudi completion.** For an arbitrary finite sequence of integers
$\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m)$, define
$$s_\mu:=\det\bigl(h_{\mu_j-j+i}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m},$$
where $h_0=1$ and $h_k=0$ for $k<0$
([[thm-jacobi-trudi-and-dual-jacobi-trudi-identities]]); for the empty sequence
the empty determinant is $1$. Every such determinant is $0$ or $\pm1$ times a
Schur function. Indeed, put $q_j:=\mu_j+m-j$. If $q_j=q_k$ for $j\ne k$, the
$j$-th and $k$-th columns of the matrix agree, so the determinant vanishes.
Otherwise let $\sigma$ be the permutation sorting $q$ into decreasing order
$q_{\sigma(1)}>\cdots>q_{\sigma(m)}$ and set $\nu_j:=q_{\sigma(j)}+j-m$; then
$\nu$ is weakly decreasing and, permuting columns with sign
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ and using
$h_{\nu_j-j+i}=h_{q_{\sigma(j)}+i-m}$, the determinant equals
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\det(h_{\nu_j-j+i})$. If $\min_jq_j<0$ then
$\nu_m<0$ and the last column of this determinant is zero, so the value is
$0$; if $\min_jq_j\ge0$ then $\nu$, after deleting trailing zero entries, is a partition of $|\mu|$
with at most $m$ parts and the Jacobi–Trudi identity gives the value
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)s_\nu$. In particular $s_{\alpha[n]}\in\Lambda^n$
for every $n\ge0$, and $s_{\alpha[n]}=0$ for $n<0$: every term of the
determinant expansion has total degree $n$, so for $n<0$ some factor has
negative index and vanishes.

**The operators $U_n$ and $V$.** The Schur functions form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of
$\Lambda$ ([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]), so there are unique
$\mathbb Z$-linear endomorphisms $U_n$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$) and $V$ of $\Lambda$
determined on the Schur basis by
$$U_n(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda[n]},\qquad V(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda+(1)},$$
where $\lambda+(1)=(\lambda_1+1,\lambda_2,\dots)$. Thus $U_n(\Lambda)\subseteq\Lambda^n$ for $n\ge0$ (and $U_n=0$ for
$n<0$), while $V$ raises degree by one; in particular $V(1)=s_{(1)}$. The operators
are extended linearly, and $V^k$ denotes the $k$-fold iterate of $V$.

**The stabilization index.** The internal product $*$ on $\Lambda$ is the
degree-preserving product of
[[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]] and
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]. For partitions
$\alpha,\beta$, define $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ to be the least
integer $n_0\ge0$ such that
$$s_{\alpha[n_0+k]}*s_{\beta[n_0+k]}=V^k\bigl(s_{\alpha[n_0]}*s_{\beta[n_0]}\bigr) \qquad\text{for all }k>0,$$
following the source. This definition records the source's convention only: it
does not assert that such an $n_0$ exists, nor that a value of $n_0$ satisfying
the display is least for any other property. Existence, least-ness and the
exact value of $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ are proved in
[[thm-exact-global-stabilization-threshold-for-a-fixed-kronecker-product]].

Let $\sigma[X]=\sum_{n\ge0}h_n[X]$ be the series of
[[def-lambda-ring-specializations-and-the-sigma-series]], and let
$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_H$ be the Hall form
([[def-hall-inner-product-on-symmetric-functions]]).

1. $\sigma[X]=\prod_{x\in X}(1-x)^{-1}$ and
   $\sigma[-X]=\prod_{x\in X}(1-x)$ for honest alphabets $X$; in particular
   $\sigma[t]=(1-t)^{-1}$ and $\sigma[-t]=1-t$ for the one-letter alphabet
   $t$, as formal series in $t$.
2. $\sigma[A+B]=\sigma[A]\,\sigma[B]$ for all specializations $A,B$, and for
   the one-letter alphabet $t$ one has $\sigma[tA]=\sum_{n\ge0}t^nh_n[A]$.
3. Cauchy identity: $\sigma[XY]=\sum_\lambda s_\lambda[X]s_\lambda[Y]
   =\sum_\lambda z_\lambda^{-1}p_\lambda[X]p_\lambda[Y]$ for all
   specializations $X,Y$, summed by degree.
4. For every specialization $A$, the operator $\sigma[AX^{\perp}]$ is the
   adjoint of multiplication by $\sigma[AX]$:
   $\sigma[AX^{\perp}]f[X]=f[X+A]$ for all $f\in\Lambda$.
5. Reproducing kernel:
   $\langle\sigma[AX]\,|\,f[X]\rangle_X=f[A]$ for all $f\in\Lambda$ and all
   specializations $A$.

Let $\alpha$ be a partition and $t$ a formal variable. With the Jacobi-Trudi
convention of [[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]]
for the integer sequences $\alpha[n]=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots)$, one
has an identity of formal Laurent series with coefficients in the symmetric
function ring
([[def-lambda-ring-specializations-and-the-sigma-series]]):
$$\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}s_{\alpha[n]}[X]\,t^n=\sigma[tX]\cdot s_\alpha[tX-1] =t^{|\alpha|}\cdot\sigma[tX]\cdot s_\alpha[X-t^{-1}],$$
where $s_\alpha[tX-1]$ is evaluated through $p_k\mapsto t^kp_k[X]-1$ and
$s_\alpha[X-t^{-1}]$ through $p_k\mapsto p_k[X]-t^{-k}$. Equivalently,
$$\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}s_{\alpha[n]}[X]\,t^n =\sigma[tX]\sum_{\mu:\ \alpha/\mu\ \text{a vertical strip}} (-1)^{|\alpha|-|\mu|}t^{|\mu|}s_\mu[X].$$

Let $A,B$ be specializations
([[def-lambda-ring-specializations-and-the-sigma-series]]).

- **(a)** For every partition $\lambda$,
  $$s_\lambda[A+B]=\sum_{\mu,\nu}c^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}\,s_\mu[A]\,s_\nu[B],$$
  the sum over pairs of partitions with $|\mu|+|\nu|=|\lambda|$, where
  $c^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}$ is the Littlewood–Richardson coefficient
  ([[def-littlewood-richardson-tableau-and-coefficient]]).
- **(b)** For every partition $\lambda$,
  $$s_\lambda[AB]=\sum_{\mu,\nu}g^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}\,s_\mu[A]\,s_\nu[B],$$
  the sum over pairs with $|\mu|=|\nu|=|\lambda|$, where
  $g^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}$ is the ordinary Kronecker coefficient
  ([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]],
  [[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]]).

Both sums are finite. No multiplicativity or bilinearity of $s_\lambda$ in
the alphabet variables, and no unproved Schur-functor decomposition, is
assumed.

For partitions $\delta,a,b,c$ with $|\delta|=|a|+|b|+|c|$, define the
**threefold Schur coefficient**
$$c^\delta_{a,b,c}:=[s_\delta]\,s_a s_b s_c,$$
the coefficient of $s_\delta$ in the ordinary product of the three Schur
functions of $\Lambda$ ([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]); when
$|\delta|\ne|a|+|b|+|c|$ the coefficient is $0$, the product being homogeneous
of degree $|a|+|b|+|c|$. Since
$s_as_b=\sum_\phi c^\phi_{a,b}s_\phi$ with
$c^\phi_{a,b}$ the Littlewood–Richardson coefficients
([[thm-littlewood-richardson-schur-product-expansion]],
[[def-littlewood-richardson-tableau-and-coefficient]]), substituting gives
$$c^\delta_{a,b,c}=\sum_\phi c^\phi_{a,b}\,c^\delta_{\phi,c} =\sum_\psi c^\psi_{a,c}\,c^\delta_{\psi,b},$$
the sums over partitions $\phi$ of $|a|+|b|$ and $\psi$ of $|a|+|c|$; hence
each $c^\delta_{a,b,c}$ is a nonnegative integer, and the two displayed
expressions agree with the definition. These coefficients are symmetric in
$a,b,c$ because the product $s_as_bs_c$ is commutative, and equivalently
$$c^\delta_{a,b,c}=\langle s_a s_b s_c,\,s_\delta\rangle_H,$$
by the orthonormality of the Schur basis
([[thm-littlewood-richardson-schur-product-expansion]]). No fourfold or
longer iterated coefficient is introduced here; iterating the two identities
above gives every nested product of three factors, and the symmetry of the
three subscripts is used throughout this page.

Let $c^\lambda_{\mu
u}$ be the Littlewood–Richardson coefficient of the inherited definition, the number of Littlewood–Richardson tableaux of shape $\lambda/\mu$ and content $
u$ ([[def-littlewood-richardson-tableau-and-coefficient]], [[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]], [[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]], [[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Then for all partitions $\mu,
u$,
$$s_\mu s_
u=\sum_{\lambda\,\supseteq\,\mu,\ |\lambda|=|\mu|+|
u|}c^\lambda_{\mu
u}s_\lambda\qquad	ext{in }\Lambda,$$
where the sum is finite and zero terms may be omitted; equivalently, for every $\lambda\supseteq\mu$,
$$s_{\lambda/\mu}=\sum_{
u}c^\lambda_{\mu
u}s_
u.$$
No choice principle is used.

For partitions $\rho,\sigma\vdash n$ one has
$$p_\rho*p_\sigma=\delta_{\rho,\sigma}\,z_\rho\,p_\rho,\qquad z_\rho=\prod_{i\ge1}i^{m_i(\rho)}m_i(\rho)!,$$
where $m_i(\rho)$ is the number of parts of $\rho$ equal to $i$. Consequently
$$s_\lambda*s_\mu=\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\,s_\nu$$
for all $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$. The internal product on $\Lambda^n$ is therefore
diagonal in the power-sum basis after extension to $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^n$,
with $z_\rho$ the diagonal scalars, and it has
the integer structure constants $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ in the Schur basis.

Extend the Hall form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_H$ on $\Lambda$
$\mathbb Q$-bilinearly to
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$. For partitions
$\lambda$ and $\mu$, let
$$z_\lambda:=\prod_{r\ge1}r^{m_r(\lambda)}m_r(\lambda)!,\qquad m_r(\lambda):=\#\{i:\lambda_i=r\}.$$
Then
$$\langle p_\lambda,p_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}z_\lambda.$$
In particular, power sums of unequal degrees are orthogonal.

Let $\operatorname{ch}:R_S\to\Lambda$ be the Frobenius characteristic restricted
to the graded ordinary representation ring of the symmetric groups
([[def-frobenius-characteristic-map]],
[[def-graded-ordinary-representation-ring-of-symmetric-groups]]). By
[[thm-frobenius-characteristic-is-an-isometric-graded-ring-isomorphism]] it is a
degree-preserving $\mathbb Z$-module isomorphism onto the stable symmetric
function ring $\Lambda=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}\Lambda^m$, so its restriction
$\operatorname{ch}:R(S_m)\to\Lambda^m$ is an isomorphism for every $m\ge0$.

For $f\in\Lambda^m$ and $g\in\Lambda^n$ define
$$f*g:=\begin{cases}\operatorname{ch}\bigl(\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(f)\cdot\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(g)\bigr),&m=n,\\[2pt]0,&m\ne n,\end{cases}$$
where $\cdot$ is the pointwise (internal tensor) product of class functions on
$S_m$; extend $*$ bilinearly to all of $\Lambda$. Call $*$ the
**internal (Kronecker) product** of symmetric functions.

**Well-definedness.** For $m=n$ the class functions $\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(f)$
and $\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(g)$ lie in $R(S_m)$, the integral span of the
irreducible characters of $S_m$
([[def-graded-ordinary-representation-ring-of-symmetric-groups]]). The
pointwise product of two honest characters of $S_m$ is again an honest
character, namely the character of the tensor product of the underlying
representations ([[thm-characters-of-direct-sums-tensor-products-and-duals]]),
and products of $\mathbb Z$-combinations of characters are computed
bilinearly; hence the pointwise product of two elements of $R(S_m)$ lies in
$R(S_m)$, and applying the isomorphism $\operatorname{ch}$ lands in $\Lambda^m$.
The product is therefore well defined and takes $\Lambda^m\times\Lambda^m$ to
$\Lambda^m$.

**Basic properties.** The product is bilinear by construction and inherits
commutativity and associativity from the pointwise product of class functions.
It preserves degrees, in the sense that $\Lambda^m*\Lambda^n\subseteq\Lambda^m$
for $m=n$ and is $0$ for $m\ne n$. On $\Lambda^n$ the unit is
$h_n=s_{(n)}=\operatorname{ch}(\text{trivial character of }S_n)$ for $n>0$,
and in degree zero it is $h_0=s_\varnothing=1$, because the
trivial character is the unit for pointwise multiplication on $R(S_n)$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]]
identifies $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^{(n)})=s_{(n)}=h_n$). The graded direct sum
$\Lambda$ has **no global unit** for $*$: if $e\in\Lambda$ had finite degree
support and $n$ were a degree with $e_n=0$ while $\Lambda^n\ne0$, then
$(e*h_n)_n=e_n*h_n=0\ne h_n$, so $e*h_n\ne h_n$; a global unit would require
$e_n$ to be a unit of $(\Lambda^n,*)$ for every $n$. In particular the ordinary
product unit $1\in\Lambda^0$ is not a unit for $*$ on the positive degrees.

**Schur expansion.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$, the definition and
the Specht character dictionary $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^\lambda)=s_\lambda$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]])
give
$$s_\lambda*s_\mu=\operatorname{ch}\bigl(\chi^\lambda\cdot\chi^\mu\bigr)=\operatorname{ch}\Bigl(\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\chi^\nu\Bigr)=\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\,s_\nu,$$
because $\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu$ is the character of
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ and its decomposition has multiplicities
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the transport goes through the
choice-free Frobenius characteristic isomorphism and finite-dimensional
representation theory of finite groups.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$ and work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be
partitions of $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ be the tensor product of their complex
Specht modules, a finite-dimensional complex $S_n$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). The
**Kronecker coefficient** $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ of a third partition
$\nu\vdash n$ is the multiplicity of $S^\nu$ in this tensor product:

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu):=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}}{\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu},$$

where $\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}$ is the isotypic
component of type $S^\nu$
([[def-isotypic-component-of-a-completely-reducible-representation]]).

**Well-definedness.** The module $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ is
finite-dimensional, and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb C=0$ does not divide the
order of the finite group $S_n$, so complex Maschke's theorem gives complete
reducibility
([[thm-maschkes-theorem-for-finite-groups-over-fields-whose-characteristic-does-not-divide-the-group-order]],
[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],
[[def-completely-reducible-representation]]). The complex Specht modules
$S^\nu$, $\nu\vdash n$, are a complete list of pairwise inequivalent
irreducible $S_n$-modules
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]],
[[cor-distinct-specht-modules-are-inequivalent]]). Consequently a decomposition
into irreducibles has the form
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu S^\nu$
with nonnegative integer multiplicities $m_\nu$, and the isotypic component of
type $S^\nu$ is the direct sum of exactly the $m_\nu$ copies of $S^\nu$
appearing in any such decomposition, by
[[thm-isotypic-decomposition-of-a-completely-reducible-representation-is-unique]]
(Proof step 2.1 identifies each grouped block with the defining isotypic sum).
In particular
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu)_{(S^\nu)}=m_\nu\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu$
and $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu>0$ because $S^\nu$ is irreducible. Hence
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=m_\nu$ is a nonnegative integer, independent of the chosen
decomposition, and $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is by definition the multiplicity of
$S^\nu$ in $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$.

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of
degrees $a$ and $b$ to a module of degree $a+b$, the internal product keeps the
rank: both inputs and the output are $S_n$-modules of the same degree $n$. The
two operations are different constructions on different data; the outer product
is mentioned here only for contrast and is not used in this definition.

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the tensor product, Maschke's theorem,
the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional
complex representation theory of a finite group.

For every $d\ge0$, the stable Schur functions $\{s_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$
form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $\Lambda^d$ and are orthonormal for the Hall form:
$$\langle s_\lambda,s_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$$
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$.

For $r\ge1$, let $p_r\in\Lambda^r$ be the compatible sequence of finite
power-sum polynomials $p_r(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=\sum_{i=1}^N x_i^r$
([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]],
[[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]). For a
partition $\lambda$, set $p_\lambda:=\prod_i p_{\lambda_i}$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Write
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$ and
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda^d$. Then
$$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[p_1,p_2,\ldots],$$
and for every $d\ge0$, the family $\{p_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$ is a
$\mathbb Q$-basis of $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$. These families are not in
general $\mathbb Z$-bases of $\Lambda^d$: in degree two,
$h_2=\tfrac12(p_{(1,1)}+p_{(2)})$ has nonintegral coordinates in the power-sum
basis.

derivations.claim: *Internal-product kernel.* For $f,g\in\Lambda^d_{\mathbb Q}$ and independent formal alphabet variables $U,V$, with any specialization $W$, one has $\langle f[U]g[V]\,|\,\sigma[UVW]\rangle_{U,V}=(f*g)[W]$. Indeed, by the power form of the Cauchy identity [F2], $\sigma[UVW]=\sum_{\rho\vdash d}z_\rho^{-1}p_\rho[U]p_\rho[V]p_\rho[W]$ in the relevant degree and the pairing is a finite sum, since only $\rho\vdash d$ matches the bidegree $(d,d)$ of $f[U]g[V]$. Writing $f=\sum_\rho a_\rho p_\rho$ and $g=\sum_\rho b_\rho p_\rho$, [F5] gives $\langle f[U]g[V],p_\rho[U]p_\rho[V]p_\rho[W]\rangle_{U,V}=a_\rho z_\rho\cdot b_\rho z_\rho\cdot p_\rho[W]$, so the left side is $\sum_{\rho\vdash d}a_\rho b_\rho z_\rho p_\rho[W]=(f*g)[W]$ by [F5].

*Finiteness of $R$.* Factor the kernel of $R$ as $\sigma[ZAB]\sigma[ZA]\sigma[ZB]\sigma[AB]$. In the $(a,b)$-bidegree of the pairing, the four factors contribute bidegrees $(j,j)$, $(m,0)$, $(0,n)$, $(l,l)$ with $j+m+l=a$ and $j+n+l=b$, so $0\le j,m,n,l\le a+b$ and the $Z$-degree is $j+m+n=b+m-l\le a+b$. For each fixed $Z$-degree only finitely many such $(j,m,n,l)$ occur, and each homogeneous component of $\sigma$ is a finite sum over partitions; hence $R_{\alpha,\beta}$ is a finite polynomial in $Z$ of degree at most $a+b$, with coefficients extracted from finitely many bidegree pieces of $\sigma$. No infinite sum of symmetric functions is evaluated.

*The generating function $F(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)t^n$.* By [F1] and [F3], the degree-$n$ part of $\sigma[A]s_\alpha[A-1]$ is $U_ns_\alpha$, and likewise for $\beta$; the bidegree-$(n,n)$ part of the product $\sigma[A]s_\alpha[A-1]\,\sigma[B]s_\beta[B-1]$ is therefore $(U_ns_\alpha)[A](U_ns_\beta)[B]$. Pairing against $\sigma[tXAB]=\sum_nt^nh_n[XAB]$ and applying step 1.1 in each degree gives $F(t)=\langle\sigma[A]s_\alpha[A-1]\,\sigma[B]s_\beta[B-1]\,|\,\sigma[tXAB]\rangle_{A,B}$, a formula in which the coefficient of $t^n$ is finite by [F1].

*Hall adjunction.* For a polynomial $u$ and a formal series $W[A]$, interpreted coefficientwise in $t$, the adjunction of [F2] with the one-letter alphabet $1$ reads $\sigma[A^{\perp}]u[A]=u[A+1]$; equivalently $\langle\sigma[A]u[A],W[A]\rangle_A=\langle u[A],W[A+1]\rangle_A$ and, in the reverse direction, $\langle u[A-1],W[A]\rangle_A=\langle u[A],\sigma[-A]W[A]\rangle_A$. Applying this in the $A$-variable and then in the $B$-variable to the identity of step 2.1 turns $\sigma[A]\sigma[B]$ into the translation $A\mapsto A+1$, $B\mapsto B+1$ of the kernel and moves the shifts $-1$ of $s_\alpha,s_\beta$ onto the kernel: $F(t)=\langle s_\alpha[A]s_\beta[B]\,|\,\sigma[tX(A+1)(B+1)-A-B]\rangle_{A,B}$. Each coefficient of $t^n$ in the kernel before translation is polynomial in $A,B$ of bidegree $(n,n)$, so both adjunctions are finite coefficientwise.

*Factorization and the coefficient identity.* Expanding $tX(A+1)(B+1)-A-B=tX+(tX-1)AB+(tX-1)A+(tX-1)B+AB$ and using $\sigma[C+D]=\sigma[C]\sigma[D]$ from the product formula [F2], the kernel of step 3.1 is $\sigma[tX]$ times $\sigma[(tX-1)AB+(tX-1)A+(tX-1)B+AB]$, so $F(t)=\sigma[tX]R_{\alpha,\beta}[tX-1]$. By [F3], the coefficient of $t^n$ in $\sigma[tX]h[tX-1]$ is $U_nh$ for every finite-degree $h$, and $R_{\alpha,\beta}[tX-1]$ is the specialization of the element $R_{\alpha,\beta}\in\Lambda_Z$ introduced in the statement, so comparing the coefficient of $t^n$ gives $(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)=U_nR_{\alpha,\beta}$ for every $n\ge0$; for $n<0$ one has $U_n=0$ by [F1], so no negative index is asserted.

*The Littlewood expression.* Expand the four factors of the kernel of $R$ with the Cauchy identity and the product-alphabet identity [F2] and [F4]: $\sigma[ZAB]=\sum_{\zeta,\delta,\epsilon}s_\zeta[Z]g^\zeta_{\delta\epsilon}s_\delta[A]s_\epsilon[B]$, $\sigma[ZA]=\sum_\sigma s_\sigma[Z]s_\sigma[A]$, $\sigma[ZB]=\sum_\rho s_\rho[Z]s_\rho[B]$ and $\sigma[AB]=\sum_\tau s_\tau[A]s_\tau[B]$. Pairing with $s_\alpha[A]s_\beta[B]$ and using the orthonormality of the Schur basis gives $R_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum g^\zeta_{\delta\epsilon}s_\zeta[Z]s_\sigma[Z]s_\rho[Z]\langle s_\delta s_\sigma s_\tau,s_\alpha\rangle_H\langle s_\epsilon s_\rho s_\tau,s_\beta\rangle_H$. By [F4] the two pairings are $c^\alpha_{\delta,\sigma,\tau}$ and $c^\beta_{\epsilon,\rho,\tau}$, and re-summing over $\sigma$ with $\rho$ fixed gives $\sum_\sigma c^\alpha_{\delta,\sigma,\tau}s_\sigma[Z]=(s_\delta s_\tau)^{\perp}s_\alpha$ by adjointness; similarly for $\beta$. Finally $\sum_\zeta g^\zeta_{\delta\epsilon}s_\zeta[Z]=s_\delta*s_\epsilon[Z]$ by [F6]. This is exactly the displayed Littlewood expression, and the sum is finite because $c$- and $g$-coefficients vanish outside the size constraints.

boundaries.evidence: Proof 1.2 covers a=b=0: only the constant bidegree of the kernel contributes, so R_(∅,∅)=1.
Proof 4.1 covers U_n=0 for negative n; the degree-zero components are included in the finite sum of step 1.2.
step 3.1 uses the one-letter alphabet 1 and the adjunction σ[A^⊥]h[A]=h[A+1], which is the normalization Z=tX-1 of the statement.
Proof 2.1 and 4.1 cover nonadmissible padding through its Jacobi–Trudi completion.
Proof 1.2 bounds the degree of R_(α,β) by a+b, making the coefficient extraction in step 4.1 finite.
step 5.1: finite sums only, with adjoints forced by nondegeneracy of the Hall form; no choice principle enters.

No converse direction is asserted.
