citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a finite Weyl group acting faithfully on its $r$-dimensional complex reflection representation $V$, and put $S=\mathbb C[V]$. Then $S^W$ is a polynomial algebra on $r$ homogeneous algebraically independent basic invariants, and $S$ is free of rank $|W|$ over $S^W$. More generally these conclusions hold for every finite subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ generated by complex reflections (nonidentity transformations fixing a hyperplane pointwise). In the Weyl case the generating root reflections have order two; no classification or Coxeter presentation is needed here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the cited invariant-theory results
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with
Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and Weyl group $W$, acting on $\mathfrak h^*$
by the root reflections of [[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]]
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]), hence on the
symmetric algebra $S=S(\mathfrak h^*)$ by graded algebra automorphisms; a nondegenerate $W$-invariant bilinear form identifies $\mathfrak h$
with $\mathfrak h^*$ and thus identifies $S$ with $S(\mathfrak h)$ as
a graded $W$-algebra. Such a form is the complexification of a positive
definite form on the real Cartan, obtained by averaging any positive
definite form over finite $W$. Fix this identification; the page writes
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$ for either presentation. Write
$$S^W_+=\bigoplus_{d>0}(S^W)_d,\qquad I:=S\,S^W_+,$$
so that $I$ is the homogeneous ideal of $S$ generated by the invariants of
positive degree; this is the specialization to the reflection group case of
the quotient construction of
[[def-finite-linear-invariant-and-coinvariant-polynomial-algebras]], because
$S^W_+$ is exactly the space of positive-degree elements of the invariant
algebra $S^W$.

The **coinvariant algebra** of the pair $(\mathfrak h,W)$ is the graded
quotient
$$C=C(\mathfrak h,W):=S/I.$$
It is a commutative graded $\mathbb C$-algebra with $C_0=\mathbb C$: the ideal
$I$ is homogeneous of positive degree, so constants survive and every
homogeneous piece of $S$ maps onto its image. The quotient map
$$\rho:S\longrightarrow C,\qquad \rho(f)=f+I,$$
is a surjective graded algebra homomorphism, and the action of $W$ on $S$
descends to a $\mathbb C$-linear action on $C$ by graded algebra
automorphisms, because $I$ is $W$-stable. The algebra $C$ is finite
dimensional: $W$ is generated by its root reflections, so
[[thm-chevalley-shephard-todd-for-finite-weyl-groups]] writes $S$ as a free
module of finite rank over the polynomial algebra $S^W$, and
[[lem-weyl-coinvariant-hilbert-series-has-order-w-dimension]] gives
$\dim_{\mathbb C}C=|W|<\infty$ with the graded Hilbert series recorded there.

**Degree normalization.** Throughout the Soergel material on this page the
Cartan generators are given degree $2$, that is $\deg\mathfrak h=2$; the
symmetric algebra $S$ is then graded with $\deg S_d=2d$ for homogeneous
polynomials of ordinary degree $d$, and $C$ inherits this doubled grading. In
particular a basic invariant of ordinary degree $d_i$ has page degree $2d_i$,
and the top nonzero degree of $C$ is $2N$ with
$N=\sum_i(d_i-1)$. The separate degree-sum lemma on this page proves
that this number equals the positive-root count.

**Auxiliary permutation model for type $A$.** For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_n$
one may instead work with the place-permuting $S_n$-action on the auxiliary
polynomial ring $S_{\mathrm{perm}}=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, where a
permutation $\sigma$ sends $x_i$ to $x_{\sigma(i)}$, and with the quotient
$$C_{\mathrm{perm}}:=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(e_1,\dots,e_n),$$
where $e_1,\dots,e_n$ are the elementary symmetric polynomials. Splitting the
permutation representation $\mathbb C^n=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathbb C\cdot(1,\dots,1)$
into its sum-zero Cartan part and its fixed average coordinate exhibits
$\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]\cong S(\mathfrak h)\otimes\mathbb C[e_1]$ with
$e_1=x_1+\cdots+x_n$ the invariant coordinate, and restriction to the hyperplane
$e_1=0$ has kernel $(e_1)$. By [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-symmetric-polynomials]], $e_1,\dots,e_n$
generate the invariant algebra and its positive-degree ideal of the permutation action, while $e_2,\dots,e_n$ restrict to basic
invariants of $S(\mathfrak h)^W$, dividing out by the positive-degree invariants
commutes with this presentation and yields a canonical isomorphism of graded
algebras
$$C(\mathfrak h,W)\cong C_{\mathrm{perm}}=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(e_1,\dots,e_n),$$
in which $x_i$ has degree $2$ and $e_i$ has degree $2i$. Elements of $C$ are
written as classes $\rho(f)$; the auxiliary model is used only for explicit
rank computations and never replaces the intrinsic definition.

The quotient and finite coordinate constructions require no additional choice;
the freeness and Hilbert-series conclusions inherit AC from their suppliers.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $G\leq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite complex reflection group, $n=\dim V$, $S=\mathbb C[V]$, and $R=S^G$. Let $f_1,\ldots,f_m$ be minimal homogeneous invariant generators of $I=SR_+$, with $d_i=\deg f_i>0$. Their common zero set is $\{0\}$, $m=n$, and they form an $S$-regular sequence. Every homogeneous lift of a homogeneous complex basis of $S/I$ is a graded free $R$-basis of $S$.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring, let $\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ be a finite ordered sequence in $R$, and let $M$ be an $R$-module. On $\bigwedge R^n$, with standard basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$, let $\delta$ be the $R$-linear graded derivation of degree $-1$ with $\delta(e_i)=x_i$ and $\delta(R)=0$; thus $\delta(ab)=\delta(a)b+(-1)^pa\delta(b)$ for homogeneous $a$ of degree $p$.

The **Koszul complex with coefficients in $M$** is $K(\mathbf x;M)=(\bigwedge R^n\otimes_R M,d)$, where $d=\delta\otimes\operatorname{id}_M$. Its degree-$p$ term is $\bigwedge^pR^n\otimes_R M$ for $0\leq p\leq n$, and zero otherwise. Explicitly,

$$d(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_p}\otimes m)=\sum_{j=1}^p(-1)^{j-1}e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\widehat{e_{i_j}}\cdots\wedge e_{i_p}\otimes x_{i_j}m.$$

The empty wedge is $1\in R$. In particular $d(e_i\otimes m)=1\otimes x_im$ in $K_0=R\otimes_R M$, canonically identified with $M$ by $r\otimes m\mapsto rm$ with inverse $m\mapsto1\otimes m$. The differential out of degree zero is zero. The derivation respects the exterior relations and the two orders of deleting distinct factors cancel in $d^2$, so these maps form a chain complex. For $n=0$ this is $M$ in degree zero under the same identification.
For a finite sequence $\mathbf x$, $H_0(K(\mathbf x;M))=M/(\mathbf x)M$, $H_i=0$ for $i>n$, and $H_n=\{m\in M:x_im=0\text{ for all }i\}$.
If $M$ is finite free and $\mathbf x$ is $M$-regular, then $K(\mathbf x;M)$ is a finite free resolution of $M/(\mathbf x)M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W\leq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite complex reflection group, in particular a finite Weyl reflection group, with $r=\dim V$. Put $S=\mathbb C[V]$, $R=S^W$, $I=SR_+$, and let $d_1,\ldots,d_r$ be the degrees of basic invariants. Then
$$\operatorname{Hilb}(S/I,t)=\prod_{i=1}^r(1+t+\cdots+t^{d_i-1}),\qquad \dim_{\mathbb C}(S/I)=\prod_i d_i=|W|.$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Define polynomial rings in finitely many commuting indeterminates recursively by

$$ R[x_1,\ldots,x_0]:=R,\qquad R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1}]:=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n][x_{n+1}]. $$

At each stage the coefficient ring embeds as the constant polynomials ([[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]]), so all preceding indeterminates remain present. The new indeterminate commutes with every coefficient by the commutativity built into [[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]], and consequently all $x_i$ commute. This iterated ring is denoted $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$.

For a right $R$-module $N$ and a left $R$-module $M$ with a specified
projective resolution $P_\bullet\twoheadrightarrow M$, define the
left-resolution construction
$$\operatorname{Tor}^{R,P}_n(N,M):=H_n(N\otimes_RP_\bullet).$$
The datum $P$ remains in the notation until the balance and
change-of-resolution results prove that it may be suppressed.

For a right $R$-module $N$ with a specified projective resolution
$Q_\bullet\twoheadrightarrow N$ and a left $R$-module $M$, define the
right-resolution construction
$$\operatorname{Tor}^{R,Q}_n(N,M):=H_n(Q_\bullet\otimes_RM).$$
The datum $Q$ remains in the notation until the balance and change-of-resolution
results prove that it may be suppressed.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]). For every right $R$-module $N$ and left
$R$-module $M$ with supplied projective resolutions $Q_\bullet\to N$ and
$P_\bullet\to M$, there is a natural isomorphism
$H_i(N\otimes_RP_\bullet)\cong H_i(Q_\bullet\otimes_RM)$.

derivations.claim: The invariant ideal is generated by the basic invariants: $I=S\,S^W_+=(w_1,\dots,w_r)$, because $S^W=\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$ and every element of $S^W_+$ is a polynomial in the $w_i$ with zero constant term. Hence $C=S/(w_1,\dots,w_r)$; since $C$ is generated by the images of the degree-two elements, its augmentation ideal satisfies $C_+=(x_1,\dots,x_r)C$.

The $r$ basic invariants form an $S$-regular sequence: they are minimal homogeneous invariant generators of $I$ (they generate $I$, and no $w_i$ lies in the ideal generated by the others, since applying the $S^W$-linear Reynolds projection to a relation in $S$ would give a relation in $\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$, where no variable belongs to the ideal generated by the others), and by [F2] the minimal homogeneous invariant generators of $I$ are $r$ in number with common zero set $\{0\}$ and form an $S$-regular sequence; consequently, by [F3], $K(\mathbf w;S)$ is a finite free resolution of $C$.
The variables $x_1,\dots,x_r$ form an $S$-regular sequence with $S/(x_1,\dots,x_r)=\mathbb C=:k$, by [F5]; consequently, by [F3], $K(\mathbf x;S)$ is a finite free resolution of $k$.

Koszul differentials vanish after base change to $k$: tensoring $K(\mathbf w;S)$ with $k$ multiplies by the images of the $w_i$ in $k$, which lie in the positive-degree part and hence act as zero; so $H_r(K(\mathbf w;S)\otimes_Sk)=K_r(\mathbf w;S)\otimes_Sk$, a one-dimensional space in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i$.

First computation: by resolution 1.2, resolving the $C$ variable, and the balance isomorphism [F6], $\operatorname{Tor}^S_r(C,k)\cong H_r(K(\mathbf w;S)\otimes_Sk)$, which by step 1.4 is one dimensional and concentrated in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i$.

Second computation: by resolution 1.3, resolving the $k$ variable, and [F6], $\operatorname{Tor}^S_r(C,k)\cong H_r(C\otimes_SK(\mathbf x;S))=H_r(K(\mathbf x;C))$; by [F3] the top homology is $\{c\in C:x_ic=0\text{ for all }i\}$, placed in internal degree $2r$ above the degrees of its elements, since $e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_r$ carries degree $2r$.

Hilbert series: applying the Euler characteristic to the finite free resolution $K(\mathbf w;S)$ of $C$ gives $$\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)=\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})\cdot\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t)=\frac{\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})}{(1-t^2)^r}=\prod_i(1+t^2+\cdots+t^{2(d_i-1)}),$$ the last equality by cancelling one factor $1-t^2$ per invariant. Hence $\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$ is a polynomial of degree $2N$ with leading coefficient $1$, so $\dim_{\mathbb C}C_{2N}=1$ and $C_j=0$ for $j>2N$; the classical formula [F4] gives the same series after substituting $t^2$ for $t$.

Comparing steps 2.1 and 2.2 through the natural isomorphism [F6] identifies the top Koszul homology of step 2.2 with a one-dimensional space in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i$; shifting back by the degree $2r$ of the top exterior generator, the space $\{c\in C:x_ic=0\text{ for all }i\}$ is one dimensional and concentrated in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i-2r=2\sum_i(d_i-1)=2N$.

Since $C_+=(x_1,\dots,x_r)C$ by step 1.1, the space of step 3.1 is exactly the socle $\operatorname{soc}(C)=\{c\in C:C_+c=0\}$; it is one dimensional in degree $2N$. The top graded piece $C_{2N}$ is one dimensional by step 2.3, and every element of $C_{2N}$ is annihilated by $C_+$ because $C$ has no degrees above $2N$; hence $0\neq C_{2N}\subseteq\operatorname{soc}(C)$ and both are one dimensional in degree $2N$, so $\operatorname{soc}(C)=C_{2N}$.

Nondegeneracy of the top pairing: let $0
eq c\in C_i$ be homogeneous and consider the nonzero graded ideal $cC$ of the finite-dimensional graded algebra $C$; let $m$ be the largest degree with $(cC)_m
eq0$, so $m\le2N$ by step 2.3. Choose $0
eq y\in(cC)_m$; then $C_+y\subseteq(cC)_{>m}=0$, so $y\in\operatorname{soc}(C)=C_{2N}$ by step 4.1, forcing $m=2N$. Writing $y=cb$ with $b\in C_{2N-i}$ gives a nonzero product $cb$, so the pairing $C_i	imes C_{2N-i}	o C_{2N}\cong\mathbb C$ has no nonzero left radical; by commutativity it has no nonzero right radical either, and finite-dimensionality of the two sides makes it a perfect pairing for every $i$. Hence $C$ is a graded Gorenstein algebra with one-dimensional socle in top degree $2N$.

[[def-finite-linear-invariant-and-coinvariant-polynomial-algebras]], because
$S^W_+$ is exactly the space of positive-degree elements of the invariant
algebra $S^W$.

The **coinvariant algebra** of the pair $(\mathfrak h,W)$ is the graded
quotient
$$C=C(\mathfrak h,W):=S/I.$$
It is a commutative graded $\mathbb C$-algebra with $C_0=\mathbb C$: the ideal
$I$ is homogeneous of positive degree, so constants survive and every
homogeneous piece of $S$ maps onto its image. The quotient map
$$\rho:S\longrightarrow C,\qquad \rho(f)=f+I,$$
is a surjective graded algebra homomorphism, and the action of $W$ on $S$
descends to a $\mathbb C$-linear action on $C$ by graded algebra
automorphisms, because $I$ is $W$-stable. The algebra $C$ is finite
dimensional: $W$ is generated by its root reflections, so
[[thm-chevalley-shephard-todd-for-finite-weyl-groups]] writes $S$ as a free
module of finite rank over the polynomial algebra $S^W$, and
[[lem-weyl-coinvariant-hilbert-series-has-order-w-dimension]] gives
$\dim_{\mathbb C}C=|W|<\infty$ with the graded Hilbert series recorded there.

**Degree normalization.** Throughout the Soergel material on this page the
Cartan generators are given degree $2$, that is $\deg\mathfrak h=2$; the
symmetric algebra $S$ is then graded with $\deg S_d=2d$ for homogeneous
polynomials of ordinary degree $d$, and $C$ inherits this doubled grading. In
particular a basic invariant of ordinary degree $d_i$ has page degree $2d_i$,
and the top nonzero degree of $C$ is $2N$ with
$N=\sum_i(d_i-1)$. The separate degree-sum lemma on this page proves
that this number equals the positive-root count.

**Auxiliary permutation model for type $A$.** For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_n$
one may instead work with the place-permuting $S_n$-action on the auxiliary
polynomial ring $S_{\mathrm{perm}}=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, where a
permutation $\sigma$ sends $x_i$ to $x_{\sigma(i)}$, and with the quotient
$$C_{\mathrm{perm}}:=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(e_1,\dots,e_n),$$
where $e_1,\dots,e_n$ are the elementary symmetric polynomials. Splitting the
permutation representation $\mathbb C^n=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathbb C\cdot(1,\dots,1)$
into its sum-zero Cartan part and its fixed average coordinate exhibits
$\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]\cong S(\mathfrak h)\otimes\mathbb C[e_1]$ with
$e_1=x_1+\cdots+x_n$ the invariant coordinate, and restriction to the hyperplane
$e_1=0$ has kernel $(e_1)$. By [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-symmetric-polynomials]], $e_1,\dots,e_n$
generate the invariant algebra and its positive-degree ideal of the permutation action, while $e_2,\dots,e_n$ restrict to basic
invariants of $S(\mathfrak h)^W$, dividing out by the positive-degree invariants
commutes with this presentation and yields a canonical isomorphism of graded
algebras
$$C(\mathfrak h,W)\cong C_{\mathrm{perm}}=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(e_1,\dots,e_n),$$
in which $x_i$ has degree $2$ and $e_i$ has degree $2i$. Elements of $C$ are
written as classes $\rho(f)$; the auxiliary model is used only for explicit
rank computations and never replaces the intrinsic definition.

The quotient and finite coordinate constructions require no additional choice;
the freeness and Hilbert-series conclusions inherit AC from their suppliers.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W\leq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite complex reflection group, in particular a finite Weyl reflection group, with $r=\dim V$. Put $S=\mathbb C[V]$, $R=S^W$, $I=SR_+$, and let $d_1,\ldots,d_r$ be the degrees of basic invariants. Then
$$\operatorname{Hilb}(S/I,t)=\prod_{i=1}^r(1+t+\cdots+t^{d_i-1}),\qquad \dim_{\mathbb C}(S/I)=\prod_i d_i=|W|.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $G\leq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite complex reflection group, $n=\dim V$, $S=\mathbb C[V]$, and $R=S^G$. Let $f_1,\ldots,f_m$ be minimal homogeneous invariant generators of $I=SR_+$, with $d_i=\deg f_i>0$. Their common zero set is $\{0\}$, $m=n$, and they form an $S$-regular sequence. Every homogeneous lift of a homogeneous complex basis of $S/I$ is a graded free $R$-basis of $S$.
Let $V$ be finite-dimensional over a field of characteristic not $2$. Every symmetric bilinear form $B$ on $V$ admits a basis whose distinct vectors are pairwise orthogonal for $B$.

derivations.claim: Choose an arbitrary positive definite symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ and average it over the finite group $W$, obtaining a $W$-invariant positive definite form $(\ ,\ )$; choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\dots,e_r$ of $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ for it. On the symmetric algebra $S=\mathbb C[e_1,\dots,e_r]$ let $\langle\ ,\ \rangle$ be the Fischer pairing, the sesquilinear form with $\langle e^{\alpha},e^{\beta}\rangle=\alpha!\,\delta_{\alpha\beta}$ on monomials $e^{\alpha}$ ($\alpha$ a multi-index); it is positive definite, and $W$ acts on $S$ by orthogonal transformations for it because the form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ is $W$-invariant. For $p\in S$ let $\partial_p=p(\partial_1,\dots,\partial_r)$ be substitution of the partial derivatives $\partial_i=\partial/\partial e_i$; then multiplication by $p$ has adjoint $\partial_{\overline p}$, i.e. $\langle pf,g\rangle=\langle f,\partial_{\overline p}g\rangle$, as checked on monomials. Choose real basic invariants: real and imaginary parts of complex invariants are invariant, and one may choose a real homogeneous basis of the indecomposables of the invariant algebra and lift it; its complexification gives basic generators. Complex conjugation preserves $S^W_+$, so simultaneous kernels are unchanged. Set $\mathcal H_d:=I_d^{\perp}$ inside the finite-dimensional space $S_d$, and $\mathcal H:=\bigoplus_d\mathcal H_d$.

The invariant ring acts on $S$ with the expected Hilbert series: $S$ has a finite homogeneous $S^W$-basis by [F1], say of degrees $m_1,\dots,m_{|W|}$; their images in $S/S^W_+S=C$ form a $\mathbb C$-basis by graded Nakayama, so $\sum_jt^{m_j}=\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$ and therefore $\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$.

By step 1.1 the spaces $S_d=I_d\oplus\mathcal H_d$ are orthogonal direct sums and $\mathcal H$ is a graded subspace; it is $W$-stable because $W$ preserves the form and $I$ is a $W$-stable homogeneous ideal, and $\mathcal H$ is a graded complement of $I$. Moreover $\mathcal H_d=\{f\in S_d:\partial_pf=0\text{ for all }p\in S^W_+\}$: since $I=(w_1,\dots,w_r)$, one has $f\in I_d^{\perp}$ exactly when $\langle f,w_ig\rangle=0$ for every $i$ and every $g\in S_{d-2d_i}$, which by adjointness is $\langle\partial_{w_i}f,g\rangle=0$ for all such $g$, hence $\partial_{w_i}f=0$ by positive definiteness; and for $p=\sum_iq_iw_i$ one has $\partial_p=\sum_i\partial_{q_i}\partial_{w_i}$, so vanishing for the $w_i$ is vanishing for all of $S^W_+$.

The restriction $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\to C$ is an isomorphism of graded vector spaces because $\rho$ has kernel $I$ and $\mathcal H$ is a complement of $I$ by step 1.1; it is a map of $W$-modules because $\rho$ is $W$-equivariant. Hence $\dim\mathcal H_d=\dim C_d$ for every $d$, and $\dim\mathcal H=\dim C=|W|$ by [F2].

Let $\varphi:S^W\otimes\mathcal H\to S$, $p\otimes h\mapsto ph$. This is a homomorphism of graded $S^W$-modules and of $W$-modules. Its reduction modulo $S^W_+$, namely $\mathcal H\to C$, $h\mapsto\rho(h)$, is surjective because it is the isomorphism $\rho|_{\mathcal H}$ of step 2.2.

The map $\varphi$ is surjective: given homogeneous $f\in S_d$, choose $h\in\mathcal H_d$ with $\rho(f)=\rho(h)$ by step 3.1; then $f-h\in I_d=\sum_i(w_iS)_d=\sum_iw_iS_{d-2d_i}$, so by induction on $d$ each $w_ig$ with $g\in S_{d-2d_i}$ lies in $S^W\cdot\mathcal H$, and adding $h$ exhibits $f$ in the image.

The map $\varphi$ is injective: by steps 1.2 and 2.2 the two sides have the same Hilbert series, $$\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W\otimes\mathcal H,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal H,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t),$$ both are graded with finite-dimensional graded pieces, and by step 4.1 the kernel of the surjective graded $S^W$-linear map $\varphi$ would otherwise contribute positive Hilbert series. Hence $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.

Steps 2.1, 2.2 and 5.1 give a $W$-stable graded complement $\mathcal H$ of $I$ with $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\cong C$ and $S^W\otimes\mathcal H\cong S$; the description of $\mathcal H$ as the simultaneous invariant differential kernel follows from the adjointness $\langle pf,g\rangle=\langle f,\partial_{\overline p}g\rangle$ of step 1.1, and $\dim\mathcal H=|W|$ by step 2.2. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the invariant-theory suppliers [F1] and [F2]; the construction itself uses only finite averages and finite-dimensional linear algebra.

risk_review.notes: Read all eight steps and CST, regular invariant generators, Hilbert and bilinear-form supplier statements. Finite W averaging gives a positive real form; degreewise Fischer orthogonal complements are W-stable, and multiplication by p has adjoint derivative of conjugate p. Real invariant generators and conjugation stability give the simultaneous invariant-derivative kernel. Degree induction proves multiplication surjective and matching finite graded Hilbert coefficients prove injectivity. The proof works for any graded W-stable complement; no false single-Laplacian characterization remains. Rank zero gives H=complex numbers, degree zero survives, and AC is inherited only from invariant theory. Current construction is sound.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, set $S=S(\mathfrak g)$, $R=S^{\mathfrak g}$, and let $\mathcal H$ be its Kostant harmonic subspace. Multiplication is an isomorphism
$$R\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathcal H\longrightarrow S$$
of graded $\mathfrak g$-modules, where $R$ carries the trivial action. The assertion includes $\mathfrak g=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra, let
$\mathfrak h\subseteq\mathfrak g$ be any Cartan subalgebra in the nilpotent self-normalizing sense, and let $W$ be its
Weyl group. Restriction to $\mathfrak h$ induces an algebra isomorphism

$$S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g} \xrightarrow{\sim} S(\mathfrak h)^W.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a finite Weyl group acting faithfully on its $r$-dimensional complex reflection representation $V$, and put $S=\mathbb C[V]$. Then $S^W$ is a polynomial algebra on $r$ homogeneous algebraically independent basic invariants, and $S$ is free of rank $|W|$ over $S^W$. More generally these conclusions hold for every finite subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ generated by complex reflections (nonidentity transformations fixing a hyperplane pointwise). In the Weyl case the generating root reflections have order two; no classification or Coxeter presentation is needed here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from invariant theory. Let $\Phi$ be a
finite reduced crystallographic root system of rank $r$ in the real Cartan
space $E$ with Weyl group $W$
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]],
[[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]]), and let
$S=\mathbb C[E]$ carry the induced graded $W$-action with Cartan generators in
ordinary degree $1$. Let $d_1,\dots,d_r$ be the ordinary degrees of basic
invariants, so that $S^W=\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$ with $w_i$ homogeneous of
degree $d_i$ ([[thm-chevalley-shephard-todd-for-finite-weyl-groups]]). Then
$$\sum_{i=1}^r(d_i-1)=|\Phi^+|.$$
With the page degree normalization $\deg E=2$ the coinvariant algebra
$S/(S^W_+S)$ has top degree $2\sum_i(d_i-1)=2|\Phi^+|=|\Phi|$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $R$ is a Noetherian Cohen--Macaulay ring, then
$R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$ is Cohen--Macaulay for every $n\ge0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(A,\mathfrak m)$ be a nonzero
Noetherian Cohen–Macaulay local ring of dimension $h$, and let
$f_1,\ldots,f_i\in\mathfrak m$ be an $A$-regular sequence.
Then $A/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)$ is nonzero and Cohen–Macaulay of
dimension $h-i$. In particular $i\le h$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

If $0\ne M$ is a finite Cohen--Macaulay module of dimension $d$ over a
Noetherian local ring $R$, then every
$\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}_R(M)$ is minimal in
$\operatorname{Supp}_R(M)$ and satisfies $\dim(R/\mathfrak p)=d$.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring, let $\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ be a finite ordered sequence in $R$, and let $M$ be an $R$-module. On $\bigwedge R^n$, with standard basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$, let $\delta$ be the $R$-linear graded derivation of degree $-1$ with $\delta(e_i)=x_i$ and $\delta(R)=0$; thus $\delta(ab)=\delta(a)b+(-1)^pa\delta(b)$ for homogeneous $a$ of degree $p$.

The **Koszul complex with coefficients in $M$** is $K(\mathbf x;M)=(\bigwedge R^n\otimes_R M,d)$, where $d=\delta\otimes\operatorname{id}_M$. Its degree-$p$ term is $\bigwedge^pR^n\otimes_R M$ for $0\leq p\leq n$, and zero otherwise. Explicitly,

$$d(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_p}\otimes m)=\sum_{j=1}^p(-1)^{j-1}e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\widehat{e_{i_j}}\cdots\wedge e_{i_p}\otimes x_{i_j}m.$$

The empty wedge is $1\in R$. In particular $d(e_i\otimes m)=1\otimes x_im$ in $K_0=R\otimes_R M$, canonically identified with $M$ by $r\otimes m\mapsto rm$ with inverse $m\mapsto1\otimes m$. The differential out of degree zero is zero. The derivation respects the exterior relations and the two orders of deleting distinct factors cancel in $d^2$, so these maps form a chain complex. For $n=0$ this is $M$ in degree zero under the same identification.
If $M$ is finite free and $\mathbf x$ is $M$-regular, then $K(\mathbf x;M)$ is a finite free resolution of $M/(\mathbf x)M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\alpha$ be a root of a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra
$\mathfrak g$ with respect to a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$
([[def-root-and-root-space-relative-to-a-cartan-subalgebra]]). Then
$\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\alpha$ be a root of a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra
$\mathfrak g$ with respect to a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, with coroot
$h_\alpha$ as in [[def-coroot-of-a-lie-algebra-root]]. Then there are
$e_\alpha\in\mathfrak g_\alpha$ and $f_\alpha\in\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ with

$$[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]=h_\alpha,\qquad [h_\alpha,e_\alpha]=2e_\alpha,\qquad [h_\alpha,f_\alpha]=-2f_\alpha .$$

Consequently the span of $e_\alpha,f_\alpha,h_\alpha$ is a copy of
$\mathfrak{sl}_2$ inside $\mathfrak g$
([[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]]).

Every finite-dimensional representation of a finite-dimensional semisimple
Lie algebra over any characteristic-zero field is completely reducible.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra, let $\mathfrak h$ be a Cartan subalgebra, and let
$\Phi=\Phi(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak h)$ be the set of roots of
[[def-root-and-root-space-relative-to-a-cartan-subalgebra]]. Then $\Phi$ is
finite and
$$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak h\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathfrak g_\alpha$$
is a direct sum of $\mathfrak h$ with the nonzero root spaces.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra, and let $B$ be its Killing form from [[def-killing-form-of-a-semisimple-lie-algebra]]. Then

$$B([x,y],z)=B(x,[y,z]) \qquad (x,y,z\in \mathfrak g),$$

and $B$ is nondegenerate.

For a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ in
characteristic zero,
$\operatorname{Der}(\mathfrak g)=\operatorname{ad}(\mathfrak g)$.
The representing element is unique because $Z(\mathfrak g)=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $G$ be an affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ ([[def-group-scheme-over-a-field]]). Then the structure morphism $G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth, that is, $G$ is a smooth group scheme over $k$ ([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]]). In particular every local ring $\mathcal O_{G,g}$ is regular and $G$ is reduced. No smoothness, reducedness or finiteness of $G$ beyond finite type is assumed, and the characteristic-zero hypothesis is essential: in characteristic $p>0$ the finite group schemes $\alpha_p$ and $\mu_p$ are not smooth.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and let $G$ be a connected affine group variety over $k$, i.e. a smooth connected affine algebraic group of finite type over $k$ ([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]], [[def-group-scheme-over-a-field]]). Then: (a) for every Borel subgroup $B\subseteq G$ the quotient $G/B$ is complete; (b) any two Borel subgroups of $G$ are conjugate by an element of $G(k)$; (c) any two maximal tori of $G$ are conjugate by an element of $G(k)$; (d) any two Borel pairs are conjugate. The assertions here are made under the stated smooth connected and algebraically closed hypotheses; no necessity claim for each hypothesis is made.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a field, let
$X$ and $Y$ be $k$-schemes that are locally standard smooth over $k$ at the
points considered below ([[def-ag-standard-smooth-algebra]]), and let
$f\colon X\to Y$ be a morphism of $k$-schemes of finite type
([[def-locally-finite-type-and-finite-type-morphism]]). Let $x\in X$ be a
$k$-rational point and put $y=f(x)$, assumed $k$-rational as well, so that
$\kappa(x)=\kappa(y)=k$ ([[def-residue-field-scheme-point]]). Write
$A=\mathcal O_{Y,y}$, $S=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, with maximal ideals
$\mathfrak m_y\subseteq A$, $\mathfrak m_x\subseteq S$, and let
$f^{*}\colon A\to S$ be the induced local homomorphism. Let
$X_y=X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$ be the scheme-theoretic fibre
([[def-scheme-theoretic-fibre]]), whose local ring at $x$ is
$S/\mathfrak m_yS$. Then:

1. **Submersion criterion.** $f$ is locally standard smooth at $x$ — that is,
   there are affine opens $\operatorname{Spec}C\subseteq X$ and
   $\operatorname{Spec}D\subseteq Y$ with $x\in\operatorname{Spec}C$,
   $f(\operatorname{Spec}C)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}D$ and $D\to C$ standard
   smooth at the prime of $C$ corresponding to $x$ — if and only if the
   $k$-linear map
   $f^{*}\colon\mathfrak m_y/\mathfrak m_y^{2}\to\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^{2}$
   induced by $f^{*}$ is injective.
2. **Flatness and fibres.** If the equivalent conditions of clause 1 hold and
   $m=\dim S$, $n=\dim A$, then $S$ is flat over $A$, that is $f$ is flat at
   $x$, and $S/\mathfrak m_yS$ is a regular local ring of dimension $m-n$; in
   other words the fibre $X_y$ is regular at $x$ of dimension $m-n$. Any
   standard smooth chart of $f$ at $x$ has relative dimension $m-n$.

The two schemes are only required to be locally standard smooth at $x$ and $y$,
not globally; $f$ is of finite type as assumed above, and no hypothesis is
imposed on the base field. The Axiom of Choice is used
through the local-flatness, regular-parameter and geometric-regularity
suppliers cited below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $R\to B$ be a finitely presented ring
map ([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]). Then the set of primes
$\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}B$ at which $B_{\mathfrak q}$ is flat over $R$
is open in $\operatorname{Spec}B$. The same statement holds with a finitely
presented $B$-module $M$ in place of $B$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes that
is flat ([[def-flat-morphism-schemes]]) and locally of finite presentation
([[def-locally-finite-presentation-morphism]]). Then $f$ is universally open
([[def-open-morphism-schemes]]); in particular $f$ is open. No further
hypothesis is imposed on $X$, $S$ or $f$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be an
algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$, let $X$ and $Y$ be
irreducible classical varieties over $k$, and let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a
dominant morphism. Regard $X$ and $Y$ as integral finite-type $k$-schemes
under
[[thm-classical-varieties-equivalent-integral-separated-finite-type-schemes]],
let $X_{\mathrm{reg}},Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ be their regular loci
([[def-singular-and-regular-loci-variety]]), and let
$$U=X_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap f^{-1}(Y_{\mathrm{reg}})\cap D(H)$$
be the nonempty open subset of $X$ produced by
[[lem-dominant-map-generic-differential-surjectivity-char-zero]], so that
$f(U)\subseteq Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $d_xf$ is surjective at every closed point
$x\in U$.

Then there are a nonempty affine open subvariety
$V\subseteq U$ of $X$ — explicitly a nonempty principal open $D_{X_0}(h')$ of
an affine chart $X_0$ of $X$ — and a nonempty affine open subvariety
$W\subseteq Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ — a nonempty principal open of an affine chart
of $Y$ — such that:

1. $f(V)\subseteq W$, and $V\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ and
   $W\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ are smooth, so that $V$ and $W$ are smooth
   affine classical varieties over $k$;
2. the restriction $f|_V\colon V\to W$ is a morphism of finite type and is
   smooth in the sense of [[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]: it is locally
   standard smooth at every point of $V$; consequently the restriction
   $f|_V\colon V\to Y$ (equivalently $V\to Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$) is smooth as
   well.

In particular $f$ is smooth at every point of the nonempty open subset $V$ of
its source. Neither $X$ nor $Y$ is assumed smooth outside its regular locus,
and the target-side statement — a dense open subset of $Y$ over which the
source is smooth — is *not* asserted here: it requires a smooth source and
fails without that hypothesis.

For an irreducible classical variety $X$ and morphism $f:X\to Y$, the reduced closure $Z=\overline{f(X)}$ is irreducible and $\dim X=\dim Z+r$, where $r$ is the common dimension of the nonempty fibres on a nonempty open of $Z$. For arbitrary nonempty $X$ with components $X_i$, $\dim X=\max_i(\dim\overline{f(X_i)}+r_i)$, with a separately chosen generic open and relative dimension $r_i$ for each $X_i$. For empty $X$ use the empty maximum $-\infty$.

Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

Let $k$ be a field, let $n\geq 0$ be finite, put $P=k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$, and let
$A=P/I$ with a specified finite generating list $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ for the
actual ideal defining the affine scheme. For a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset
A$, write $L=A/\mathfrak m$. Let $J(\mathfrak m)$ be the $r\times n$ matrix over
$L$ obtained by mapping the formal partial derivatives $\partial f_i/\partial
t_j$ through $P\to A\to L$.

If $k$ is perfect, then $L/k$ is finite separable and
$$
\operatorname{rank}_L J(\mathfrak m)=n-\dim A_{\mathfrak m}
$$
if and only if $A_{\mathfrak m}$ is a regular local ring. For any field $k$,
the same equivalence holds at a $k$-rational point, where $L=k$, without a
perfectness assumption. If $I=I(X)$ for a reduced classical affine algebraic
set $X$ over an algebraically closed field and $\mathfrak m$ corresponds to a
closed point $x$, then, assuming AC,
$$
\dim A_{\mathfrak m}=\dim_xX=\max_{x\in X_i}\dim X_i,
$$
where $X_i$ ranges over the irreducible components through $x$. The finite
generating list need not be minimal, and $I$ need not be radical in the first
two assertions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). A regular local ring $R$ of dimension $d$ is a domain and Cohen–Macaulay. For every regular system $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$, the tuple is $R$-regular and $R/(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$ is regular local of dimension $d-c$ for all $0\le c\le d$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring.
The natural map
$$R\longrightarrow\prod_{\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}(R)}R_{\mathfrak q}$$
is injective. For each $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}(R)$,
the local ring $R_{\mathfrak q}$ has a nonzero element
annihilated by its maximal ideal $\mathfrak qR_{\mathfrak q}$;
in particular it has depth zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, the enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak g)$ is a free left, hence also right, module over its center $Z(U(\mathfrak g))$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: If $\mathfrak g=0$ then $r=0$ and $A=\mathbb C$, so all assertions hold; assume otherwise. By [F1], $S(\mathfrak g)$ is free over the polynomial invariant algebra $\mathbb C[p_1,\ldots,p_r]$. After quotienting by the first $j$ generators it remains free over $\mathbb C[p_{j+1},\ldots,p_r]$; hence multiplication by the next generator is injective and all successive quotients are nonzero. Thus the $p_i$ form a regular sequence, rather than merely a sequence of algebraically independent elements. The Koszul Euler characteristic gives $\operatorname{Hilb}(A,t)=\prod_i(1-t^{d_i})/(1-t)^{\dim\mathfrak g}$. At any rational maximal ideal containing the $p_i$, the ambient polynomial local ring has dimension $\dim\mathfrak g$: the chain of translated coordinate ideals gives this lower bound at a rational point, and [[cor-dimension-of-a-finite-polynomial-ring-over-a-field]] gives the upper bound, and [F2] gives quotient dimension $\dim\mathfrak g-r$. At every prime the same regular sequence localizes and [F2] makes the quotient Cohen--Macaulay. In particular $\dim A=\dim\mathfrak g-r=2N$ by root-space decomposition. The Hilbert series has pole order $2N$ at $t=1$; it is not a polynomial of degree $2N$.

Choose for every simple root $\alpha_i$ an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple $(e_i,f_i,h_i)$ and write $2\rho^\vee=\sum_i c_i h_i$ in the simple-coroot basis, so $\sum_i c_i\alpha_j(h_i)=2$ for every simple root $\alpha_j$, and put $e=\sum_i e_i$, $h=2\rho^\vee$, $f=\sum_i c_i f_i$. Distinct simple-root differences are not roots, so $[e_i,f_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$, and consequently $[h,e]=2e$, $[h,f]=-2f$ and $[e,f]=h$. The eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}h$ are $2\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$ and zero, hence all are even. Complete reducibility for this $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ subalgebra writes the adjoint module as a direct sum of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-strings $L(2m_1)\oplus\cdots$; each string contributes exactly one vector killed by $h$, and $\ker\operatorname{ad}h=\mathfrak h$ has dimension $r$, so there are exactly $r$ strings; a string with $m_j=0$ would consist of a nonzero vector killed by $e$ and $h$, i.e. a nonzero element of $\mathfrak h$ commuting with all $e_i$, which is central in $\mathfrak g$, hence zero; so all $m_j\ge1$ and counting dimensions gives $\sum_j(2m_j+1)=\dim\mathfrak g=2N+r$, that is $\sum_jm_j=N$. The highest vector of a string has $\operatorname{ad}h$-eigenvalue $2m_j>0$, hence lies in $\mathfrak n^+=\bigoplus_{\alpha>0}\mathfrak g_\alpha$; therefore $\ker\operatorname{ad}e$ is the $r$-dimensional span of the highest vectors and lies in $\mathfrak n^+$, and the lowest vectors span $z_f:=\ker\operatorname{ad}f\subseteq\mathfrak n^-$ with $\mathfrak g=[\mathfrak g,e]\oplus z_f$.

Let $\varphi_t(x)=t\cdot\operatorname{Ad}(t^{-\rho^\vee})(x)$ for $t\in\mathbb C^\times$. Since $p_i$ is $\mathfrak g$-invariant, $p_i(\varphi_tx)=t^{d_i}p_i(x)$ for all $x\in\mathfrak g$; since $\operatorname{Ad}(t^{-\rho^\vee})f_i=tf_i$, the map $\varphi_t$ preserves $z_f$, so with $q_i(y):=p_i(e+y)$ one has $q_i(\varphi_ty)=p_i(\varphi_t(e+y))=t^{d_i}q_i(y)$: each $q_i$ is weighted-homogeneous of weighted degree $d_i$ for the weights $\deg y_j=m_j+1$ on $z_f$; indeed a root vector of height $t$ has $\varphi$-weight $1-t$, so the lowest vector $y_j$ has weight $m_j+1\ge2$.

The group constructions needed below are explicit. Order the height spaces of $\mathfrak g$ by root height, with $\mathfrak h$ at height zero. The endomorphisms $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak n^+$ strictly raise height. Exponential and logarithm are finite inverse polynomials on the corresponding strictly triangular matrices. For a unipotent automorphism $u$ which raises height relative to the identity, $\exp(t\log u)$ preserves the Lie bracket for every integer $t$ since it equals $u^t$; the bracket equations are polynomial in $t$, so they hold for all complex $t$. Differentiating at zero shows that $\log u$ is a derivation. By [F4] it equals $\operatorname{ad}x$; comparison of the height components shows $x\in\mathfrak n^+$, because negative-root components lower height and a Cartan component acts in height zero, and $\operatorname{ad}$ is injective. Thus $N_+=\exp(\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak n^+)$ is exactly the closed subgroup of $G$ defined by these strict-height unipotence equations; it is polynomially isomorphic to $\mathfrak n^+$, hence connected. Let $H=(\mathbb C^\times)^r$ act by fixing $\mathfrak h$ and multiplying $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ by $\prod_i t_i^{a_i}$ when $\alpha=\sum_i a_i\alpha_i$. Root brackets show this is a closed torus of automorphisms, with Lie algebra $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak h$. It normalizes $N_+$; $B=HN_+$ is closed, since the diagonal entries determine its $H$ factor and the remaining strict-height unipotent equations determine its $N_+$ factor. It is connected and solvable, with Lie algebra $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak b$. Any Lie subalgebra containing $\mathfrak b$ is $\mathfrak h$-stable and splits into root spaces; if it is larger it contains a negative root space and hence, together with its positive root space, a root $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, so it cannot be solvable. Thus $B$ is maximal among connected solvable closed subgroups (a larger such subgroup would have larger solvable Lie algebra), and is a Borel. The connected group $G=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)^0$ is smooth and irreducible of dimension $\dim\mathfrak g$ by [F4], and its Borels are conjugate. These explicit tori also give the height scalings used in step 1.3.

The central reduction has associated graded $A$: fix a central character $\chi:Z\to\mathbb C$ with kernel $\mathfrak m_\chi$, and let $J=\mathfrak m_\chi U(\mathfrak g)$. By [F6], $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)=S(\mathfrak g)$, $\operatorname{gr}Z=S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}$, and the leading symbol of any $z\in\mathfrak m_\chi$ lies in $S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}_+=(p_1,\dots,p_r)$; conversely each $p_i$ is the leading symbol of an element of $\mathfrak m_\chi$, for instance of $z_i-\chi(z_i)$ for a central element $z_i$ of leading symbol $p_i$ (the scalar term has lower filtration degree because $d_i>0$). Therefore $\operatorname{gr}J=(p_1,\dots,p_r)S(\mathfrak g)$ and the natural graded surjection $S(\mathfrak g)/(p_1,\dots,p_r)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{gr}(U(\mathfrak g)/J)$ is an isomorphism: both sides have the Hilbert series of step 1.1, since the filtered free harmonic decomposition of [F6] restricts to a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)/J$ whose symbols have exactly the Hilbert series $\prod_i(1-t^{d_i})/(1-t)^{\dim\mathfrak g}$. Hence the PBW associated graded of $U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$ is canonically $A$.

The morphism $\Psi:G\times z_f\to\mathfrak g$, $(g,y)\mapsto g\cdot(e+y)$, is dominant. Its differential at $(1,0)$ is $(\xi,y)\mapsto[\xi,e]+y$ for $\xi\in T_1G=\mathfrak g$ (using $G$-equivariance of the action), with image $[\mathfrak g,e]+z_f=\mathfrak g$ by step 1.2; hence the cotangent map is injective and, by the submersion criterion at the rational points $(1,0)$ and $e$, $\Psi$ is locally standard smooth, hence flat, at $(1,0)$; the flat locus is open and flat morphisms of finite presentation are open, so the image of $\Psi$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathfrak g$; since $\mathfrak g$ is irreducible, $\Psi$ is dominant.

If $\operatorname{ad}x$ is nilpotent, $U_x=\{\exp(t\operatorname{ad}x):t\in\mathbb C\}$ is a closed connected unipotent subgroup of $G$: for $x\ne0$ logarithm identifies it with the closed line $\mathbb C\operatorname{ad}x$; for $x=0$ it is trivial. Among connected solvable closed subgroups containing it choose one of maximal dimension; any strictly larger connected closed subgroup has larger dimension, so it is a Borel. Conjugacy from [F4] moves it into the $B$ constructed in step 2.1. Every unipotent element of that triangular group has diagonal entries all one, hence trivial $H$ factor, and lies in $N_+$. Its logarithm therefore belongs to $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak n^+$ by step 2.1. Injectivity and equivariance of $\operatorname{ad}$ show that $x$ is conjugate into $\mathfrak n^+$. Conversely the invariant $p_i$ vanishes on $\mathfrak n^+$: the torus automorphism multiplying height $j$ by $t^j$ sends every $n\in\mathfrak n^+$ to zero as $t\to0$, while invariance preserves $p_i(n)$. Thus $p_i(n)=p_i(0)=0$. Lie invariance implies $G$-invariance here: the differential of $g\mapsto p_i(gx)$ vanishes on the connected smooth group, and in characteristic zero a regular function with zero differential on an irreducible variety is constant.

The restrictions $q_1,\dots,q_r\in\mathbb C[z_f]$ are algebraically independent: the pullback $\Psi^*$ is injective because $\Psi$ is dominant, and $\Psi^*(p_i)=q_i$ by $G$-invariance of the $p_i$; if a nonzero polynomial $F$ satisfied $F(q_1,\dots,q_r)=0$, then $\Psi^*(F(p_1,\dots,p_r))=0$, hence $F(p_1,\dots,p_r)=0$ in $S(\mathfrak g)$, contradicting the algebraic independence of $p_1,\dots,p_r$ from [F1].

The common zero set $\mathcal N=\{x:p_i(x)=0\text{ for all }i\}$ equals $G\cdot\mathfrak n^+$: the inclusion $\supseteq$ is step 3.2, and conversely if all $p_i$ vanish then every invariant polynomial of positive degree vanishes, so the invariant traces $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{ad}x)^k)$, $k\ge1$, vanish because each is invariant with zero constant term; Newton's identities express every coefficient of the characteristic polynomial of $\operatorname{ad}x$ polynomially in these traces, so the characteristic polynomial is $T^{\dim\mathfrak g}$, hence $\operatorname{ad}x$ is nilpotent and $x$ is conjugate into $\mathfrak n^+$ by step 3.2. Also $\mathcal N$ is the underlying set of $\operatorname{Spec}A$.

The map $q=(q_1,\dots,q_r):\mathbb A^r\to\mathbb A^r$ is dominant by step 4.1, and $\mathbb A^r$ is smooth, so generic smoothness provides a dense open subset of $\mathbb A^r$ on which the differential of $q$ is surjective; in particular the Jacobian determinant $D=\det(\partial q_i/\partial y_j)$ is not identically zero.

Weights: $D$ is weighted-homogeneous of weighted degree $\sum_id_i-\sum_j(m_j+1)=\sum_i(d_i-1)-\sum_jm_j=N-N=0$ by steps 1.2 and 1.3, because the derivative with respect to $y_j$ lowers weighted degree by $m_j+1$; a nonzero polynomial all of whose monomials have positive weights $m_j+1$ and total weighted degree zero is a nonzero constant. Hence $D$ is a nonzero constant, and in particular the linear map $z_f\to\mathbb C^r$, $y\mapsto(dp_1(e)(y),\dots,dp_r(e)(y))$, given by the matrix $(\partial q_i/\partial y_j)(0)$, is invertible.

The Jacobian matrix of the presentation $A=S(\mathfrak g)/(p_1,\dots,p_r)$ at the rational maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $e$ has rank exactly $r$: its rows are the differentials $dp_i(e)$, which are linearly independent by step 6.1. Since $\dim A_{\mathfrak m}=\dim A=\dim\mathfrak g-r$ by step 1.1, the Jacobian criterion in the form $\operatorname{rank}J(\mathfrak m)=n-\dim A_{\mathfrak m}$ identifies $A_{\mathfrak m}$ as a regular local ring.

The set $\mathcal N$ is irreducible: step 4.2 identifies its closed points with the image of the irreducible variety $G\times\mathfrak n^+$, so its closure is irreducible and equals the underlying space of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ ([[cor-closed-points-dense-in-affine-spectra]] and [[cor-weak-nullstellensatz-algebraically-closed-coordinate-form]] give density of its complex rational closed points). In particular there is a unique minimal prime $\mathfrak p_0$. The regular local ring $A_{\mathfrak m_e}$ of step 7.1 localizes further to $A_{\mathfrak p_0}$; localizations of regular local rings are regular by [[cor-localisations-of-regular-local-rings-are-regular]]. Since $\mathfrak p_0$ is minimal, that localization has dimension zero and is a field. This proves generic reducedness without needing an assertion about openness of the regular orbit.

There are no embedded associated primes. For $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}(A)$ choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\supseteq\mathfrak q$. An element with annihilator $\mathfrak q$ remains nonzero at $\mathfrak m$ and has annihilator $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak m}$, so this is an associated prime of $A_{\mathfrak m}$. That local ring is Cohen--Macaulay by step 1.1, and the associated-prime theorem in [F2] makes $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak m}$ minimal. Any strict smaller prime of $A$ below $\mathfrak q$ would remain strict after localization at $\mathfrak m$, so $\mathfrak q$ itself is minimal. Hence the only possible associated prime is the unique $\mathfrak p_0$ of step 8.1. The associated-localization detection map in [F5] therefore injects $A$ into the field $A_{\mathfrak p_0}$, proving that $A$ is an integral domain and in particular reduced. The Cohen--Macaulay argument is essential here; generic reducedness alone would not exclude embedded nilpotents.

Combining steps 1.1, 2.2, 9.1: $A$ is a reduced integral domain of dimension $\dim\mathfrak g-r=2N=2|\Phi^+|$ with the displayed Hilbert series, and every central reduction has associated graded $A$. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the invariant-theory, group-theoretic and geometric suppliers [F1], [F4], [F5] and [F6]; the conclusions themselves are choice-free statements about $\mathfrak g$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published block theory
([[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]],
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Work in category $\mathcal O$ of a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie
algebra $\mathfrak g$ with the conventions of [[def-bgg-category-o]]: a Cartan
subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, a positive system with simple roots $\alpha_i$, the
Weyl group $W$ of [[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]], the Weyl
vector $\rho$, and the dot action $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$. Write
$Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$ and $\mu\le\lambda$ when
$\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$.

**The fixed weight.** Fix a weight $\lambda$ which is **integral**,
**dot-regular** and **dominant**: $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z$
for every root $\alpha$ (so the integral Weyl group $W_\lambda$ of
[[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]] is all of $W$), and
$\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\neq0$, respectively $>0$, for every
root, respectively every positive root ([[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]]).
The set $\Phi_\lambda$ of [[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]] is therefore
the full root system and $W_\lambda=W$.

**The block.** The regular point $\lambda+\rho$ lies in an open chamber. An element fixing
it preserves that chamber, so [[thm-the-weyl-group-acts-simply-transitively-on-weyl-chambers]]
makes its stabilizer trivial; hence the linkage class
$$C=W_\lambda\cdot\lambda=W\cdot\lambda$$
has exactly $|W|$ elements. The **regular integral block** is the full
subcategory
$$\mathcal O_\lambda:=\mathcal O_C$$
of objects of $\mathcal O$ whose simple composition factors have labels in
$C$, as in [[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]]; it is
nonzero, abelian and extension-closed as a block, and
$K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$ is the subgroup of $K_0(\mathcal O)$ of
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]] spanned by the classes
of objects of the block.

**Its labelled objects.** For $w\in W$ define the standard and costandard
objects and the simple object by
$$\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):=M(w\cdot\lambda),\qquad \nabla(w\cdot\lambda):=D(M(w\cdot\lambda)),\qquad L(w\cdot\lambda):=M(w\cdot\lambda)/J(w\cdot\lambda),$$
where $M$ is the Verma module of [[def-verma-module]], $D$ the restricted dual
of [[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], and $J(w\cdot\lambda)$
the sum of all proper submodules, so that $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ is the unique
simple quotient of $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ by
[[thm-verma-module-has-a-unique-simple-quotient]]. By
[[thm-simple-objects-of-category-o-are-highest-weight-modules]] the simple
objects of $\mathcal O_\lambda$ are exactly the $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ for
$w\in W$, pairwise non-isomorphic. Let $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ denote a projective
cover of $L(w\cdot\lambda)$, which may be chosen inside the linkage class of
$w\cdot\lambda$ and is unique up to isomorphism and indecomposable
([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]); every such $P(w\cdot\lambda)$
carries a finite Verma flag
([[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]],
[[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]).

**Triangularity of the Verma-flag matrix.** For all $v,w\in W$,
$$[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):L(v\cdot\lambda)]\neq0\ \Longrightarrow\ v\cdot\lambda\le w\cdot\lambda,\qquad [\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]=1,$$
where the multiplicity is the composition multiplicity of
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]]. Indeed
$(P(v\cdot\lambda):\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))=[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):L(v\cdot\lambda)]$
by [[thm-bgg-reciprocity]] and
$(P(v\cdot\lambda):\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))\neq0$ forces
$w\cdot\lambda-v\cdot\lambda\in Q^+$ while
$(P(v\cdot\lambda):\Delta(v\cdot\lambda))=1$ by
[[cor-projective-standard-labels-lie-above-the-head]].

**The antidominant weight.** Let $w_0\in W$ be the longest element. Since
$\langle w_0\cdot\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle
=\langle\lambda+\rho,w_0^{-1}\alpha^\vee\rangle<0$ for every positive root
$\alpha$, the antidominant Verma module $\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)$ is simple
([[cor-antidominant-verma-modules-are-simple]]), so
$$\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)=L(w_0\cdot\lambda)$$
and this is the unique standard object of the block that is simple: for
$w\neq w_0$ the regular weight $w\cdot\lambda$ is not antidominant, so some
positive root $\alpha$ has
$\langle w\cdot\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$, and
[[thm-verma-embedding-for-an-arbitrary-positive-root]] embeds
$M(s_\alpha\cdot(w\cdot\lambda))$ as a proper submodule of
$\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$. The weight $w_0\cdot\lambda$ is called the
**antidominant weight** of the block and $\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)$ its
antidominant Verma module.

**Grothendieck group.** By [[prop-the-grothendieck-group-of-o-has-simple-and-standard-bases]]
applied to the finite label set $C=W\cdot\lambda$, both the classes
$[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]$ and the classes $[L(w\cdot\lambda)]$, $w\in W$,
form $\mathbb Z$-bases of $K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$, and the transition matrix
between them is unitriangular for any linear order of $W$ extending the order
on the dot orbit induced by $\le$.

Every statement above uses the published block, Verma, duality and
projective-cover theory named in the citations, and that theory assumes the
Axiom of Choice; the definition itself selects nothing further.

For a $\mathfrak g$-module $V$, sending a homomorphism $T:M(\lambda)\to V$
to $T(v_\lambda)$ is a bijection onto the vectors $v\in V$ of weight
$\lambda$ annihilated by $\mathfrak n^+$.  Here $M(\lambda)$ is
[[def-verma-module]].  The nonzero vectors in this target are precisely the
highest-weight vectors of weight $\lambda$ from
[[def-highest-weight-vector-and-cyclic-highest-weight-module]]; the zero vector
corresponds to the zero homomorphism.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published block theory
([[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Fix a regular integral block $\mathcal O_\lambda$ as in
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]], with
inclusion $\operatorname{incl}_\lambda:\mathcal O_\lambda\to\mathcal O$ and
exact projection $\operatorname{pr}_\lambda:\mathcal O\to\mathcal O_\lambda$
of [[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]], so that
$\operatorname{pr}_\lambda\circ\operatorname{incl}_\lambda=\operatorname{id}$;
the block is a direct summand of $\mathcal O$ and contains the projective
covers $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ of [[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]. For a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module $E$ define
the endofunctor
$$F_E:=\operatorname{pr}_\lambda\circ(E\otimes-)\circ\operatorname{incl}_\lambda\colon\mathcal O_\lambda\longrightarrow\mathcal O_\lambda .$$

**Basic properties.** The functor $F_E$ is well defined and additive:
$E\otimes-$ is an exact endofunctor of $\mathcal O$ and maps $\mathcal O$ into
itself ([[prop-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-category-o]]),
and $\operatorname{pr}_\lambda$ is exact. Hence $F_E$ is exact as a composite of
exact functors. It preserves projective objects: if $P\in\mathcal O_\lambda$ is
projective, then $E\otimes P$ is projective in $\mathcal O$
([[lem-tensoring-a-projective-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-is-projective]]),
and $\operatorname{pr}_\lambda$ preserves projectives
([[lem-block-projection-preserves-projectives]]). The zero module $E=0$
gives the zero functor, and $E=\mathbb C$ the identity functor, since the
one-dimensional trivial module acts by the identity.

**Projective functors.** A **projective functor** on
$\mathcal O_\lambda$ is an endofunctor of $\mathcal O_\lambda$ isomorphic to a
direct summand of some $F_E$, $E$ finite dimensional and
$\mathfrak h$-semisimple. Write $\mathcal F_\lambda$ for the full subcategory
of the endofunctor category of $\mathcal O_\lambda$ whose objects are the
projective functors, with arbitrary natural transformations as morphisms; it is
additive with the pointwise biproducts of [[def-additive-category]], and
"direct summand" means natural maps $i:F\to F_E$, $p:F_E\to F$ with $pi=1_F$;
then $ip$ is an idempotent natural transformation.

**Closure properties.** The class of projective functors is closed under
finite direct sums, composition, direct summands and passage to adjoints:

1. $F_{E\oplus E'}\cong F_E\oplus F_{E'}$, since tensoring with a direct sum
distributes over direct sums and $\operatorname{pr}_\lambda$ is additive.
2. $F_E\circ F_{E'}$ is a natural direct summand of $F_{E\otimes E'}$:
the natural block decomposition of $E'\otimes X$ splits off its
$\lambda$-component before applying $E\otimes-$ and the final projection.
Its complementary blocks can return to $\mathcal O_\lambda$, so an
isomorphism with the entire $F_{E\otimes E'}$ is not asserted.
3. $F_{E^*}$ is both a left and a right adjoint of $F_E$: this is
[[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]] applied to

apply the splitting to the image of each object. Hence every projective functor

functors a summand of the composite of their ambient tensor functors. Clause 2

corresponding adjoint summand of $F_{E^*}$.

of $\mathcal O$ has a finite Verma flag
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]).

[[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]] is a direct summand of the
projective object $\operatorname{pr}_C(E\otimes M(\lambda))$ of
[[lem-finite-dimensional-tensors-reach-every-block-simple]], which is a
direct summand of $E\otimes M(\lambda)$; a general projective object has
finite length, hence is a finite direct sum of indecomposable projectives,
each of which is a projective cover of its simple head.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). If a projective object
$P$ of $\mathcal O$ admits an epimorphism $P\twoheadrightarrow L$ onto a
simple object $L$, then some indecomposable direct summand of $P$ maps onto
$L$, and that summand is a projective cover of $L$ (an essential epimorphism
with projective source, [[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]]).
Any two projective covers of $L$ are isomorphic, although not canonically so,
and the endomorphism ring of a projective cover is local. In particular, for
every simple $L$ there is at most one isomorphism class of indecomposable
projectives with head $L$; when such a cover exists it is written $P(L)$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category in which every object has finite
length, and define an object to be **indecomposable** when it is nonzero and
every decomposition $X\cong Y\oplus Z$ has $Y=0$ or $Z=0$. Then:

   objects;
2. the endomorphism ring of an indecomposable object is local, and for an
   endomorphism $f$ of an indecomposable object either $f$ is an isomorphism
   or $f$ is nilpotent;
3. the decomposition is unique up to isomorphism and permutation of the
   summands;
4. an indecomposable projective object $P$ of $\mathcal A$ has a unique
   maximal proper subobject $J(P)$, its quotient $P/J(P)$ is simple, and $P$
   is a projective cover of $P/J(P)$

   under submodules, essentiality is the superfluous-kernel condition of the
   cited module definition; projectivity in the ambient module category is
   not asserted).

regular integral block $\mathcal O_\lambda$ of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]] the
assignment
$$c\colon K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z[W],\qquad[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]\longmapsto w,$$
is an isomorphism of abelian groups, and for every simple reflection $s$ the
wall-crossing functor $\theta_s$ of
[[def-wall-crossing-functor-and-unit-counit]] satisfies
$$c\,[\theta_sX]=c\,[X]\cdot(1+s)\qquad\text{for all }X\in\mathcal O_\lambda,$$
right multiplication by $1+s$ in the integral group ring $\mathbb Z[W]$.
Consequently, for a reduced word $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ one has
$$c\,[\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}\Delta(\lambda)]=(1+s_1)(1+s_2)\cdots(1+s_k),$$
the sum of all subexpression products with their actual multiplicities; its top
Bruhat term is $w$ once and all other terms have strictly smaller labels. With
the composition $\theta_{s_1}\cdots\theta_{s_k}$ instead, the factors are
multiplied in the reverse order.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published items. Let
$\theta_s$ be the wall-crossing functor of
[[def-wall-crossing-functor-and-unit-counit]] attached to the simple reflection

object $\theta_s\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ has a finite Verma flag with exactly two
factors, namely $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ and $\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)$, each with
multiplicity one; in the Grothendieck group
$$[\theta_s\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]=[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]+[\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)].$$

Verma flags: if $X$ has a finite Verma flag with multiplicities
$(X:\Delta(v\cdot\lambda))$, then $\theta_sX$ has one with multiplicities
$(\theta_sX:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))=(X:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))+(X:\Delta(us\cdot\lambda))$,
and the same formula holds in $K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$. The resulting flag is
not in general split; splitting is neither asserted nor used.

$\lambda$ and $\mu$,
$$(P(\lambda):\Delta(\mu))=[\Delta(\mu):L(\lambda)]=[M(\mu):L(\lambda)],$$
where $P(\lambda)$ is the projective cover of $L(\lambda)$, the left-hand
multiplicity is the Verma-flag multiplicity of
[[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]], and the right-hand
multiplicity is the simple composition multiplicity of the Verma module
$M(\mu)$ ([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]]).

$(P(\lambda):\Delta(\mu))$ is nonzero then $\mu\ge\lambda$, that is,
$\mu-\lambda\in Q^+$. Moreover $(P(\lambda):\Delta(\lambda))=1$, so exactly
one factor of every Verma flag of $P(\lambda)$ has label $\lambda$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

If $[M(\lambda):L(\mu)]\ne0$, then $\mu\uparrow\lambda$.

For the simple reflections of a finite reduced crystallographic root system, word length equals inversion length: $\ell(w)=|\operatorname{Inv}(w)|$. If a root reflection $t$ satisfies $\ell(tw)<\ell(w)$, every reduced word for $w$ loses exactly one letter to give $tw$. Every nonreduced word admits deletion of two letters without changing its group element.

More precisely, for $\beta\in\Phi^+$, $\ell(s_\beta w)<\ell(w)$ if and only if $w^{-1}\beta<0$. In this case one letter can be deleted from any word for $w$ to give $s_\beta w$, although the resulting word need not be reduced. Also $\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)\pm1$, with the minus sign exactly when $w\alpha_i<0$. These are assertions for the geometric reflection group, without an assumed Coxeter presentation or exchange axiom.

For the geometric finite Weyl group and its simple reflections, define $u\le v$ when a reduced expression for $v$ contains a reduced expression for $u$ as an ordered subword: choose positions in increasing order, multiply their letters in that order, and require their number to be $\ell(u)$. The empty subword represents the identity.

The following proof shows this condition is independent of the reduced expression for $v$ and is equivalent to a chain $u=w_0,w_1,\ldots,w_k=v$ with $w_{j+1}=t_jw_j$, each $t_j$ a root reflection and $\ell(w_{j+1})=\ell(w_j)+1$. Thus it is a partial order, called **strong Bruhat order**. A zero-length chain is allowed. Assume the Axiom of Choice.

For weights $\lambda,\mu$, a nonzero homomorphism $M(\mu)\to M(\lambda)$ exists if and only if $\mu\uparrow\lambda$.

No summand $P(x\cdot\lambda)$ with $x\not\le w$ occurs: the diagonal entry of the BGG matrix gives $(P(x\cdot\lambda):\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))=1$ by [F3], so such a summand would contribute a standard factor $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$ to $Y$ with $x\not\le w$, contradicting step 1.1.

The full subexpression contributes $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ with multiplicity one to the product class, and no other summand $P(x\cdot\lambda)$ with $x\le w$, $x\neq w$ contributes to the multiplicity of $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$: $(P(x\cdot\lambda):\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))\neq0$ forces $w\le x$ by [F3], so with $x\le w$ it forces $x=w$. The remaining multiplicities $m_x$, $x<w$, are determined recursively from the product class: the coefficient of $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$ in the class of $Y$ equals $m_x+\sum_{x<z}m_z(P(z\cdot\lambda):\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))$, whose second term involves only strictly larger labels already determined; solving downward in the finite Bruhat order gives all $m_x$.

Every indecomposable projective is a summand of such a word: the decomposition of step 1.1 with diagonal support realizes each $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ as a summand of $\theta_{\underline w}\Delta(\lambda)$ for any reduced word $w$, which is the stated generation statement.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in category
$\mathcal O$ with the conventions of [[def-bgg-category-o]], and write
$\Delta(\mu)=M(\mu)$ for the standard objects of
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], i.e. the Verma modules
of [[def-verma-module]].

A **finite Verma flag** of an object $X$ of $\mathcal O$ — also called a
**standard flag** or a **$\Delta$-flag** — is a finite increasing sequence of
subobjects
$$0=X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$$
such that each quotient $X_i/X_{i-1}$ is isomorphic to a Verma module
$\Delta(\mu_i)=M(\mu_i)$, for $i=1,\dots,n$. An object admitting such a flag is
called **Verma-filtered**. Since the flag is exhausted by its factors, its
class in the Grothendieck group
$K_0(\mathcal O)$ of [[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]
is
$$[X]=\sum_{i=1}^n[\Delta(\mu_i)].$$

For a Verma-filtered object $X$ and a weight $\mu$, the **multiplicity**
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is the number of indices $i$ with $\mu_i=\mu$ in a Verma
flag of $X$. This number is independent of the chosen flag by
[[lem-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-independent-of-the-flag]], so the notation
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is well-defined for Verma-filtered $X$.

The zero object has the empty flag, and every multiplicity of the zero object
is zero; a nonzero Verma-filtered object has at least one factor. A one-step
flag of $X$ is exactly an isomorphism $X\cong\Delta(\mu)$ for a single weight
$\mu$, so the objects with a one-step flag are the Verma modules themselves.
The flag is a chain of subobjects of $X$ in the module category; it is not
required to split, and later examples show that it need not.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). If $X\in\mathcal O$
admits two finite Verma flags with corresponding multiplicities
$m_\mu$ and $m'_\mu$
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]), then $m_\mu=m'_\mu$ for every
weight $\mu$. Hence the multiplicity $(X:\Delta(\mu))$ of
[[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]] is well defined.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

For the abelian category [[thm-category-o-is-abelian-and-extension-closed]], define $K_0(\mathcal O)$ as the free abelian group on isomorphism classes $[M]$, modulo $[B]=[A]+[C]$ for every short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$. A set of representatives suffices: every finitely generated $U(\mathfrak g)$-module is a quotient of some $U(\mathfrak g)^n$, and those quotients form a set up to isomorphism.

Define the formal character by $\operatorname{ch}M=\sum_\mu(\dim M_\mu)e^\mu$. By [[prop-equivalent-support-description-of-category-o]], its integer coefficients are finite and supported in finitely many downward cones. Let $\mathscr R$ be the group of all such integer coefficient families, with pointwise addition. It is a ring with $e^\mu e^\nu=e^{\mu+\nu}$: at a fixed resulting weight, in any pair of cones the equation $\beta+\gamma=\eta$ with $\beta,\gamma\in Q^+$ has finitely many solutions, since every simple-root coefficient is bounded. Taking weight spaces is exact, so character gives a well-defined homomorphism $K_0(\mathcal O)\to\mathscr R$. The zero object's class and character are zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). If $X=X_1\oplus X_2$
is a direct sum decomposition in $\mathcal O$ and $X$ is Verma-filtered
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]), then both $X_1$ and $X_2$ are
Verma-filtered.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $E$ be a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module with weight
multiplicities $\dim E_\eta$
([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]). For every
weight $\mu$, the object $E\otimes\Delta(\mu)$ has a finite Verma flag
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]) whose factors are $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$,
the factor $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$ occurring $\dim E_\eta$ times; the factors can be
ordered so that a real-linear height $\ell$ with $\ell(\alpha_i)=1$ is nonincreasing.

Consequently, if $X\in\mathcal O$ has a finite Verma flag with multiplicities
$(X:\Delta(\nu))$, then $E\otimes X$ has a finite Verma flag and
$$(E\otimes X:\Delta(\mu))=\sum_\eta\dim E_\eta\,(X:\Delta(\mu-\eta)).$$

Let $X$ be Verma-filtered with finite flag $0=X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$ and factors $\Delta(v_i\cdot\lambda)$. Exactness of $\theta_s$ by [F2] makes $0=\theta_sX_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\theta_sX_n=\theta_sX$ an increasing chain of subobjects, and each quotient $\theta_sX_i/\theta_sX_{i-1}\cong\theta_s(X_i/X_{i-1})\cong\theta_s\Delta(v_i\cdot\lambda)$ carries the two-factor flag of step 1.1; concatenating these two-step flags through the chain yields a finite Verma flag of $\theta_sX$ with factor multiplicities $(X:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))+(X:\Delta(us\cdot\lambda))$, where the independence of the flag [F2] makes the count well defined.

Summing the classes along the flag of step 2.1 gives $[\theta_sX]=\sum_i([\Delta(v_i\cdot\lambda)]+[\Delta(v_is\cdot\lambda)])=[X]+\sum_i[\Delta(v_is\cdot\lambda)]$, which is the stated formula $(\theta_sX:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))=(X:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))+(X:\Delta(us\cdot\lambda))$; no splitting of the two-step extensions is used, and the claim extends to direct summands of $\theta_sX$ whenever they are Verma-filtered, by [F3].
