Put
$$\mathfrak p=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r,\qquad \mathfrak h=\mathfrak g_0,\qquad \mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r,$$
and for rows $1\le i,j\le n$ define the shift $s_{i,j}=p_j-p_i$ if $i\le j$
and $s_{i,j}=0$ if $i\ge j$, together with the centralizer elements
$$e_{i,j;r}=\sum_{\substack{\mathrm{row}(h)=i,\ \mathrm{row}(k)=j\\ \mathrm{col}(k)-\mathrm{col}(h)=r}}e_{h,k} \qquad(s_{i,j}\le r<p_j).$$
Finally let $\chi\colon\mathfrak m\to\mathbb C$ be $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$,
where the trace is the trace of the $N\times N$ matrix.

The verification below records the properties of this data that are used
throughout this page. $e\in\mathfrak g_1$ has Jordan type $\lambda$; $\mathfrak p$
is a parabolic subalgebra with Levi factor
$\mathfrak h\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{q_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{q_l}$ and
nilradical $\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$, while $\mathfrak m$ is the
nilradical of the opposite parabolic; the elements $e_{i,j;r}$ with
$s_{i,j}\le r<p_j$ form a basis of the centralizer
$\mathfrak g^e=\{X\in\mathfrak g:[X,e]=0\}$; the box set
$J=\{(a,b)\in\{1,\dots,N\}^2:\mathrm{col}(a)\le\mathrm{col}(b),\ R(b)=\emptyset\}$
is in bijection with $K=\{(i,j,r):1\le i,j\le n,\ s_{i,j}\le r<p_j\}$ via
$(a,b)\mapsto(\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b),\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a))$, and
$$\xi_{a,b}:=\sum_{t=0}^{\mathrm{col}(a)-1}e_{L^t(a),L^t(b)}=e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)};$$
and $\chi$ is a Lie algebra character, $\chi([\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m])=0$. This
grading is the type-A pyramid good grading in the degree-one convention:
$\operatorname{ad}e:\mathfrak g_r\to\mathfrak g_{r+1}$ is injective for
$r<0$ and surjective for $r\ge0$. For $e\ne0$ it differs from the standard
Dynkin grading, in which $e$ has degree $2$ rather than $1$. For $e=0$ all
boxes lie in one column or there are no boxes, and the pyramid grading and
the trivial Dynkin grading both concentrate $\mathfrak g$ in degree zero.
If $N=0$, take $\mathfrak{gl}_0=0$: the box set and both centralizer index
sets are empty, $e=0$, $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak h=\mathfrak m=0$, and
$\chi=0$. These conventions also permit an empty row list.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

For a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ over $k$ and a $\mathfrak g$-module $M$,
the degree-$n$ **Chevalley–Eilenberg cochains** are

$$C^n(\mathfrak g,M)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\Lambda^n\mathfrak g,M)\quad(n\geq0).$$

Set $C^n(\mathfrak g,M)=0$ for $n<0$. Since
$\Lambda^0\mathfrak g=k$, evaluation at $1$ identifies
$C^0(\mathfrak g,M)$ with $M$. Cochains may equivalently be viewed as
alternating $n$-linear maps $\mathfrak g^n\to M$. No finite-dimensionality
or characteristic hypothesis is needed. If $n>\dim\mathfrak g$ in the
finite-dimensional case, the exterior power and hence the cochain space are
zero.

For $f\in C^n(\mathfrak g,M)$ define $df\in C^{n+1}(\mathfrak g,M)$ by

$$\begin{aligned}(df)(x_0,\ldots,x_n)={}&\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^i x_i f(x_0,\ldots,\widehat{x_i},\ldots,x_n)\\&+\sum_{0\leq i<j\leq n}(-1)^{i+j}f([x_i,x_j],x_0,\ldots,\widehat{x_i},\ldots,\widehat{x_j},\ldots,x_n).\end{aligned}$$

This fixes a zero-based sign convention. A hat means omission, and in the
second sum the bracket is inserted as the first argument. Empty sums are
zero. Thus for $m\in C^0=M$, $(dm)(x)=xm$. Alternation of the formula makes
it factor through $\Lambda^{n+1}\mathfrak g$; the next theorem proves that
successive differentials compose to zero.

The **Lie algebra cohomology** of $\mathfrak g$ with coefficients in the
$\mathfrak g$-module $M$ is the cohomology of its Chevalley–Eilenberg
cochain complex:

$$H^n(\mathfrak g,M)=\frac{\ker(d:C^n\to C^{n+1})}{\operatorname{im}(d:C^{n-1}\to C^n)}.$$

The containment of the denominator in the numerator is supplied by
[[thm-the-chevalley-eilenberg-differential-squares-to-zero]]. For $n<0$ all
cochain groups, and hence all cohomology groups, are zero by convention. This
definition is valid without finite-dimensionality or a characteristic
restriction.
$$H^0(\mathfrak g,M)=M^{\mathfrak g}=\{m\in M:xm=0\text{ for every }x\in\mathfrak g\}.$$

For finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$ and a short exact sequence
$0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$ of $\mathfrak g$-modules, the induced CE
complexes form a degreewise short exact sequence and yield the natural long
exact sequence

$$\cdots\to H^n(\mathfrak g,M')\to H^n(\mathfrak g,M)\to H^n(\mathfrak g,M'')\to H^{n+1}(\mathfrak g,M')\to\cdots.$$

Keep the type-A pyramid data
$(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak p,\mathfrak h,\mathfrak m,e,\chi)$ of
[[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]], with
$\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$, transpose
$q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, and $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$ on $\mathfrak m$.
Let $\eta\colon U(\mathfrak p)\to U(\mathfrak p)$ be the algebra automorphism
with
$$\eta(e_{i,j})=e_{i,j}+\delta_{i,j}\bigl(n-q_{\mathrm{col}(j)}-q_{\mathrm{col}(j)+1}-\cdots-q_l\bigr)$$
for all matrix units $e_{i,j}\in\mathfrak p$. Let $I_\chi$ be the kernel of the
algebra homomorphism $\chi\colon U(\mathfrak m)\to\mathbb C$ extending the Lie
character $\chi$, that is, the two-sided ideal generated by $x-\chi(x)$,
$x\in\mathfrak m$ ([[def-universal-enveloping-algebra]],
[[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]),
and let $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ be the left ideal it generates in
$U(\mathfrak g)$.

The **type-A finite W-algebra** is
$$W(\lambda)=\{u\in U(\mathfrak p):[x,\eta(u)]\in U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi\ \text{for all }x\in\mathfrak m\}.$$
It is a subalgebra of $U(\mathfrak p)$, and
$Q_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ is a
$(U(\mathfrak g),W(\lambda))$-bimodule with right action
$\bar v\cdot u=\overline{v\,\eta(u)}$. This is a module quotient by a left ideal; no quotient-ring multiplication is imposed.

The **Whittaker category** $\mathcal C(\lambda)$ is the category of
$\mathfrak g$-modules on which $x-\chi(x)$ acts locally nilpotently for every
$x\in\mathfrak m$ ([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). For
$M\in\mathcal C(\lambda)$ the **Whittaker vectors**
$$\mathrm{Wh}(M)=\{v\in M:xv=\chi(x)v\ \text{for all }x\in\mathfrak m\}$$
form a $W(\lambda)$-module with $u\cdot v=\eta(u)v$, and
$\mathrm{Wh}(M)=0$ implies $M=0$.

The verification below establishes the algebra and module structures just
stated. The associated graded of the loop filtration on $U(\mathfrak p)$ makes
$W(\lambda)$ a filtered deformation of $U(\mathfrak g^e)$; that statement is
proved later on this page
([[thm-the-loop-filtration-on-the-type-a-finite-w-algebra-has-associated-graded-u-of-g-e]]),
and the filtration used is the loop (good) filtration, not the Kazhdan
filtration.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a Lie algebra over $k$. In $T(\mathfrak g)$, regard
$[x,y]\in\mathfrak g$ as an element of tensor degree one, and let $I$ be the
two-sided ideal generated by

$$x\otimes y-y\otimes x-[x,y]\qquad(x,y\in\mathfrak g).$$

The **universal enveloping algebra** is

$$U(\mathfrak g)=T(\mathfrak g)/I.$$

Write

$$\iota_{\mathfrak g}:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow U(\mathfrak g)$$

for the composite of the degree-one inclusion with the quotient map. This
definition makes $U(\mathfrak g)$ a unital associative algebra and $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ a
linear map. It does not assert that $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ is injective; that conclusion will
come from PBW.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]) and let $I$ be a set.
The set $R[x_i:i\in I]$ consists of the functions

$$c:\mathcal M(I)\longrightarrow R$$

with finite support, where $\mathcal M(I)$ is the monoid of
[[def-monomials-on-an-index-set]]. We write such a function as the formal sum
$\sum_a c_a x^a$. Addition is pointwise. Multiplication is the convolution

$$(cd)_u:=\sum_{a+b=u}c_a d_b,$$

where only pairs in $\operatorname{supp}(c)\times\operatorname{supp}(d)$
contribute and the sum is the finite sum of
[[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]. The constant $r\in R$ is the
coefficient family supported at the zero monomial with value $r$, and the
indeterminate $x_i$ is supported at the exponent family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere.

The convolution is well defined and these operations make the displayed set a
commutative ring by [[thm-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-is-a-commutative-ring]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: **Positive-weight transverse product.** Choose the usual rowwise $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ triple. On $\operatorname{Hom}(R_b,R_a)$ the strings have highest $h$-weight $p_a+p_b-2k$, $1\le k\le\min(p_a,p_b)$. Since the pyramid grading element differs from $h$ by row scalars, their highest and lowest grading weights are $2(p_b-k)\ge0$ and $-2(p_a-k)\le0$. Thus the negative-degree part is injected by $\operatorname{ad}e$ and gives the direct-sum complement of [F1]. The differential of $\alpha(u,z)=uzu^{-1}$ at $(1,e)$ is $(x,y)\mapsto[x,e]+y$, an isomorphism. Use weight $-H$ on $\mathfrak m$ and weight $2-H$ on the translated slice and target coordinates; these are positive. In homogeneous coordinates of increasing weight, each component of $\alpha$ is an invertible linear block in the variables of that weight plus a polynomial in lower-weight variables. Successive substitution constructs its polynomial inverse. In particular derivative invertibility alone is not being used as a global inverse theorem.

**Detection.** The shifted operators $x-\chi(x)$ form a representation of the nilpotent Lie algebra $\mathfrak m$, because $\chi$ kills brackets. A nonzero central element has a nonzero kernel on any nonzero locally nilpotent module: apply its largest nonvanishing power to a nonzero vector. That kernel is stable, and the quotient Lie algebra acts on it with the same local nilpotence. Induction on $\dim\mathfrak m$ therefore gives a common nonzero invariant. The case $\mathfrak m=0$ is immediate.

**The actual graded complex.** PBW and [F3] give $\operatorname{gr}Q_\chi=\mathbb C[e+\mathfrak m^\perp]$, with no additional symbol factor. Step 1.1 identifies this with $\mathbb C[M_{\mathrm{unip}}]\otimes\mathbb C[S]$. Infinitesimal conjugation acts by invariant vector fields on the first factor and trivially on the slice factor. Giving the exterior dual of a grading-degree $-2r$ vector weight $2r$ makes the twisted Chevalley–Eilenberg differential filtration preserving. Its graded complex is the polynomial de Rham complex of $M_{\mathrm{unip}}$, tensored with $\mathbb C[S]$: invariant vector fields trivialize the tangent bundle and the bracket terms are precisely the de Rham differential. Polynomial exponential coordinates identify this unipotent group with affine space. On a polynomial form of positive total degree $t$, $t^{-1}\iota_{\mathrm{Euler}}$ is a contracting homotopy; constants are the only surviving degree-zero classes.

**Filtered lifting and right freeness.** A positive-degree cocycle in the actual complex has a graded leading term which is a boundary by step 2.1. Lift that boundary and subtract it, strictly lowering the integer filtration degree; boundedness below terminates this process. The same procedure lifts every graded invariant, using vanishing of graded degree-one cohomology to remove its differential. Hence $H^{>0}(\mathfrak m,Q_\chi)=0$ and $\operatorname{gr}W=\mathbb C[S]$, since $H^0(\mathfrak m,Q_\chi)=W$ by the defining invariant realization. Using the fixed PBW vector-space identification $U(\mathfrak p)\to Q_\chi$, take homogeneous coordinate representatives in $U(\mathfrak p)$ and form their ordered products there before projecting to $Q_\chi$. This never multiplies abstract classes in a left-ideal quotient. Their projected ordered monomials, acted on by the right $W$ bimodule action, span $Q_\chi$ by finite descending leading-term subtraction. A finite relation among them would give a relation between distinct monomials over $\operatorname{gr}W$; independence of polynomial monomials rules this out. Thus $Q_\chi$ is right $W$-free. All statements include the independent scalar coordinate of $\mathfrak{gl}_N$.

**Transfer to every module without graded-flatness assumptions.** The finite augmented cochain complex $0\to W\to C^0\to\cdots\to C^{\dim\mathfrak m}\to0$, where $C^j=Q_\chi\otimes\bigwedge^j\mathfrak m^*$, is exact by step 3.1 and is a complex of right $W$-modules. Its differentials are right $W$-linear because the right action commutes with the twisted left $\mathfrak m$ action. Each term is right $W$-free. Starting at the last term, split each surjection onto the already-projective boundary module; descending induction makes every boundary projective and splits every short exact sequence, including $W\hookrightarrow C^0$. These splittings supply a right $W$-linear contraction of the augmented complex. Tensor the contraction with an arbitrary left $W$-module $X$. This remains a contraction, and the resulting complex is exactly the twisted Chevalley–Eilenberg complex of $Q_\chi\otimes_W X$. Consequently its positive cohomology vanishes and its degree-zero cohomology is $X$ via $x\mapsto1_\chi\otimes x$. No filtration or flatness of $X$ is assumed. The splittings use exactly [F4].

The preceding steps prove the three assertions with the doubled even grading. In particular there is no degree $-1$ symplectic or Clifford contribution. If $e=0$, then $\mathfrak m=0$ and the product, augmentation and all cohomology identities reduce to their degree-zero identities.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $e$ be a nilpotent endomorphism of a
finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$ ([[def-nilpotent-endomorphism]]),
let $X=\overline{\mathrm{GL}(V)\cdot e}$ be the closure in
$\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ of its conjugacy orbit
([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]), and let
$\partial X=X\setminus\mathrm{GL}(V)\cdot e$. Then $\mathbb C[X]$ is a reduced
irreducible normal domain and $\operatorname{codim}_X\partial X\ge2$. This
holds for every Jordan type, not only the regular nilpotent cone.

The proof uses the *chain schemes*: if the Jordan partition of $e$ has column
lengths $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_t>0$, put $n_i=q_t+\cdots+q_{t-i+1}$ and
$U_i=\mathbb C^{n_i}$ for $0\le i\le t$. Let $M=\prod_{i=1}^{t-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Hom}(U_i,U_{i+1})\times\operatorname{Hom}(U_{i+1},U_i)\bigr)$
with coordinates $(A_i,B_i)$ and let $Z\subseteq M$ be the closed subscheme
$B_1A_1=0$, $B_iA_i=A_{i-1}B_{i-1}$ $(2\le i<t)$. Then $Z$ is a complete
intersection, smooth outside a closed subset of codimension $\ge2$, reduced,
irreducible and normal, and the invariant ring $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ under
$H=\prod_{i<t}\mathrm{GL}(U_i)$ is the coordinate ring of $X$ via the end map
$\theta=A_{t-1}B_{t-1}$ when $t\ge2$. For the empty Jordan diagram ($V=0$,
$t=0$) and the single-column diagram ($e=0$, $t=1$), the chain has no
variables or equations: take $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$, $H$ trivial
and $\theta=0$; the equation list above is imposed only on existing links.
In these cases $X$ is a point, its boundary is empty, and its boundary
codimension is $+\infty$.

An endomorphism $N:V\to V$ is **nilpotent** if $N^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$. Its **nilpotency index** is the least positive integer $r$ such that $N^r=0$; this least exponent exists by the well-ordering principle ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

The unique endomorphism of the zero space is nilpotent. With the same least-positive-exponent convention, its nilpotency index is $1$ because its identity and zero endomorphisms coincide.

Every nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ has an ordered basis that is the concatenation of Jordan strings for $N$ at $0$. For $V=0$, this is the empty basis and the empty family of strings.
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every commutative Noetherian integrally closed domain satisfies $(S_2)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring and let $M\ne0$ be a finite
$R$-module. Then
$$\operatorname{depth}(M)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathfrak m\in\operatorname{Ass}_R(M).$$

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, let $M$ be a finitely generated left
$R$-module, and let $S \subseteq R$ be multiplicative. Then
$$ \operatorname{Ass}_{S^{-1}R}(S^{-1}M)=\{S^{-1}\mathfrak p : \mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass}_R(M),\ \mathfrak p \cap S=\varnothing\}. $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $R$ be Noetherian, let $M$ be finite, let $I$ lie in the Jacobson radical,
and let $x\in I$ be $M$-regular. Then
$$\operatorname{depth}_I(M/xM)=\operatorname{depth}_I(M)-1,$$
with $\infty-1=\infty$.

Assume Dependent Choice. Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring and let $M$ be a left $R$-module. Then
the set of zero divisors on $M$ is
$$ \bigcup_{\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass}_R(M)}\mathfrak p. $$
If the Axiom of Choice also holds and $M$ is finitely generated, this is a finite union.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $I \trianglelefteq R$ be an ideal, and let
$\mathfrak p_1,\dots,\mathfrak p_n$ be prime ideals with $n \ge 1$. If
$$ I\subseteq \mathfrak p_1\cup\cdots\cup \mathfrak p_n, $$
then $I\subseteq \mathfrak p_i$ for some $i$.

Every finite-dimensional representation of a finite-dimensional semisimple
Lie algebra over any characteristic-zero field is completely reducible.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, let $n\ge0$, and let
$E:=V^{\otimes n}$ carry the left place action of $S_n$
([[def-commuting-symmetric-and-linear-actions-on-tensor-power]]). Let $A$ be
the image of the algebra homomorphism $\mathbb C[S_n]\to\operatorname{End}(E)$
extending the place action, and let
$B:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{g^{\otimes n}:g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)\}$
be the linear span of the diagonal operators
$g^{\otimes n}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=gv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_n$.
Then:

1. **(Mutual centralizers.)** $B=\{F\in\operatorname{End}(E):F a=aF\text{ for
   all }a\in A\}$ and $A=\{F\in\operatorname{End}(E):F b=bF\text{ for all
   }b\in B\}$.
2. **(Uniqueness of the identification.)** $B$ is a unital
   $\mathbb C$-subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}(E)$ and equals the image of
   the diagonal action of the universal enveloping algebra
   $U(\mathfrak{gl}(V))$, that is the unital subalgebra generated by the
   operators $\Delta(T)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes T\otimes
   \mathbf 1^{\otimes(n-i)}$, $T\in\operatorname{End}(V)$
   ([[lem-tensor-place-operators-span-the-symmetric-centralizer]]).

All statements include $n=0$, where $E=\mathbb C$.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.

derivations.claim: **The zero-dimensional case.** If $V=0$, its orbit closure is a point and its boundary is empty by [F1]. For $d=0$, $V^{\otimes d}=\mathbb C$ and every fixed operator is a scalar, extended by the constant polynomial map; the empty permutation and empty tensor product give the asserted normal form. For $d>0$, $V^{\otimes d}=0$ and its endomorphism space has only the zero operator, extended by the zero map; the normal form is the empty sum. Thus both assertions hold without a largest Jordan block. Henceforth $V\ne0$, so its largest block length $l$ exists.

Hartogs lifting. Let $A=\mathbb C[X]$ and let $f\in\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ be regular on $O$, hence regular off a closed subset of $X\setminus O$; since $\partial X$ has codimension $\ge2$ in $X$ by the normality lemma [F1], $f$ is regular in codimension $1$ and therefore extends to $A$ by [F2]. Applying this coordinatewise to maps into a finite-dimensional vector space shows that every regular map $O\to W$ into a finite-dimensional vector space extends uniquely to a regular map $X\to W$.

The equivariant map on $O$. Fix $B\in\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})^{G_e}$ and define, for $g\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, $F(g\,e\,g^{-1}):=(g^{\otimes d})\,B\,(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}\in\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$. This is well defined: if $g_1e g_1^{-1}=g_2eg_2^{-1}$, then $g_2^{-1}g_1\in G_e$, so $(g_2^{-1}g_1)^{\otimes d}B(g_2^{-1}g_1)^{-\otimes d}=B$ by $G_e$-invariance, which rearranges to $(g_1^{\otimes d})B(g_1^{-1})^{\otimes d}=(g_2^{\otimes d})B(g_2^{-1})^{\otimes d}$. The map $F$ is $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant by construction: $F(hXh^{-1})=(h^{\otimes d})F(X)(h^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ for $X\in O$.

Regularity of $F$ on $O$. The ranks of $X^0,X^1,\dots,X^{l-1}$ are constant on $O$. Cover $O$ by open charts where fixed minors used to select bases of the kernels and images, their quotient complements and Jordan top vectors are nonzero. Gaussian elimination on such a chart gives a Jordan basis for $X$ with entries regular in $X$. Let $g(X)$ carry a fixed Jordan basis for $e$ to this chosen Jordan basis for $X$, with the same ordered string lengths. Then $g(X)e g(X)^{-1}=X$. Restricting to the open chart where the Jordan-basis determinant is nonzero makes both $g(X)$ and $g(X)^{-1}$ regular, since their entries have only the fixed nonvanishing minors and determinant as denominators. Thus $X\mapsto(g(X)^{\otimes d})B(g(X)^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ is the map of step 1.3 and is regular on each chart. These charts cover $O$; on overlaps $g_2(X)^{-1}g_1(X)\in G_e$, so the expressions agree by $G_e$-invariance of $B$. Hence $F$ is regular on $O$.

Extension to $X$. By steps 1.2 and 2.1 the map $F\colon O\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ is a regular equivariant map on the dense orbit; by step 1.2 it extends uniquely to a regular map $F\colon X\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$. Since $\mathbb C[X]=\mathbb C[\operatorname{End}(V)]/I(X)$ and $X$ is an affine closed subset of the affine space $\operatorname{End}(V)$, the coordinate functions of $F$ are restrictions of polynomial functions on $\operatorname{End}(V)$; fixing representatives gives a polynomial map $\Phi\colon\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ extending $F$.

Equivariance of $\Phi$. For fixed $g\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, both sides of $\Phi(gXg^{-1})=(g^{\otimes d})\Phi(X)(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ are polynomial maps in $X$; they agree on the dense orbit $O$ by step 1.3 and hence on all of $X$. Consequently the class of $\Phi$ in the finite-dimensional space of polynomial maps $\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ of degree at most $K$ (for $K$ at least the degree of $\Phi$), modulo the $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-stable subspace of maps vanishing on $X$, is invariant for the conjugation action. By the invariant-lifting property of complete reducibility [F3], this class has an invariant representative $\Phi'$ of degree at most $K$; then $\Phi'$ is a $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant polynomial map on $\operatorname{End}(V)$ agreeing with $F$ on $X$, and $\Phi'(e)=F(e)=B$ since $e\in O$, which is assertion (1).

Polarization. Write $\Phi=\sum_k\Phi_k$ for its homogeneous components of degree $k$; each $\Phi_k$ is equivariant. Fix $k$ and assume for the structure argument that $\Phi$ is homogeneous of degree $k$. Polarize the $k$ matrix variables $X_1,\dots,X_k$ of $\Phi$ and pair the output in $\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ with $d$ independent matrices $Y_1,\dots,Y_d$ using the nondegenerate trace pairing on each tensor factor; this produces a multilinear $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-invariant $P(X_1,\dots,X_k;Y_1,\dots,Y_d)\in\mathbb C$ in $(k+d)$ matrix arguments.

Tensor invariants are permutation contractions. By the Schur-Weyl description [F3], every multilinear invariant of the matrix arguments is a linear combination of contractions: each argument contributes one upper and one lower index, an invariant pairs each upper index with a lower index of another argument, and the invariant is a product over the cycles of the resulting permutation of traces of the corresponding cyclically ordered product of matrices.

Covariant normal form. Depolarize in the $k$ identical variables $X_i=X$ and read each contraction cycle. A cycle that uses only $X$-arguments contributes a scalar invariant polynomial in $X$; a cycle that uses some $Y$-arguments alternates blocks of $X$'s and single $Y$'s, so its trace is precisely the trace pairing of $Y_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Y_d$ with a place permutation of $X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d}$. By nondegeneracy of the trace pairing, the operator identity $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h(X)\,\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$ follows, with $h_i\ge0$, $\sigma_h$ a place permutation and $c_h$ a scalar invariant polynomial (a polynomial in the traces $\operatorname{tr}(X^m)$); summing over the homogeneous components gives assertion (2).

Evaluation at $e$. Since $e^l=0$ for the largest Jordan block length $l$ of $e$, evaluating the normal form at $X=e$ kills every term with some $h_i\ge l$; the surviving terms are place permutations applied to a tensor product of nonnegative powers $e^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e^{h_d}$ multiplied by the scalar invariants $c_h(e)$, which are complex constants; since $\operatorname{tr}(e^m)=0$ for every positive $m$, the scalar invariant polynomials satisfy $c_h(e)=c_h(0)$. This gives the concrete description of the $G_e$-fixed endomorphisms used by the double centralizer theorem.

Let $(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak p,\mathfrak h,\mathfrak m,e,\chi)$, $W(\lambda)$, $Q_\chi$ and $\mathcal C(\lambda)$ be as in [[def-the-type-a-finite-w-algebra-and-whittaker-category]].

The operators $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ commute with the $\mathfrak g$-action and are natural in $M$, and satisfy all the defining relations of the degenerate affine Hecke algebra [[def-degenerate-affine-hecke-algebra]]: the Coxeter relations for the $s_i$; $s_ix_j=x_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$; $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i+1$ and $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$; and the polynomial commutation $[x_i,x_j]=0$.

Every nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ has an ordered basis that is the concatenation of Jordan strings for $N$ at $0$. For $V=0$, this is the empty basis and the empty family of strings.

Work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ be a partition
of $N\ge0$ with transpose $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, where $l=p_n$ for a
nonempty row list and $l=0$ for an empty row list. Zero-length rows have no
boxes. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with matrix units
$e_{i,j}$ in the standard basis
$v_1,\dots,v_N$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]). Number the
boxes of the diagram of $\lambda$ by $1,\dots,N$ down columns from the left,
and for a box $i$ write $\mathrm{row}(i),\mathrm{col}(i)$ for its row and
column, $L(i)$ for the box immediately to its left (or $\emptyset$ if absent),
and $R(i)$ for the box immediately to its right (or $\emptyset$ if absent).
Define the nilpotent endomorphism
$$e=\sum_{i:\ L(i)\ne\emptyset}e_{L(i),i}\in\mathfrak g,\qquad ev_i=v_{L(i)},$$
and declare $\deg e_{i,j}=\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)$ for all $i,j$, so
that $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_r$ with
$\mathfrak g_r=\operatorname{span}\{e_{i,j}:\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)=r\}$.
Put
$$\mathfrak p=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r,\qquad \mathfrak h=\mathfrak g_0,\qquad \mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r,$$
and for rows $1\le i,j\le n$ define the shift $s_{i,j}=p_j-p_i$ if $i\le j$
and $s_{i,j}=0$ if $i\ge j$, together with the centralizer elements
$$e_{i,j;r}=\sum_{\substack{\mathrm{row}(h)=i,\ \mathrm{row}(k)=j\\ \mathrm{col}(k)-\mathrm{col}(h)=r}}e_{h,k} \qquad(s_{i,j}\le r<p_j).$$
Finally let $\chi\colon\mathfrak m\to\mathbb C$ be $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$,
where the trace is the trace of the $N\times N$ matrix.

The verification below records the properties of this data that are used
throughout this page. $e\in\mathfrak g_1$ has Jordan type $\lambda$; $\mathfrak p$
is a parabolic subalgebra with Levi factor
$\mathfrak h\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{q_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{q_l}$ and
nilradical $\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$, while $\mathfrak m$ is the
nilradical of the opposite parabolic; the elements $e_{i,j;r}$ with
$s_{i,j}\le r<p_j$ form a basis of the centralizer
$\mathfrak g^e=\{X\in\mathfrak g:[X,e]=0\}$; the box set
$J=\{(a,b)\in\{1,\dots,N\}^2:\mathrm{col}(a)\le\mathrm{col}(b),\ R(b)=\emptyset\}$
is in bijection with $K=\{(i,j,r):1\le i,j\le n,\ s_{i,j}\le r<p_j\}$ via
$(a,b)\mapsto(\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b),\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a))$, and
$$\xi_{a,b}:=\sum_{t=0}^{\mathrm{col}(a)-1}e_{L^t(a),L^t(b)}=e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)};$$
and $\chi$ is a Lie algebra character, $\chi([\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m])=0$. This
grading is the type-A pyramid good grading in the degree-one convention:
$\operatorname{ad}e:\mathfrak g_r\to\mathfrak g_{r+1}$ is injective for
$r<0$ and surjective for $r\ge0$. For $e\ne0$ it differs from the standard
Dynkin grading, in which $e$ has degree $2$ rather than $1$. For $e=0$ all
boxes lie in one column or there are no boxes, and the pyramid grading and
the trivial Dynkin grading both concentrate $\mathfrak g$ in degree zero.
If $N=0$, take $\mathfrak{gl}_0=0$: the box set and both centralizer index
sets are empty, $e=0$, $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak h=\mathfrak m=0$, and
$\chi=0$. These conventions also permit an empty row list.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_r$ be an ordered basis of a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Then the monomials

$$x_1^{a_1}x_2^{a_2}\cdots x_r^{a_r} \qquad (a_i\in \mathbb N_0)$$

form a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)$. In particular, multiplication identifies $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)$ with the symmetric algebra $S(\mathfrak g)$ on the symbols of the $x_i$.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a Lie algebra over $k$. In $T(\mathfrak g)$, regard
$[x,y]\in\mathfrak g$ as an element of tensor degree one, and let $I$ be the
two-sided ideal generated by

$$x\otimes y-y\otimes x-[x,y]\qquad(x,y\in\mathfrak g).$$

The **universal enveloping algebra** is

$$U(\mathfrak g)=T(\mathfrak g)/I.$$

Write

$$\iota_{\mathfrak g}:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow U(\mathfrak g)$$

for the composite of the degree-one inclusion with the quotient map. This
definition makes $U(\mathfrak g)$ a unital associative algebra and $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ a
linear map. It does not assert that $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ is injective; that conclusion will
come from PBW.

Keep the type-A pyramid data
$(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak p,\mathfrak h,\mathfrak m,e,\chi)$ of
[[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]], with
$\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$, transpose
$q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, and $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$ on $\mathfrak m$.
Let $\eta\colon U(\mathfrak p)\to U(\mathfrak p)$ be the algebra automorphism
with
$$\eta(e_{i,j})=e_{i,j}+\delta_{i,j}\bigl(n-q_{\mathrm{col}(j)}-q_{\mathrm{col}(j)+1}-\cdots-q_l\bigr)$$
for all matrix units $e_{i,j}\in\mathfrak p$. Let $I_\chi$ be the kernel of the
algebra homomorphism $\chi\colon U(\mathfrak m)\to\mathbb C$ extending the Lie
character $\chi$, that is, the two-sided ideal generated by $x-\chi(x)$,
$x\in\mathfrak m$ ([[def-universal-enveloping-algebra]],
[[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]),
and let $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ be the left ideal it generates in

The **type-A finite W-algebra** is
$$W(\lambda)=\{u\in U(\mathfrak p):[x,\eta(u)]\in U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi\ \text{for all }x\in\mathfrak m\}.$$
It is a subalgebra of $U(\mathfrak p)$, and
$Q_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ is a
$(U(\mathfrak g),W(\lambda))$-bimodule with right action
$\bar v\cdot u=\overline{v\,\eta(u)}$. This is a module quotient by a left ideal; no quotient-ring multiplication is imposed.

The **Whittaker category** $\mathcal C(\lambda)$ is the category of
$\mathfrak g$-modules on which $x-\chi(x)$ acts locally nilpotently for every

$$\mathrm{Wh}(M)=\{v\in M:xv=\chi(x)v\ \text{for all }x\in\mathfrak m\}$$
form a $W(\lambda)$-module with $u\cdot v=\eta(u)v$, and
$\mathrm{Wh}(M)=0$ implies $M=0$.

the image of the algebra homomorphism $\mathbb C[S_n]\to\operatorname{End}(E)$
extending the place action, and let
$B:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{g^{\otimes n}:g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)\}$
be the linear span of the diagonal operators
$g^{\otimes n}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=gv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_n$.
Then:

1. **(Mutual centralizers.)** $B=\{F\in\operatorname{End}(E):F a=aF\text{ for
   all }a\in A\}$ and $A=\{F\in\operatorname{End}(E):F b=bF\text{ for all
   }b\in B\}$.
2. **(Uniqueness of the identification.)** $B$ is a unital
   $\mathbb C$-subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}(E)$ and equals the image of
   the diagonal action of the universal enveloping algebra
   $U(\mathfrak{gl}(V))$, that is the unital subalgebra generated by the
   operators $\Delta(T)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes T\otimes
   \mathbf 1^{\otimes(n-i)}$, $T\in\operatorname{End}(V)$
   ([[lem-tensor-place-operators-span-the-symmetric-centralizer]]).

All statements include $n=0$, where $E=\mathbb C$.

derivations.claim: **Empty chains.** If $V=0$, take $t=0$; if $e=0$ on a nonzero space, its Jordan diagram has a single column and $t=1$. In either case there are no chain variables or equations, $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$, $H$ is trivial and $\theta=0$. Its image is the point orbit closure, its coordinate ring is a normal domain, and the empty equation sequence is regular. The boundary is empty and has codimension $+\infty$. All conclusions follow in these cases. Henceforth $t\ge2$.

**The open chain locus.** Put $c=\sum_{i<t}n_i^2$ and $D=2\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}-c$. The differential of the chain equations is $Y_iA_i+B_iX_i-X_{i-1}B_{i-1}-A_{i-1}Y_{i-1}$, with the index-zero terms zero. If each $A_i$ is injective or $B_i$ is surjective, these equations can be solved successively for any prescribed right-hand sides: use a left inverse of $A_i$ to choose $Y_i$, or a right inverse of $B_i$ to choose $X_i$, after the preceding pair is fixed. Thus the open locus $Z^\circ$ with this condition is smooth of dimension $D$ by [F4]. It is nonempty: use $U_i=\operatorname{im}e^{t-i}$, inclusions $A_i$, and restrictions $B_i=e|_{U_{i+1}}$, transported to the fixed spaces. These maps satisfy the equations and have end map $e$.

**Alternating strings and their stabilizers.** For a nilpotent pair $A:U\to W$, $B:W\to U$, the odd operator $T$ on $U\oplus W$ with these components has a homogeneous Jordan-string decomposition: kernels and images of its powers are graded, so the complements in the Jordan construction may be chosen homogeneous. Every string alternates letters $a$ from $U$ and $b$ from $W$. Removing all $b$ letters gives the Jordan rows of $BA$, and removing all $a$ letters gives those of $AB$. The ranks of alternating composites recover the numbers of strings of each length and starting letter, so a diagram determines one pair orbit and there are finitely many diagrams in fixed dimensions. The pair stabilizer is the unit group of its even endomorphism algebra, an open subset of a vector space and hence smooth and irreducible. On a string $A$ kills exactly a terminal $a$ and $B$ misses exactly an initial $a$; consequently $A$ is injective iff every string ends in $b$, and $B$ is surjective iff every string begins in $b$.

**Even orbit drops.** Distinct dominated types have strictly smaller orbit dimension. One can move from a dominating partition to a dominated one by repeatedly moving a box from an earlier row to a later allowable row: choose an excess row and a subsequent deficit row, taking the last row of the source plateau and the first allowed destination to preserve the partition inequalities, and repeat until the target is reached. A move from row $i$ to row $j>i$ increases $\sum_r(2r-1)\mu_r$ by $2(j-i)$ and therefore decreases the orbit dimension by that positive even number. Each allowable unit move from row lengths $a,b$ with $a\ge b+2$ is realized by a one-parameter degeneration. On chains $u_1,\ldots,u_{a-1}$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_{b+1}$ of the destination type, keep the usual lowering maps except send $v_{b+1}$ to $v_b+z u_{a-1}$, with $v_0=0$. At $z=0$ the type is $(a-1,b+1)$; for $z\ne0$ the ranks of powers are those of $(a,b)$ (the chain generated by $v_{b+1}$ has length $a$, and the remaining chain has length $b$). Keeping other strings fixed proves that dominated types belong to the top orbit closure. Hence a drop of exactly two consists of one box moved to the next row; any other drop is at least four. Equivalently, parity also follows from $\sum_j(\mu'_j)^2\equiv\sum_j\mu'_j=N\pmod2$ for the total sum; individual summands in a difference of square sums need not be even.

**The pair-orbit dimension.** Write $m=\dim U$, $n=\dim W$, and let $E,O$ be the dimensions of the even and odd centralizers of $T$. A homomorphism between Jordan strings of lengths $L,L'$ has $\min(L,L')$ possible shifts. Counting the parity of those shifts, odd strings of the same endpoint type contribute $+1$ to the even-minus-odd count, and odd strings of opposite type contribute $-1$; the two opposite Hom directions for an odd/even pair cancel, and even/even pairs contribute zero. Summing gives $E-O=(m-n)^2$, because the difference between the numbers of odd $a$-type and odd $b$-type strings is $m-n$. The pair orbit therefore has dimension $m^2+n^2-E=\tfrac12((m+n)^2-E-O)$, half the dimension of the ordinary orbit of $T$. If a string has $r_j$ letters $a$ and $s_j$ letters $b$, then $\min(r_j+s_j,r_k+s_k)=\min(r_j,r_k)+\min(s_j,s_k)$ except for equal odd lengths with opposite endpoint types, where the left side is larger by one. Let $a_l,b_l$ count the odd strings of length $l$ beginning with the two respective letters, and put $\Delta=\sum_{l\text{ odd}}a_lb_l$. The ordinary Jordan centralizer counts now give $\dim O_{(A,B)}=mn+\tfrac12(\dim C_{BA}+\dim C_{AB})-\Delta$. This is a dimension identity for the orbit, not for the full matrix space minus the pair orbit.

**Chain strata.** Stratify $Z$ by its compatible alternating-string diagrams at every link. Compatibility means that the $b$-diagram of one link equals the $a$-diagram of the next. These are finitely many locally closed strata. Pair-orbit projections to either ordinary Jordan orbit are smooth homogeneous fibrations: their fibers are quotients of the ordinary centralizer unit group by the pair stabilizer. Both groups are smooth connected open subsets of finite-dimensional endomorphism spaces, so these fibers are irreducible. Iterating these fibrations proves each nonempty chain stratum $Z_\delta$ smooth and irreducible. The dimension at each fiber-product step is the preceding dimension plus the pair-orbit dimension minus the shared Jordan-orbit dimension. The intermediate orbit dimensions cancel in the formula of step 2.1, giving $\dim Z_\delta=\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12\dim C_\sigma-\sum_{i<t}\Delta_i$, where $\sigma$ is the type of its final end map.

**Dominance and the top stratum.** The chain equations make $\theta^k$ factor through $U_{t-k}$, so $\operatorname{rank}\theta^k\le n_{t-k}$ and $\theta^t=0$. Thus its type $\sigma$ is dominated by $\eta$ by [F3]. For a $b$-diagram $\sigma$, every row must first be filled internally by alternating $a$ letters; this requires exactly $|\sigma|-\ell(\sigma)$ letters, the size of the diagram obtained by deleting its first column. Over the top diagram $\eta$, this equals $n_{t-1}$, leaving no extra letters: every string starts and ends in $b$ and the lower diagram is exactly the first-column deletion of $\eta$. Repeat down the chain. There is exactly one top stratum; it has both maximal-rank maps at every link, lies in $Z^\circ$, and has every $\Delta_i=0$. Finally, expanding $q_j=n_{t-j+1}-n_{t-j}$ gives $\tfrac12\dim C_\eta=\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}-\sum_{i<t}n_i^2$, so its dimension is $D$.

**Drops of at least four.** By the stratum formula and the nonnegativity of all $\Delta_i$, a final orbit drop of at least four gives $\dim Z_\delta\le\sum n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12(\dim C_\eta-4)=D-2$. Every non-top stratum has dimension at most $D-1$. This latter estimate establishes uniqueness of the dense top stratum but does not assert that every non-top stratum has codimension two: some are smooth divisors inside $Z^\circ$.

**Drops of two and the nonsmooth-locus bound.** Suppose $\sigma$ is obtained from $\eta$ by moving a box to the next row. Let $\eta'$ and $\sigma'$ denote first-column deletions and let $m=|\eta'|$, $m'=|\sigma'|$. At the last link the available number of $a$ letters is $m$ and its $a$-diagram must be dominated by $\eta'$, since its powers factor through the shorter chain. If the receiving row was nonempty, $m=m'$: internal filling consumes every $a$, all strings begin and end in $b$, and the same next-row degeneration passes to the shorter chain. If a new singleton row is created, $m=m'+1$. After internal filling there is one extra $a$. It can be attached at either end of the shortened last row, at either end of the new singleton $b$ row, or placed in a new singleton $a$ row. No earlier row can receive it: its $a$-diagram would gain a box earlier than the removed last-row box and violate dominance by $\eta'$. In the first four placements one map is maximal rank; the lower diagram is either $\eta'$ or its next-row degeneration. In the fifth placement both maps fail maximal rank, and singleton strings of both types occur, giving $\Delta_i\ge1$. This remains valid when the shortened row is itself a singleton, when there can be more than one singleton $b$. Inducting through the shorter chain shows that either every link has a maximal-rank map and $Z_\delta\subseteq Z^\circ$, or some $\Delta_i\ge1$. In the latter case the dimension formula gives $\dim Z_\delta\le\sum n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12(\dim C_\eta-2)-1=D-2$. Together with step 5.1, this proves $\dim(Z\setminus Z^\circ)\le D-2$.

**Complete intersection and reducedness.** Every irreducible component of the scheme cut out by its $c$ equations has dimension at least $\dim M-c=D$ by [F4]. The top stratum has dimension $D$ and all other strata have smaller dimension by step 5.1, so every component has dimension $D$. Thus the equation ideal has height $c$. Its homogeneous generators form a regular sequence in the polynomial ring: at the homogeneous maximal ideal, every prefix of length $k$ has height at least $k$, since adjoining the remaining $c-k$ equations raises height by at most $c-k$; the opposite inequality is Krull's bound. Complete the generators to a system of parameters and apply the Cohen-Macaulay parameter theorem in [F4]. Homogeneous localization detects a kernel in a multiplication map, so regularity is global. The quotient is Cohen-Macaulay, hence satisfies $S_1$ and $S_2$. Every component meets the smooth open $Z^\circ$ by step 6.1, so it satisfies $R_0$; [F5] implies reducedness.

**Irreducibility and normality of the chain.** The unique top stratum is irreducible. Its closure contains every component: otherwise a component of dimension $D$ would have a nonempty open subset outside that closure, contained in a finite union of strata of dimensions at most $D-1$, which is impossible. Thus the reduced chain ring is a domain. Its singular locus is contained in $Z\setminus Z^\circ$, of codimension at least two by step 6.1, so it satisfies $R_1$; it satisfies $S_2$ by step 7.1. Serre's criterion [F5] gives normality.

**The invariant quotient.** For one pair $A:U\to W$, $B:W\to U$, invariants under $\mathrm{GL}(U)$ are generated by entries of $AB$: the scalar matrices force equal polynomial degrees in $A,B$, polarization turns a bihomogeneous invariant into a mixed tensor invariant, and [F6] expresses it as permutation contractions. Each contraction is a product of entries of $AB$, with possible cyclic traces also polynomials in those entries. For rational finite-dimensional $\mathrm{GL}(U)$ modules, the central scalar torus splits the space into integer weight spaces. On each weight space apply the semisimple Lie algebra complete-reducibility theorem [F6] to $\mathfrak{sl}(U)$; an invariant complement then respects the center as well. It respects the group because elementary unipotents and diagonal matrices generate $\mathrm{GL}(U)$. Thus rational quotient invariants lift by complete reducibility in bounded polynomial degree, so the same description applies to a stable closed subscheme with its induced relations. Eliminate vertices in order. At the first vertex the invariant generators are $A_1B_1$ and the remaining variables; the chain equation replaces $A_1B_1$ by $B_2A_2$. The quotient is consequently the graph over the remaining variables with the induced rank and nilpotency relations, and eliminating the next vertex applies the same one-pair calculation. Repeating leaves precisely the entries of $\theta$. Thus $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ is generated by those entries, and is the coordinate ring of the closure of $\theta(Z)$. The rank bounds of step 4.1 put the image in the orbit closure of $e$, while the inclusion/restriction construction of step 1.2, applied to every conjugate of $e$, puts its full orbit in the image. Hence that closure is $X$ and $\mathbb C[Z]^H\cong\mathbb C[X]$.

**Normality and boundary of the orbit closure.** An element of $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb C[Z]^H)$ integral over $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ is also integral over the normal domain $\mathbb C[Z]$, hence belongs to it. Being a fraction of invariant elements it is fixed by $H$, so it belongs to $\mathbb C[Z]^H$; no equality between the full invariant fraction field and the fraction field of the invariant ring is needed. Therefore $\mathbb C[X]$ is a normal domain, reduced and irreducible. The finitely many boundary nilpotent orbits have positive even dimension drops by step 1.4, so their union has codimension at least two. The point cases and their empty boundary were proved in step 1.1. This proves all chain and orbit conclusions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and work with the finite
classical $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ tableau blocks of
[[def-integral-parabolic-category-o-block-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]],
and with the general translation machinery of
[[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]] and
[[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]].

Let $V$ be the natural $\mathfrak{gl}_n$-module and $V^{*}$ its dual. For a
residue $i$ define the **residue translation functor** $f_i$ on
$\mathcal O^\Lambda$ by tensoring with $V$ and projecting onto the entry-multiset
central character in which exactly one entry $i$ is replaced by $i+1$; define
$e_i$ by tensoring with $V^{*}$ and the reverse character change ($i+1\mapsto i$,
with the signs of the natural form). Concretely, on a block
$\mathcal O^\Lambda_\alpha$ the functor is the exact block projection
$\operatorname{pr}_{\alpha+\alpha_i}(-\otimes V)$ for $f_i$ and
$\operatorname{pr}_{\alpha-\alpha_i}(-\otimes V^{*})$ for $e_i$, where
$\alpha_i$ is the Fock root label of the dictionary item
([[def-the-fock-convention-dictionary-for-finite-type-a-quantum-modules]]).

On the direct sum $\mathcal O^\Lambda$ of the blocks these functors are exact
and biadjoint, preserve projective and injective objects, and commute with the
restricted transpose duality
([[prop-restricted-duality-is-an-exact-involution-on-category-o]]).
Equivalently, $f_i$ is the generalized $i$-eigencomponent of the tensor
Casimir (including the place factors), and $e_i$ is the generalized
$-n-i$-eigencomponent on the dual tensor product.

The functors are **special residue translations**, not automatically ordinary
regular-wall translations; the Fock root label shifts by $\pm\alpha_i$, and
that label is not the classical $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ highest weight.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and work with the finite
classical $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ category $\mathcal O$ of
[[def-integral-parabolic-category-o-block-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]],
distinct from the Fock algebra $\mathfrak{gl}_{I^+}$.

Let $x_j$ be the tensor Casimir acting on the $j$-th natural factor of
$M\otimes V^{\otimes r}$ together with all preceding factors, and let $T_j$ be
the adjacent place swap. Then the **degenerate affine Hecke relations** hold:
the $x_j$ commute, the $T_j$ satisfy the symmetric-group braid and quadratic
relations, $T_jx_j-x_{j+1}T_j=-1$, and distant generators commute. They restrict
naturally to the repeated residue functors $f_i^r$ of
[[def-residue-translation-functors-on-the-sum-of-parabolic-o-blocks]], where
$x_j-i$ is locally nilpotent; the dual actions are the biadjoint mates on
$e_i^r$. Finite Levi tensor decomposition and exact PBW induction give
multiplicity-free generalized-standard flags for the entry moves $i\to i+1$ and
$i+1\to i$.

The standard-class map $[\Delta(A)]\mapsto M_A$ gives the full integral Fock
$K_0$ action, its Chevalley/Serre relations and local integrability; each root's
biadjoint functors therefore give a positive, locally finite
$\mathfrak{sl}_2$ action on the simple-class basis. The ground-state class
generates the highest constituent, not generally the entire tensor Fock module.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The exact residue
functors of
[[def-residue-translation-functors-on-the-sum-of-parabolic-o-blocks]] on the
genuine finite-$n$ parabolic blocks have multiplicity-free
generalized-standard flags given by the valid single-entry moves $i\to i+1$ and
$i+1\to i$.

(1) Their $K_0$ operators are the full integrable $\mathfrak{gl}_{I^+}$ Fock
Chevalley action, satisfying the integral Chevalley/Serre relations on the
standard basis.

(2) For each simple $L(A)$, a residue translate vanishes exactly when the
corresponding crystal edge is absent; otherwise it is a self-dual
indecomposable with simple equal head and socle $L(\tilde f_iA)$, respectively
$L(\tilde e_iA)$.

(3) The full tensor Fock module is represented by all standard classes; the
ground-state class, with
$M(A_\Lambda)=L(A_\Lambda)=P(A_\Lambda)$, generates only its multiplicity-one
highest constituent.

No action on labels alone proves the $K_0$ relations or the head/socle
statement.

Assume inherited AC [[def-axiom-of-choice]] for the invoked cyclotomic PBW supplier. Fix a multiset of complex roots $\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_l)$ with $l\ge1$, allowing repeated roots. Write $B=H_d(\mathbf a)$ and $A=H_{d+1}(\mathbf a)$ for [[def-degenerate-cyclotomic-hecke-algebra]]. The generator-preserving tower map embeds $B$ in $A$.

For every generalized eigenvalue $i$ of $x_{d+1}$ in the regular representation of $A$, let $u_i\in\mathbb C[x_{d+1}]$ be its polynomial generalized-eigenspace projector. All such eigenvalues lie in $\bigcup_j(a_j+\mathbb Z)$. These are additive residue chains, separately indexed in each coset of $\mathbb C/\mathbb Z$; coincident roots do not give extra projectors. The $u_i$ are mutually orthogonal, sum to one, commute with $B$ and satisfy $u_i^*=u_i$. They need not be central in $A$.

For finite-dimensional left modules define the residue functors
$$e_i(M)=u_iM,\qquad f_i(N)=Au_i\otimes_BN.$$
Here the first functor takes its $B$-action from the tower inclusion and the second takes its $A$-action from the first factor. They are exact and biadjoint and commute naturally with the generator-fixing $*$-duality. Consequently they preserve projectives and induce adjoint operators for the projective/module Hom pairing. Projecting further by source and target content idempotents gives the supported-block functors. Neither primitivity of a central content projector nor equality $B=u_iAu_i$ is needed or asserted here. Actual image towers in admissible stable realizations use the compatible projected tensor actions of [[def-stable-range-and-block-idempotent-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]].

For level zero use $H_0(\varnothing)=\mathbb C$ and $H_d(\varnothing)=0$ for $d>0$. The map $H_0\to H_1$ is the zero homomorphism $\mathbb C\to0$, so it is not an embedding. Every positive-degree residue induction and restriction functor is zero; all biadjunction and exactness assertions then hold for zero functors.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For admissible origins $c$ the genuine Whittaker functor $V$ of
[[def-the-whittaker-functor-from-the-relevant-parabolic-o-summand]] is exact
on $\mathcal O_c^d$, and
$$\gamma\colon\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(T,-)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{W}(V_c^{\otimes d},V(-))$$
is a natural isomorphism, where $T=P_c\otimes V^{\otimes d}$. Both $V$ and the
Hecke quotient $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(T,-)$ are fully faithful on
all projective objects of the relevant summand, and the quotient is also fully
faithful on tiltings. $T$ is a self-dual prinjective detecting object
containing all standard-labelled projective-injective covers, each individually self-dual, but it need not be a
generator of the entire category-$\mathcal O$ summand. $V(T)=V_c^{\otimes d}$
is a projective generator of $W_d$-mod, and $V$ preserves projectivity on
$\operatorname{add}(T)$; it need not send every projective of $\mathcal O$ to
a projective $W$-module. The composite of $V$ with the Morita equivalence is
the Serre quotient killing exactly the off-standard simples.

Work over $\mathbb C$ and assume the Axiom of Choice where projective covers,
duality and locally unital assemblies enter. Let
$\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ be a pyramid with columns
$q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, let $c=(c_1,\dots,c_l)$ be admissible in the sense that
$c_i-c_j\in\mathbb Z$ implies $c_i=c_j$, and let
$\mathcal O_c^d$ be the relevant summand of the genuine parabolic
category $\mathcal O$ attached to the labels $c$ and the degree $d$: its
objects are the modules whose column-strict labels have nonnegative integral
differences from the ground entries of each column, i.e. the labels with
$\Lambda$-diagram content $c_j+q_j-n$ in the sense of
[[def-degenerate-cyclotomic-hecke-algebra]] (the ambient categories are the
ones of [[def-integral-parabolic-category-o-block-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]]
and [[def-parabolic-category-o-for-a-standard-parabolic]]).

For a $U(\mathfrak m)$-finitely-generated object $N$ of genuine parabolic
$\mathcal O$, the **Whittaker functor** is the covariant finite-dimensional dual
$$V(N):=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak m}(N,\mathbb C_\chi)^*.$$
Its $W(\lambda)$ action is obtained from the continuous $\chi$-part of the right
linear dual, then the reflected head/tail identification proved below. In the
notation $D_{\mathrm{row}}\mathrm{Wh}D_{\mathrm{row}}$, the middle Whittaker
operation is performed on this continuous $\chi$-part, not on the uncompleted
ordinary row-restricted dual. Write $N(A)$ for source standard objects,
$L_{\mathcal O}(A)$ for source simples, and $L_W(A)$ for the resulting
nonzero simple $W$-modules. These namespaces are distinct.

The verification below records the properties used on this page: $V$ is exact
on the $U(\mathfrak m)$-finitely-generated objects of genuine parabolic
$\mathcal O$ and intertwines finite tensoring, the Casimir and the flips; $V$
is distinct from the Hecke quotient $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(T,-)$
constructed later; for the ground simple projective-injective $P_c$ and
$T=P_c\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ one has $V(P_c)=\mathbb C_c$ and
$V(T)=V_c^{\otimes d}$; and $V(L_{\mathcal O}(A))$ is the simple $W$-module $L_W(A)$ for
standard labels $A$ and zero otherwise. Nonintegral origins use the typed
equivalence of the all-weight Harish-Chandra comparison of the source; no
arbitrary complex $c$ is identified with an integral block. After fixing the
ground identification $i_0\colon V(P_c)\to\mathbb C_c$, the compatible functor
and the maps $j_d$ are unique up to the normalized unique natural isomorphism;
without this normalization scalar automorphisms prevent literal uniqueness.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ be a pyramid with columns
$q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, let $c$ be an admissible origin, let $P_c$ be the ground
simple projective-injective of the relevant summand of the parabolic category
$\mathcal O$ of
[[def-integral-parabolic-category-o-block-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]],
and let $T=P_c\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ with $V=\mathbb C^N$. Write
$B_d=\psi_d(H_d(\Lambda))$ for the image of the right cyclotomic Hecke action of
[[def-degenerate-cyclotomic-hecke-algebra]] and $B_\alpha$ for its central
components. Then the right Hecke action gives an algebra isomorphism
$$\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}(T)^{\mathrm{op}}=B_d,$$
and on each central component, cut by the central idempotents $f_\alpha$ of
$B_d$ acting on $T=\bigoplus_\alpha T_\alpha$,
$$\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}(T_\alpha)^{\mathrm{op}}=B_\alpha =f_\alpha H_\alpha(\mathbf a)f_\alpha,$$
where $H_\alpha(\mathbf a)$ is the corresponding block of the cyclotomic Hecke
algebra. For a nonempty pyramid, in the stable range $q_l\ge d$ the image is the full cyclotomic
algebra, $B_d=H_d(\mathbf a)$ and $B_\alpha=H_\alpha(\mathbf a)$; a single
component is not identified with the entire degree-$d$ algebra. Outside the
stable range the central-corner identification uses the admissible-origin
corner of [[def-stable-range-and-block-idempotent-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]].
The maps $H_d(\mathbf a)\twoheadrightarrow B_d$ are surjective in all cases,
and the full action $H_d(\mathbf a)\to\operatorname{End}(V_c^{\otimes d})$ is
injective precisely when $q_l\ge d$ for a nonempty pyramid. For the empty pyramid $l=N=0$, the degree-zero objects and algebras are $T_0=U_0=H_0=\mathbb C$, and for $d>0$ they are $T_d=U_d=H_d=0$. All endomorphism identities hold there, and the raw action is faithful in every degree, including the zero-algebra action; $q_l$ is not defined in this branch.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix an admissible origin $c$. Let
$\pi=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(T,-)$ be the Schur functor of
[[def-the-higher-level-schur-weyl-projective-generator-and-schur-functor]],
$T=P_c\otimes V^{\otimes d}$. Use the current category-O namespace:
$N(A):=M(A)$ is the generalized standard, $K(A):=\nabla(A)$ the costandard,
$L(A)$ the category-O simple and $P(A)$ its projective cover, as in
[[def-integral-parabolic-category-o-block-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]].
The source17 symbol $K(A)$ denotes our $L(A)$, not our costandard $K(A)$.
Write $\mathsf L(A):=\mathrm{Wh}(L(A))$ for the finite-W image of the
category-O simple; for $A\in\mathrm{Std}$ this is the source finite-W simple
appearing in the Whittaker/Morita contract of
[[thm-the-whittaker-functor-is-exact-and-fully-faithful-on-the-required-projectives]].
In particular the $W_d$-Hom below takes a finite-W module as its second
argument. Let $\mathrm{Std}$ be the standard labels. Then:

1. For every label $A$, the Schur image of the standard object $N(A)$ is the
   intrinsic affine-induced Specht module
   $$S(A)=H_d\otimes_{H_{d_1,\dots,d_l}}\Bigl(\bigotimes_j \mathrm{ev}^*_{a_j}S^{\mu^{(j)}}\Bigr),\qquad a_j=c_j+q_j-n,$$
   where $\mu^{(j)}$ is the partition of $d_j$ read from the nonnegative
   ground differences in the $j$-th column of $A$ and the factors are induced
   along the affine Young subalgebra $H_{d_1,\dots,d_l}=H_{d_1}\otimes\cdots
   \otimes H_{d_l}$. Its affine action factors through the cyclotomic image $B_d$, so the same module is obtained by replacing $H_d$ in this tensor product by $H_d(\mathbf a)$.
2. For $A\in\mathrm{Std}$ the module
   $D(A)=\pi(L(A))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{W_d}(V_c^{\otimes d},\mathsf L(A))$ is
   simple, the modules $D(A)$, $A\in\mathrm{Std}$, form a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simples of the Hecke image $B_d$, and
   $\pi(L(A))=0$ for $A\notin\mathrm{Std}$.
3. For $A\in\mathrm{Std}$, $\pi(P(A))$ is the projective cover $Y(A)$ of
   $D(A)$, and $\pi^*\pi(P(A))\cong P(A)$; ambient off-standard projectives
   still have their genuine images, and no projective-preservation assertion
   is made for them.
4. Images of tiltings carry the opposite-parabolic standard/Specht flag
   coefficients, and $\pi$ is fully faithful on tiltings.
5. For $A\in\mathrm{Col}$ and $B\in\mathrm{Std}$,
   $[S(A):D(B)]=[N(A):L(B)]=d_{B,A}(1)$, where $d_{B,A}$ is the typed
   canonical-basis coefficient of the Fock-space dictionary; for $B\notin
   \mathrm{Std}$ the symbol $D(B)$ is not a Hecke simple. All interfaces are
   ungraded at parameter $1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and that $I$ is bounded
below, so $n_j=m_j+1-\inf(I)$ and $n=\sum_jn_j$ are finite; the upper end of
$I$ may remain unbounded. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)$ and let
the standard parabolic $\mathfrak p$ have Levi
$\mathfrak{gl}_{n_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{n_l}$
([[def-standard-parabolic-and-levi-subalgebras-from-simple-roots]]).
For a tableau $A$ let $a_1,\dots,a_n$ be its ordinary highest-weight
reading: read columns from left to right and each column from top to bottom,
so its entries are strictly decreasing. This is also the normally ordered column reading of
[[def-higher-level-wedge-tensor-fock-module]]. Put
$$\lambda_A=\sum_{j=1}^{n}(a_j+j-1)\,\varepsilon_j .$$
Strict columns make $\lambda_A$ Levi-dominant, so that the simple highest weight
module $L(A)$ of [[thm-simple-objects-of-category-o-are-highest-weight-modules]]
and the induced generalized standard
$M(A)=M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda_A)$ of
[[def-parabolic-category-o-for-a-standard-parabolic]] belong to the genuine
parabolic category $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ of
[[thm-parabolic-category-o-is-a-highest-weight-category]].

Use the published **half-sum convention**
$\rho_j=(n+1-2j)/2$; then
$$\lambda_{A,j}+\rho_j=a_j+\frac{n-1}{2},$$
so the $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ Harish-Chandra shifted-coordinate multiset of the
block is the tableau-entry multiset plus the common scalar $(n-1)/2$, and this
multiset together with the displayed scalar $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ centre labels the
central character ([[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]). The Fock
weight $\sum_j\delta_{a_j}=\Lambda-\alpha$ of the Fock item belongs to the
different $\mathfrak{gl}_{I^+}$ weight lattice and indexes that entry multiset;
it is **not** a literal $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ highest weight.

For an entry multiset $\alpha$ the corresponding **finite parabolic central
block** $\mathcal O^\Lambda_\alpha$ has labels
$\mathrm{Col}^\Lambda_\alpha$, generalized standards $M(A)$, simples $L(A)$,
projective covers $P(A)$ and costandards $\nabla(A)$, with the BGG reciprocity,
restricted duality and highest-weight structure inherited from
[[thm-parabolic-category-o-is-a-highest-weight-category]]; by
[[lem-type-a-tableau-central-summands-are-single-linkage-blocks]] it is a single
linkage block. Its simple and standard classes form bases of its Grothendieck
group, and its numerical multiplicities include repeated-entry singular central
characters. The direct sum over the admitted entry multisets is
$\mathcal O^\Lambda$. **Opposite blocks** use the reversed Levi order and the
reverse-column reading, with the correspondingly reversed label order
([[lem-the-parabolic-semi-regular-duality-and-reverse-column-label-map]]).

derivations.claim: **Restriction uses the dual natural module.** For $N$ in the degree-$(d+1)$ summand and a basis $v_a$ of $V$ with dual basis $v^a$, tensor adjunction gives the natural map $\rho_N:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(T_{d+1},N)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(T_d,N\otimes V^*)$, $\rho_N(h)(t)=\sum_a h(t\otimes v_a)\otimes v^a$. Its inverse sends $g$ to $(t\otimes v)\mapsto(1\otimes\operatorname{ev}_v)g(t)$. These maps are basis-independent by coevaluation and evaluation and commute with the first $d$ tower generators, acting on the $T_d$ factors. Thus they identify restriction of $\pi_{d+1}N$ with $\pi_d(N\otimes V^*)$ after the appropriate degree/block projection. The natural and dual natural modules are distinct $\mathfrak{gl}_n$-modules; no identification between them is used.

**The induction map is an actual tensor map.** For $M$ of degree $d$, put $\tau_M:B_{d+1}\otimes_{B_d}\pi_dM\to\pi_{d+1}(M\otimes V)$, $b\otimes f\mapsto(f\otimes\mathrm{id}_V)\circ R_b$, where $R_b$ is the right action on $T_{d+1}$. The first $d$ generators act on $T_d$, so this expression is balanced over $B_d$ and is $B_{d+1}$-linear for the left-module convention; naturality follows by postcomposition. To prove it invertible, on the finite-W side form $\sigma_X(b\otimes g)=(g\circledast\mathrm{id}_V)\circ\mu_d^{-1}\circ R_b$. For $X=U_d$ this is the regular-module isomorphism $B_{d+1}\otimes_{B_d}B_d\cong B_{d+1}$. It remains an isomorphism on finite sums and summands. Every finite-W image object has a finite projective presentation by summands of finite sums of $U_d$, and both sides are right exact: induction is right exact, tensoring with $V$ is exact and Hom from $U_d,U_{d+1}$ is exact. Passing to cokernels proves $\sigma_X$ invertible for all $X$. The coherent $\gamma,\nu,\mu$ square of [F3] sends $1\otimes f$ by either route to $(\mathrm{Wh}(f)\circledast\mathrm{id}_V)\mu_d^{-1}$; $B_{d+1}$-linearity then makes the square commute on every $b\otimes f$. Consequently $\tau_M$ is invertible for every $M$. This presentation argument takes place in the finite-W image category, where $U_d$ is a full projective generator; it does not assert that $T_d$ is a full category-O generator.

**The two residue projectors.** The tower's last dot on $T_d\otimes V$ is the tensor Casimir, with the normalization of [F1]. Hence $\tau$ intertwines its generalized-$i$ eigenprojector with the projector defining $f_i^{\mathcal O}$. On the dual tensor factor one has the actual operator identity $\Omega_{N,V^*}\rho_N(h)=-\rho_N(h\Omega_{T_d,V})-n\rho_N(h)$. Indeed $E_{ba}v^c=-\delta_{bc}v^a$ and equivariance of $h$ give the first term $-\sum_{a,b}h(E_{ab}t\otimes v_b)\otimes v^a$ and the second term $-n\sum_a h(t\otimes v_a)\otimes v^a$, exactly that identity. Thus the last-dot generalized-$i$ projector corresponds to the dual-Casimir generalized-$(-n-i)$ projector, including its nilpotent part. This is the actual adjunction mate and agrees with the flag normalization in [F1]. Under $\rho$ the last-dot projector therefore corresponds to the generalized-$(-n-i)$ projector defining $e_i^{\mathcal O}$. Applying the source content projector $e_\alpha$ and target projector $e_{\alpha+\alpha_i}$ to steps 1.1–1.2 gives $u_{\alpha,i}\pi_{\alpha+\alpha_i}N\cong\pi_\alpha e_i^{\mathcal O}N$ and $B_{\alpha+\alpha_i}u_{\alpha,i}\otimes_{B_\alpha}\pi_\alpha M\cong\pi_{\alpha+\alpha_i}f_i^{\mathcal O}M$. Polynomial generalized-eigenspace projectors commute with these natural maps because the maps intertwine the operators, proving the asserted residue compatibility.

**The natural duality comparison.** The ordinary category-O duality $D$ uses matrix transpose and restricted weight-space duals. The product of the ground contravariant form and the natural-factor forms gives a nondegenerate detector form $(xtb,t')=(t,x^{\mathrm{tr}}t'b^*)$; the Casimir, crossings and content projectors are self-adjoint. Put $\delta M=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(M,T_d)$ with $(bf)(m)=f(m)b^*$ and $X^\#=\operatorname{Hom}_{B_d}(X,B_d)$ with the same twist. The detector form gives an actual isomorphism $\beta:T_d\cong DT_d$, $\beta(t)(t')=(t,t')$. Exact restricted contravariant duality, with its canonical bidual map, consequently gives $\delta M=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(M,T_d)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(M,DT_d)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(T_d,DM)=\pi_dDM$. Its explicit map is $f\mapsto[t\mapsto(m\mapsto(t,f(m)))]$; its inverse sends $g:T_d\to DM$ to $\beta^{-1}\circ Dg\circ\operatorname{bidual}_M:M\to T_d$. These maps are inverse by the symmetry and nondegeneracy of the form and the bidual identities, and the form's $*$-invariance makes them Hecke-linear. This is a canonical natural Hom-duality isomorphism; it requires neither dimensions of simple images nor self-duality of individual projective summands. Tensor-Hom gives $\delta\pi_d^*\cong\#$, while the symmetric trace of [F2] gives $\#\cong D_H$ by $h\mapsto\mathrm{tr}\circ h$. Define $\theta_M:M\to D\pi_d^*\delta M$ by $\theta_M(m)(t\otimes f)=(t,f(m))$. The displayed form identity makes it balanced over $B_d$ and $\mathfrak g$-linear. Applying $\pi_d$ gives a natural transformation $\pi_d\to\pi_dD\pi_d^*\delta\cong\#\pi_dD$ between exact functors. It is an isomorphism on $T_d$ and hence on its finite sums and summands. Apply the copresentations in [F3] to prove it an isomorphism on every projective, by exactness and kernels; then apply projective presentations to prove it on every object, by cokernels. Dualizing yields the natural comparison $\pi_dD\cong D_H\pi_d$. The product forms, tensor evaluation and trace form are the same forms used for the dual adjunctions; consequently this comparison identifies their dual unit/counit squares. Since the residue projectors are self-adjoint, it also commutes with each $f_i,e_i$ separately. Thus $Df_i\cong f_iD$ and $De_i\cong e_iD$. None of this identifies the usual tensor dual $V^*$ with $V$.

**Grothendieck operators and quotient.** Exactness of $\pi$ and of the residue functors makes the natural isomorphisms of step 2.1 induce $[f_i^H][\pi]=[\pi][f_i^{\mathcal O}]$ and $[e_i^H][\pi]=[\pi][e_i^{\mathcal O}]$. On $G_0$, the source simple-class basis shows that $\ker[\pi]$ is exactly the span of the off-standard simple classes, and the induced map from this quotient onto $G_0(H)$ is an isomorphism. No isomorphism from the entire category-O Grothendieck group is asserted. On split projective groups only $\operatorname{add}(T)$ is equivalent to Hecke projectives; an ambient off-standard projective need not have projective image. These distinctions leave the displayed operator equalities intact.

**Adjunction maps.** The first tensor unit is the coevaluation $m\mapsto\sum_a(m\otimes v_a)\otimes v^a$, and the tensor counit is evaluation. The induction/restriction unit is $z\mapsto1\otimes z$, and the counit is $b\otimes z\mapsto bz$. Substituting these formulas into $\tau$ and $\rho$ gives the same composite maps, term by term: coevaluation is precisely the sum in $\rho$, and evaluation cancels that sum by $v^a(v_b)=\delta_{ab}$. Restricting the commuting squares by the content and residue projectors proves compatibility for $f_i\dashv e_i$. For the reverse adjunction use the biadjoint mate maps supplied by [F1] and the symmetric-trace reverse adjunction of [F2]; transport the latter through $\tau,\rho$. The transported evaluation and coevaluation pair is the O-side biadjoint pair, since its dot and crossing mates agree with those in [F1], with the same trace normalization. Equivalently the reverse unit and counit are the dual mates of the first pair, so the same squares commute. The two pairs are thus compared with their transported normalizations; this is stronger than asserting abstract uniqueness of adjoints across a quotient.

**Filtrations and boundaries.** Applying exact $\pi$ to the O-side residue standard flags preserves their successive quotients, and the intertwined generalized-eigenvalue projectors select the corresponding residue pieces. Admissible nonintegral origins retain the typed coset realization of [F4]; an integral highest-weight Fock interpretation is used only on its actual integral residue component. All comparisons here are ungraded at parameter one. Together with steps 2.1–3.2 this proves the statement.
