Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix the pyramid $\lambda$ with columns
$q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, an origin $c\in\mathbb C^l$, and $d\ge0$, and let
$V_c^{\otimes d}$ be the truncated tensor space of
[[def-deformed-tensor-space-for-the-type-a-finite-w-algebra]]. Let
$W_d=\varphi_d(W(\lambda))\subseteq\operatorname{End}(V_c^{\otimes d})$ be the
image of the finite W-algebra and let
$B_d=\psi_d(H_d(\Lambda))$ be the image of the cyclotomic Hecke algebra of
[[def-degenerate-cyclotomic-hecke-algebra]] under the right action. Then:

1. $W_d$ and $B_d$ are mutual centralizers on $V_c^{\otimes d}$, for every
   complex origin $c$ and every $d$, and their associated graded image
   algebras are the corresponding images of $U(\mathfrak g^e)$ and of the
   truncated polynomial/permutation algebra.
2. For a nonempty pyramid, if $q_l\ge d$, then the action of the full cyclotomic algebra
   $H_d(\mathbf a)$ is faithful.
3. If $c$ is admissible (that is, $c_i-c_j\in\mathbb Z$ implies $c_i=c_j$),
   then the tensor module is a progenerator and
   $\operatorname{Hom}_{W_d}(V_c^{\otimes d},-)$ is a Morita equivalence
   between $W_d$-mod and $B_d$-mod.

Mutual centralizers alone do not imply Morita for arbitrary $c$: the explicit
example with $c=(0,1)$, $q=(1,1)$, $d=2$ in step 7.1 below has a
nonprojective left $W_d$-module.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ be a pyramid with columns
$q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, let $c$ be an admissible origin, let $P_c$ be the ground
simple projective-injective of the relevant summand of the parabolic category
$\mathcal O$ of
[[def-integral-parabolic-category-o-block-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]],
and let $T=P_c\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ with $V=\mathbb C^N$. Write
$B_d=\psi_d(H_d(\Lambda))$ for the image of the right cyclotomic Hecke action of
[[def-degenerate-cyclotomic-hecke-algebra]] and $B_\alpha$ for its central
components. Then the right Hecke action gives an algebra isomorphism
$$\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}(T)^{\mathrm{op}}=B_d,$$
and on each central component, cut by the central idempotents $f_\alpha$ of
$B_d$ acting on $T=\bigoplus_\alpha T_\alpha$,
$$\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}(T_\alpha)^{\mathrm{op}}=B_\alpha =f_\alpha H_\alpha(\mathbf a)f_\alpha,$$
where $H_\alpha(\mathbf a)$ is the corresponding block of the cyclotomic Hecke
algebra. For a nonempty pyramid, in the stable range $q_l\ge d$ the image is the full cyclotomic
algebra, $B_d=H_d(\mathbf a)$ and $B_\alpha=H_\alpha(\mathbf a)$; a single
component is not identified with the entire degree-$d$ algebra. Outside the
stable range the central-corner identification uses the admissible-origin
corner of [[def-stable-range-and-block-idempotent-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]].
The maps $H_d(\mathbf a)\twoheadrightarrow B_d$ are surjective in all cases,
and the full action $H_d(\mathbf a)\to\operatorname{End}(V_c^{\otimes d})$ is
injective precisely when $q_l\ge d$ for a nonempty pyramid. For the empty pyramid $l=N=0$, the degree-zero objects and algebras are $T_0=U_0=H_0=\mathbb C$, and for $d>0$ they are $T_d=U_d=H_d=0$. All endomorphism identities hold there, and the raw action is faithful in every degree, including the zero-algebra action; $q_l$ is not defined in this branch.

Keep the pyramid and admissible origins $c$ of
[[def-the-whittaker-functor-from-the-relevant-parabolic-o-summand]], the
ground object $P_c$, the tensor object $T=P_c\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ and its
central decomposition. For a charge $\alpha\in Q^+$ with $\mathrm{ht}(\alpha)=d$
let $I_\alpha$ be the finite set of residue sequences of content $\alpha$, and
let $T_\alpha$ be the corresponding central component of $T$; in the integral
model
$$T_\alpha=\sum_{i\in I_\alpha}f_{i_d}\cdots f_{i_1}P_c,$$
the sum of the residue-induction images of the ground object. Put
$$B_\alpha:=\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}(T_\alpha)^{\mathrm{op}},$$
the corresponding central component of the Hecke image algebra (the opposite
convention is fixed here), and define the **Schur functor** of the block by
$$\pi_\alpha:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(T_\alpha,-)\colon\mathcal O_\alpha^d\to B_\alpha\text{-mod}.$$
Its left adjoint is $\pi^*_\alpha:=T_\alpha\otimes_{B_\alpha}-$.

For the whole polynomial $\mathrm{Col}_c^d$ summand, use the distinct finite projective generator
$$G_d=\bigoplus_{A\in\mathrm{Tab}^d}Z(A,c),$$
with actual prefix symmetric modules $Z(A,c)$ as constructed independently from the raw inducing modules in steps 1.2, 2.2, 3.2 and 4.1 of
[[thm-the-whittaker-functor-is-exact-and-fully-faithful-on-the-required-projectives]]. Every category-O
projective cover is a summand of $G_d$; every $Z(A,c)$ embeds in $T_d$ with a
standard-filtered quotient. Exact projection gives $G_\alpha$ on the entire
central block. The tensor detector $T_\alpha$ remains the object defining
$\pi_\alpha$; $G_\alpha$ generates all Col labels, while $T_\alpha$ contains
the standard-labelled projective-injective covers. These roles are distinct.

The verification below records the properties used on this page and marks the
boundaries explicitly: $\pi_\alpha$ is exact, being Hom from a projective
object; its left adjoint is right exact but not exact in general; it sends
$B_\alpha$-projectives to projective objects and $\pi^*_\alpha\pi_\alpha$
recovers $\operatorname{add}(T_\alpha)$, including every standard-labelled
prinjective; neither exactness of $\pi^*_\alpha$ nor recovery of every
category-$\mathcal O$ projective is asserted, both failing in the two-equal-charge
rank-one computation in step 3.1 below. The components assemble as a locally
unital sum over the charges, and all ambient labels, including those killed by
$\pi$, remain in the category $\mathcal O$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For admissible origins $c$ the genuine Whittaker functor $V$ of
[[def-the-whittaker-functor-from-the-relevant-parabolic-o-summand]] is exact
on $\mathcal O_c^d$, and
$$\gamma\colon\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(T,-)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{W}(V_c^{\otimes d},V(-))$$
is a natural isomorphism, where $T=P_c\otimes V^{\otimes d}$. Both $V$ and the
Hecke quotient $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(T,-)$ are fully faithful on
all projective objects of the relevant summand, and the quotient is also fully
faithful on tiltings. $T$ is a self-dual prinjective detecting object
containing all standard-labelled projective-injective covers, each individually self-dual, but it need not be a
generator of the entire category-$\mathcal O$ summand. $V(T)=V_c^{\otimes d}$
is a projective generator of $W_d$-mod, and $V$ preserves projectivity on
$\operatorname{add}(T)$; it need not send every projective of $\mathcal O$ to
a projective $W$-module. The composite of $V$ with the Morita equivalence is

Central components. This is column strict, has total degree $d$, and is standard: for columns with the same charge, the changed rightmost entry is at least every unchanged entry to its left in that row; different charge cosets are incomparable. Work over $\mathbb C$ and fix $n\ge1$ together with a shift matrix
$\sigma=(s_{i,j})_{1\le i,j\le n}$ of nonnegative integers satisfying
$s_{i,j}+s_{j,k}=s_{i,k}$ whenever $i\le j\le k$ or $i\ge j\ge k$, and
$s_{i,i}=0$. The **shifted Yangian** $Y_n(\sigma)$ is the associative unital
$\mathbb C$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) generated by the
shifted Drinfeld generators $D_i^{(r)}$ ($1\le i\le n$, $r\ge1$),
$E_i^{(r)}$ ($1\le i<n$, $r>s_{i,i+1}$), and
$F_i^{(r)}$ ($1\le i<n$, $r>s_{i+1,i}$). For $i<j$, the higher-root
coefficients $E_{i,j}^{(r)}$ have range $r>s_{i,j}$ and
$F_{j,i}^{(r)}$ have range $r>s_{j,i}$; they are defined recursively by
adjacent-root commutators, not declared as a duplicate independent family.
Put $D_i^{(0)}=1$, $D_i(u)=\sum_{r\ge0}D_i^{(r)}u^{-r}$ and $\widetilde D_i(u)=-D_i(u)^{-1}$. The defining relations are the following, for every index for which all displayed generators exist (in particular the $E$ and $F$ indices exceed their respective shifts):

$$[D_i^{(r)},D_j^{(s)}]=0,\qquad [E_i^{(r)},F_j^{(s)}]=\delta_{ij}\sum_{t=0}^{r+s-1}\widetilde D_i^{(t)}D_{i+1}^{(r+s-1-t)}.$$

$$[D_i^{(r)},E_j^{(s)}]=(\delta_{ij}-\delta_{i,j+1})\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}D_i^{(t)}E_j^{(r+s-1-t)}.$$

$$[D_i^{(r)},F_j^{(s)}]=(\delta_{i,j+1}-\delta_{ij})\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}F_j^{(r+s-1-t)}D_i^{(t)}.$$

$$[E_i^{(r)},E_i^{(s+1)}]-[E_i^{(r+1)},E_i^{(s)}]=E_i^{(r)}E_i^{(s)}+E_i^{(s)}E_i^{(r)}.$$

$$[F_i^{(r+1)},F_i^{(s)}]-[F_i^{(r)},F_i^{(s+1)}]=F_i^{(r)}F_i^{(s)}+F_i^{(s)}F_i^{(r)}.$$

$$[E_i^{(r)},E_{i+1}^{(s+1)}]-[E_i^{(r+1)},E_{i+1}^{(s)}]=-E_i^{(r)}E_{i+1}^{(s)}.$$

$$[F_i^{(r+1)},F_{i+1}^{(s)}]-[F_i^{(r)},F_{i+1}^{(s+1)}]=-F_{i+1}^{(s)}F_i^{(r)}.$$

For $|i-j|>1$, $[E_i^{(r)},E_j^{(s)}]=[F_i^{(r)},F_j^{(s)}]=0$. For $|i-j|=1$ impose

$$[E_i^{(r)},[E_i^{(s)},E_j^{(t)}]]+[E_i^{(s)},[E_i^{(r)},E_j^{(t)}]]=0,$$

$$[F_i^{(r)},[F_i^{(s)},F_j^{(t)}]]+[F_i^{(s)},[F_i^{(r)},F_j^{(t)}]]=0.$$

The higher roots are specified without new independent generators by $E_{i,i+1}^{(r)}=E_i^{(r)}$, $F_{i+1,i}^{(r)}=F_i^{(r)}$, and, for $j>i+1$,

$$E_{i,j}^{(r)}=[E_{i,j-1}^{(r-s_{j-1,j})},E_{j-1}^{(s_{j-1,j}+1)}],\qquad F_{j,i}^{(r)}=[F_{j-1}^{(s_{j,j-1}+1)},F_{j-1,i}^{(r-s_{j,j-1})}].$$

These are [BK, Section 2.1, (2.7)–(2.18), and Section 2.2, (2.21)–(2.22)], with the negative root written in matrix-row order here. Two filtrations are fixed on it: the **canonical
filtration**, in which each generator of upper index $r$ has degree $r$, and
the **loop filtration**, in which it has degree $r-1$; their associated
graded algebras are different (the canonical one is commutative polynomial,
the loop one is a current algebra).

For the pyramid $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ with conjugate
$q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$ ([[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]])
the relevant shift matrix is $s_{i,j}=p_j-p_i$ for $i\le j$ and $s_{i,j}=0$
for $i\ge j$, and the **type-A finite W-algebra** is the quotient
$$W(\lambda)=Y_n(\sigma)/\bigl(D_1^{(r)},\ r>p_1\bigr)$$
of $Y_n(\sigma)$ by the two-sided ideal generated by the higher modes of
$D_1$ beyond $p_1$.

Write the Gauss decomposition $T(u)=F(u)D(u)E(u)$ of the generating matrix,
with $T(u)=\sum_{r\ge0}T_{i,j}^{(r)}u^{-r}$, $T_{i,j}^{(0)}=\delta_{i,j}$, and
**no** additional factor $u^{s_{i,j}}$: the coefficient of $u^{-r}$ is the
mode $T_{i,j}^{(r)}$. Its modes satisfy $T_{i,j}^{(r)}=0$ for
$0<r\le s_{i,j}$, and in the finite quotient also $T_{i,j}^{(r)}=0$ for
$r>S_{i,j}:=s_{i,j}+p_{\min(i,j)}$, so the finite quotient has the PBW basis
of ordered monomials
$$T_{i,j}^{(r)},\qquad s_{i,j}<r\le S_{i,j}.$$
The auxiliary signed path polynomials used in the source to construct the
Gauss generators are not all identified with these shifted $T$-modes; the root
of $T_{i,j}^{(r)}$ is the weight $\varepsilon_i-\varepsilon_j$, and the
surviving modes have loop leading term $(-1)^{r-1}e_{i,j;r-1}$ in the
centralizer basis of the pyramid.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_r$ be an ordered basis of a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Then the monomials

$$x_1^{a_1}x_2^{a_2}\cdots x_r^{a_r} \qquad (a_i\in \mathbb N_0)$$

form a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)$. In particular, multiplication identifies $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)$ with the symmetric algebra $S(\mathfrak g)$ on the symbols of the $x_i$.

Keep the pyramid data $(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak p,\mathfrak h,\mathfrak m,e,\chi)$
of [[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]] and
the finite W-algebra $W(\lambda)$, the bimodule $Q_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$
and the Whittaker category of
[[def-the-type-a-finite-w-algebra-and-whittaker-category]]. Double the pyramid
grading by declaring the degree of $e_{i,j}$ to be
$2(\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i))$; then $e$ has degree $2$ and the
degree $-1$ part of $\mathfrak g$ is zero. Let
$\mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r>0,\ r\ \mathrm{even}}\mathfrak g_{-r}$ in the doubled
grading (the strictly negative even part), carrying the character $\chi$. Then:

1. There is a homogeneous transverse complement
   $S=e+\ker(\operatorname{ad} f)$ for a suitable $f\in\mathfrak g$, and the
   conjugation map $M_{\mathrm{unip}}\times S\to e+\mathfrak m^\perp$,
   $(u,s)\mapsto usu^{-1}$, is a polynomial isomorphism; the Kazhdan
   associated graded of $Q_\chi$ is $\mathbb C[M_{\mathrm{unip}}]\otimes\mathbb C[S]$
   and $\operatorname{gr}W(\lambda)=\mathbb C[S]$.
2. Assuming the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]], for every $W(\lambda)$-module $X$, the twisted $\mathfrak m$-cohomology of
   $Q_\chi\otimes_{W(\lambda)}X$ vanishes in positive degree and its degree-zero
   part is $X$.
3. Every nonzero module on which all $x-\chi(x)$, $x\in\mathfrak m$, act
   locally nilpotently has a nonzero simultaneous invariant vector; in
   particular $\mathrm{Wh}(M)=0$ implies $M=0$ for $M$ in the Whittaker
   category.

These assertions use the doubled good grading; no nondegenerate alternating
form on the original degree $-1$ space is asserted.

Let $A$ be a unital algebra with an increasing **multiplicative filtration**

$$0=F_{-1}A\subseteq F_0A\subseteq F_1A\subseteq\cdots,$$

where $1\in F_0A$ and $(F_mA)(F_nA)\subseteq F_{m+n}A$. Its
**associated graded algebra** is

$$\operatorname{gr}_F A=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}F_nA/F_{n-1}A,$$

with multiplication on homogeneous classes

$$ (a+F_{m-1}A)(b+F_{n-1}A)=ab+F_{m+n-1}A.$$

This product is well-defined. Indeed, if $a$ changes by
$u\in F_{m-1}A$ and $b$ by $v\in F_{n-1}A$, the product changes by
$ub+av+uv\in F_{m+n-1}A$. Associativity and the unit class descend from $A$.

derivations.claim: **RTT spanning and the actual coproduct.** In the unshifted RTT algebra the commutator of modes $r,s$ has canonical degree at most $r+s-1$, so induction on total degree and the number of unordered pairs rewrites every word into ordered monomials. Matrix-unit brackets verify RTT for $L_a(u)=I+E^{(a)}/u$ in the $a$th factor of $U(\mathfrak{gl}_n)^{\otimes l}$. Multiplication of RTT matrices with commuting coefficient algebras preserves RTT: moving the two middle commuting tensor factors past each other allows the first RTT identity, then the second. Thus the iterated evaluation map is $T(u)\mapsto L_1(u)\cdots L_l(u)$. More generally shifted evaluation points give the ordered product $\prod_{a=1}^l(I+E^{(a)}/(u-c_a))$, in increasing factor order. Its $u^{-r}$ coefficient when all $c_a=0$ is $\sum_{a_1<\cdots<a_r}E^{(a_1)}\cdots E^{(a_r)}$, homogeneous of enveloping PBW degree $r$.

We first prove invariance of the actual path generators for both column arrangements, independently of generation. For a box a write c(a) for its column, $\rho_c=n-\sum_{d\ge c}q_d$ and $\widetilde E_{ab}=(-1)^{c(b)-c(a)}(E_{ab}+\delta_{ab}\rho_{c(a)})$. The negative PBW projection $\operatorname{pr}:U(\mathfrak g)=U(\mathfrak p)U(\mathfrak m)\to U(\mathfrak p)$ applies χ to the right factor. Its elementary rules are $\operatorname{pr}(ZB)=\chi(Z)B+\operatorname{pr}([Z,B])$ and $\operatorname{pr}(BZ)=B\chi(Z)$ for a negative matrix unit Z and a p-factor B. The bracket is $[\widetilde E_{ab},\widetilde E_{hk}]=\delta_{bh}(\widetilde E_{ak}-\delta_{ak}\rho_{c(a)})-\delta_{ak}(\widetilde E_{hb}-\delta_{hb}\rho_{c(b)})$, and $\chi(\widetilde E_{ab})=-\delta_{\operatorname{row}(a),\operatorname{row}(b)}$ at adjacent negative columns, zero at greater distance. Define $P_{ij;x}^{(r)}$ as the sum of products $E_{a_1b_1}\cdots E_{a_sb_s}$ with total degree $\sum(c(b_t)-c(a_t)+1)=r$, p-factors, shared intervening rows, starting/ending rows i,j, strict forward joins when the intervening row exceeds x and weak reverse joins otherwise, and sign $(-1)^{r-s}$ times one minus for every intervening row at most x. Its $\eta_{\rm tail}$ image replaces each factor by $E_{ab}+\delta_{ab}\rho_{c(a)}$. Equivalently, in the $\widetilde E$ factors its only external sign is one minus for every intervening row at most x, since their product already contributes $(-1)^{r-s}$. Invariance means $\operatorname{pr}([z,\eta_{\rm tail}(P)])=0$. If an element B is invariant, then $(z-\chi(z))B=B(z-\chi(z))+[z,B]$ proves $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi B\subseteq U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$; hence invariant elements form a subalgebra, and products, commutators and coefficients of inverse series with identity constant are invariant.

The local Gan–Ginzburg supplier is stated for the original left-justified diagram; we derive the reflected version by an actual graded Lie isomorphism. Let f reflect boxes, $\tau(E_{ab})=E'_{f(b),f(a)}$ reverse products, and let S on the reflected space be diagonal with $S_{bb}=(-1)^{\operatorname{col}'(b)}$. The linear map $\phi(x)=S(-\tau(x))S^{-1}$ is a Lie isomorphism, because $[\tau(x),\tau(y)]=-\tau([x,y])$. It preserves grading degrees, p and m, and the trace pairing. The diagonal-conjugation sign on every positive adjacent arrow is −1, so $\phi(e)=e'$ and $\chi'\phi=\chi$. It extends to an ALGEBRA isomorphism of enveloping algebras and takes $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ to $U(\mathfrak g')I_{\chi'}$. Thus it takes the entire untwisted left reduction $A=\eta_{\rm tail}(W)$ to $A'$: each defining commutator condition is equivalent under φ. The chart map is the explicit algebra isomorphism $\beta=\eta_{\rm tail}'^{-1}\phi\eta_{\rm tail}:W\to W'$. Scalar translations have smaller positive Kazhdan degree, so $\operatorname{gr}\beta=\operatorname{gr}\phi$. The doubled good grading, sl2 triple, trace-orthogonal slice and transverse product transport under φ. Consequently the proved original polynomial-slice and cohomological statements imply the reflected statements in its actual grading, including the homogeneous coordinate weights. The polynomial-slice part used here is choice-free; for consumers assuming AC as in the cohomological supplier, its left Skryabin quotient, local-nilpotence category, invariant space and equivalence maps also transport first through φ and then through β. **Index and inverse sign in the abstract quotient.** Write $A_i(u)=D_i(u)^{-1}=\sum_{t\ge0}A_i^{(t)}u^{-t}$, so $A_i^{(0)}=1$, while the defining relation uses $\widetilde D_i(u)=-A_i(u)$ with constant $-1$. In the commutative symbol algebra of $U(\mathfrak{gl}_n)^{\otimes l}$ write $P_r(X_1,\ldots,X_l)=\sum_{a_1<\cdots<a_r}X_{a_1}\cdots X_{a_r}$. Deleting the last column embeds the smaller shifted matrix units into the current ones; on unshifted diagonal units this compensates the rho difference by a scalar translation, and on negative units it preserves χ. Keep the pyramid data $(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak p,\mathfrak h,\mathfrak m,e,\chi)$
of [[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]] and
the finite W-algebra $W(\lambda)$, the bimodule $Q_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$
and the Whittaker category of
[[def-the-type-a-finite-w-algebra-and-whittaker-category]]. Double the pyramid
grading by declaring the degree of $e_{i,j}$ to be
$2(\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i))$; then $e$ has degree $2$ and the
degree $-1$ part of $\mathfrak g$ is zero. Let
$\mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r>0,\ r\ \mathrm{even}}\mathfrak g_{-r}$ in the doubled
grading (the strictly negative even part), carrying the character $\chi$. Then:

1. There is a homogeneous transverse complement
   $S=e+\ker(\operatorname{ad} f)$ for a suitable $f\in\mathfrak g$, and the
   conjugation map $M_{\mathrm{unip}}\times S\to e+\mathfrak m^\perp$,
   $(u,s)\mapsto usu^{-1}$, is a polynomial isomorphism; the Kazhdan
   associated graded of $Q_\chi$ is $\mathbb C[M_{\mathrm{unip}}]\otimes\mathbb C[S]$
   and $\operatorname{gr}W(\lambda)=\mathbb C[S]$.
2. Assuming the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]], for every $W(\lambda)$-module $X$, the twisted $\mathfrak m$-cohomology of
   $Q_\chi\otimes_{W(\lambda)}X$ vanishes in positive degree and its degree-zero
   part is $X$.
3. Every nonzero module on which all $x-\chi(x)$, $x\in\mathfrak m$, act
   locally nilpotently has a nonzero simultaneous invariant vector; in
   particular $\mathrm{Wh}(M)=0$ implies $M=0$ for $M$ in the Whittaker
   category.

These assertions use the doubled good grading; no nondegenerate alternating
form on the original degree $-1$ space is asserted.

Keep the type-A pyramid data
$(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak p,\mathfrak h,\mathfrak m,e,\chi)$ of
[[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]], with
$\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$, transpose
$q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, and $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$ on $\mathfrak m$.
Let $\eta\colon U(\mathfrak p)\to U(\mathfrak p)$ be the algebra automorphism
with
$$\eta(e_{i,j})=e_{i,j}+\delta_{i,j}\bigl(n-q_{\mathrm{col}(j)}-q_{\mathrm{col}(j)+1}-\cdots-q_l\bigr)$$
for all matrix units $e_{i,j}\in\mathfrak p$. Let $I_\chi$ be the kernel of the
algebra homomorphism $\chi\colon U(\mathfrak m)\to\mathbb C$ extending the Lie
character $\chi$, that is, the two-sided ideal generated by $x-\chi(x)$,
$x\in\mathfrak m$ ([[def-universal-enveloping-algebra]],
[[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]),
and let $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ be the left ideal it generates in
$U(\mathfrak g)$.

The **type-A finite W-algebra** is
$$W(\lambda)=\{u\in U(\mathfrak p):[x,\eta(u)]\in U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi\ \text{for all }x\in\mathfrak m\}.$$
It is a subalgebra of $U(\mathfrak p)$, and
$Q_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ is a
$(U(\mathfrak g),W(\lambda))$-bimodule with right action
$\bar v\cdot u=\overline{v\,\eta(u)}$. This is a module quotient by a left ideal; no quotient-ring multiplication is imposed.

The **Whittaker category** $\mathcal C(\lambda)$ is the category of
$\mathfrak g$-modules on which $x-\chi(x)$ acts locally nilpotently for every
$x\in\mathfrak m$ ([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). For
$M\in\mathcal C(\lambda)$ the **Whittaker vectors**
$$\mathrm{Wh}(M)=\{v\in M:xv=\chi(x)v\ \text{for all }x\in\mathfrak m\}$$
form a $W(\lambda)$-module with $u\cdot v=\eta(u)v$, and
$\mathrm{Wh}(M)=0$ implies $M=0$.

The verification below establishes the algebra and module structures just
stated. The associated graded of the loop filtration on $U(\mathfrak p)$ makes
$W(\lambda)$ a filtered deformation of $U(\mathfrak g^e)$; that statement is
proved later on this page
([[thm-the-loop-filtration-on-the-type-a-finite-w-algebra-has-associated-graded-u-of-g-e]]),
and the filtration used is the loop (good) filtration, not the Kazhdan
filtration.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a Lie algebra over $k$. In $T(\mathfrak g)$, regard
$[x,y]\in\mathfrak g$ as an element of tensor degree one, and let $I$ be the
two-sided ideal generated by

$$x\otimes y-y\otimes x-[x,y]\qquad(x,y\in\mathfrak g).$$

The **universal enveloping algebra** is

$$U(\mathfrak g)=T(\mathfrak g)/I.$$

Write

$$\iota_{\mathfrak g}:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow U(\mathfrak g)$$

for the composite of the degree-one inclusion with the quotient map. This
definition makes $U(\mathfrak g)$ a unital associative algebra and $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ a
linear map. It does not assert that $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ is injective; that conclusion will
come from PBW.

For a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ over $k$ and a $\mathfrak g$-module $M$,
the degree-$n$ **Chevalley–Eilenberg cochains** are

$$C^n(\mathfrak g,M)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\Lambda^n\mathfrak g,M)\quad(n\geq0).$$

Set $C^n(\mathfrak g,M)=0$ for $n<0$. Since
$\Lambda^0\mathfrak g=k$, evaluation at $1$ identifies
$C^0(\mathfrak g,M)$ with $M$. Cochains may equivalently be viewed as
alternating $n$-linear maps $\mathfrak g^n\to M$. No finite-dimensionality
or characteristic hypothesis is needed. If $n>\dim\mathfrak g$ in the
finite-dimensional case, the exterior power and hence the cochain space are
zero.

For finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$ and a short exact sequence
$0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$ of $\mathfrak g$-modules, the induced CE
complexes form a degreewise short exact sequence and yield the natural long
exact sequence

$$\cdots\to H^n(\mathfrak g,M')\to H^n(\mathfrak g,M)\to H^n(\mathfrak g,M'')\to H^{n+1}(\mathfrak g,M')\to\cdots.$$

Work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ be a partition
of $N\ge0$ with transpose $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, where $l=p_n$ for a
nonempty row list and $l=0$ for an empty row list. Zero-length rows have no
boxes. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with matrix units
$e_{i,j}$ in the standard basis
$v_1,\dots,v_N$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]). Number the
boxes of the diagram of $\lambda$ by $1,\dots,N$ down columns from the left,
and for a box $i$ write $\mathrm{row}(i),\mathrm{col}(i)$ for its row and
column, $L(i)$ for the box immediately to its left (or $\emptyset$ if absent),
and $R(i)$ for the box immediately to its right (or $\emptyset$ if absent).
Define the nilpotent endomorphism
$$e=\sum_{i:\ L(i)\ne\emptyset}e_{L(i),i}\in\mathfrak g,\qquad ev_i=v_{L(i)},$$
and declare $\deg e_{i,j}=\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)$ for all $i,j$, so
that $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_r$ with
$\mathfrak g_r=\operatorname{span}\{e_{i,j}:\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)=r\}$.
Put
$$\mathfrak p=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r,\qquad \mathfrak h=\mathfrak g_0,\qquad \mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r,$$
and for rows $1\le i,j\le n$ define the shift $s_{i,j}=p_j-p_i$ if $i\le j$
and $s_{i,j}=0$ if $i\ge j$, together with the centralizer elements
$$e_{i,j;r}=\sum_{\substack{\mathrm{row}(h)=i,\ \mathrm{row}(k)=j\\ \mathrm{col}(k)-\mathrm{col}(h)=r}}e_{h,k} \qquad(s_{i,j}\le r<p_j).$$
Finally let $\chi\colon\mathfrak m\to\mathbb C$ be $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$,
where the trace is the trace of the $N\times N$ matrix.

The verification below records the properties of this data that are used
throughout this page. $e\in\mathfrak g_1$ has Jordan type $\lambda$; $\mathfrak p$
is a parabolic subalgebra with Levi factor
$\mathfrak h\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{q_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{q_l}$ and
nilradical $\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$, while $\mathfrak m$ is the
nilradical of the opposite parabolic; the elements $e_{i,j;r}$ with
$s_{i,j}\le r<p_j$ form a basis of the centralizer
$\mathfrak g^e=\{X\in\mathfrak g:[X,e]=0\}$; the box set
$J=\{(a,b)\in\{1,\dots,N\}^2:\mathrm{col}(a)\le\mathrm{col}(b),\ R(b)=\emptyset\}$
is in bijection with $K=\{(i,j,r):1\le i,j\le n,\ s_{i,j}\le r<p_j\}$ via
$(a,b)\mapsto(\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b),\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a))$, and
$$\xi_{a,b}:=\sum_{t=0}^{\mathrm{col}(a)-1}e_{L^t(a),L^t(b)}=e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)};$$
and $\chi$ is a Lie algebra character, $\chi([\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m])=0$. This
grading is the type-A pyramid good grading in the degree-one convention:
$\operatorname{ad}e:\mathfrak g_r\to\mathfrak g_{r+1}$ is injective for
$r<0$ and surjective for $r\ge0$. For $e\ne0$ it differs from the standard
Dynkin grading, in which $e$ has degree $2$ rather than $1$. For $e=0$ all
boxes lie in one column or there are no boxes, and the pyramid grading and
the trivial Dynkin grading both concentrate $\mathfrak g$ in degree zero.
If $N=0$, take $\mathfrak{gl}_0=0$: the box set and both centralizer index
sets are empty, $e=0$, $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak h=\mathfrak m=0$, and
$\chi=0$. These conventions also permit an empty row list.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

derivations.claim: **Unit, membership and counit.** The shifted $\mathfrak m$ action on $Q_\chi$ lowers the bounded-below Kazhdan filtration: $(x-\chi(x))u1_\chi=[x,u]1_\chi$, and for negative doubled degree $-2r$ the commutator lowers filtration by $2r>0$. This proves local nilpotence on $Q_\chi\otimes_W M$ too, so the adjunction lands in $\mathcal C(\lambda)$. By [F1], its unit $M\to\mathrm{Wh}(Q_\chi\otimes_W M)$ is an isomorphism. For $N\in\mathcal C(\lambda)$, the triangle identity makes $\mathrm{Wh}(c_N)$ an isomorphism. Left exactness gives $\mathrm{Wh}(\ker c_N)=0$, hence $\ker c_N=0$ by detection. Now the short exact sequence with this injective counit has $H^1$ of its domain zero by [F1]; its cohomology sequence gives $\mathrm{Wh}(\operatorname{coker}c_N)=0$. Detection makes that cokernel zero. Thus the unit and counit are isomorphisms, proving the equivalence without presuming exactness of $\mathrm{Wh}$.

Exactness and detection. Exactness of $\mathrm{Wh}$ follows because it is inverse to the exact functor $Q_\chi\otimes_{W(\lambda)}-$ (tensoring with the right-free module $Q_\chi$ proved in the local cohomology supplier [F1]), and the detection statement is the case $H^0=0$ of [F1].

The transported tensor functor. For $M\in W(\lambda)$-mod and finite-dimensional $X$, the functor $M\mapsto\mathrm{Wh}((Q_\chi\otimes_{W(\lambda)}M)\otimes X)$ is exact in $M$ because the composed functors are exact; it is the transport of $?\otimes X$ across the equivalence.

**Invertibility of the displayed tensor map.** Let $M$ be a $\mathfrak p$-module and put $N=Q_\chi\otimes_W M$. PBW gives representatives $\eta(u)1_\chi$, and $\psi_M(\eta(u)1_\chi\otimes m)=um$ is balanced because right multiplication by $\eta(w)$ changes $u$ to $uw$. Hence $\mu_{M,X}=(\psi_M\otimes1)|_{\mathrm{Wh}}$ is a defined linear map. Use [F4]'s finite flag of $X$. Each quotient of $N\otimes X_j$ by $N\otimes X_{j-1}$ is a finite direct sum of $N$, with trivial $\mathfrak m$ action on its finite factor. By [F1] it has vanishing positive twisted cohomology and invariants $M\otimes(X_j/X_{j-1})$. Induction and the long exact sequence give the same vanishing on each $N\otimes X_j$, and give short exact sequences on their invariant spaces. The map $\mu$ preserves these filtrations. On each successive quotient, the invariants are represented by $1_\chi\otimes m\otimes\bar x$ and $\psi_M$ sends them to $m\otimes\bar x$. Thus its quotient maps are identities; induction through the finite short exact sequences makes $\mu$ bijective. This argument holds for arbitrary $M$ and needs no cofree realization or completion of $M$.

Associativity. The associativity isomorphisms of the transported functor are obtained by inserting the canonical associativity isomorphisms of the tensor product of $\mathfrak g$-modules into the definition of $\circledast$ and applying the inverse equivalence; they are compatible by the naturality of the unit and counit of the adjunction and by the coherence of the tensor associativity in $\mathcal C(\lambda)$.

**Balancing and $W$-linearity.** PBW gives unique representatives $\eta(u)1_\chi$, $u\in U(\mathfrak p)$, in $Q_\chi$. Define $\psi_M(\eta(u)1_\chi\otimes m)=um$. Since the right action of $w\in W\subset U(\mathfrak p)$ sends this representative to $\eta(uw)1_\chi$, the formula is right-$W$-balanced: $(uw)m=u(wm)$. Moreover $\psi_M(\eta(v)q\otimes m)=v\psi_M(q\otimes m)$ for $v\in U(\mathfrak p)$. The shift $\eta$ adds a Lie character on $\mathfrak p$, so on its primitive generators, and hence multiplicatively on $U(\mathfrak p)$, $(\eta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(v)=\Delta\eta(v)$. The $W$ action on the source Whittaker subspace is therefore $\Delta\eta(w)$, while the target restricted $\mathfrak p$-module $M\otimes X$ has action $\Delta(w)$. Applying $\psi_M\otimes\mathrm{id}$ to the displayed coproduct identity proves $\mu_{M,X}(wz)=w\mu_{M,X}(z)$. Together with step 2.1 this proves the actual stated $W$-module isomorphism. No equality with cofree evaluation or citation-only character-equation argument is used.

Independence of the order. For $X=V^{\otimes d}$ the isomorphism $\mu_d$ is the composite of the single-step maps $\mu_{\bullet,V}$; two different parenthesizations differ by the associativity isomorphisms of step 2.2, and both are restrictions of the balanced evaluation maps of step 3.1, applied with the same iterated coproduct on $U(\mathfrak p)$; coassociativity and the displayed shift identity make these maps equal. Therefore the resulting isomorphism $\mathbb C_c\circledast V^{\circledast d}\to V_c^{\otimes d}$ is independent of the composed associativity isomorphisms.

Work over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]],
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Fix $N\ge1$, let
$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with its matrix units $E_{ij}$ and the
trace form $B(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, which is symmetric, nondegenerate and
invariant ([[prop-trace-forms-are-symmetric-and-invariant]]), and let
$$z:=\sum_{i=1}^NE_{ii}\in\mathfrak g$$
be the central element (the identity matrix). The dual basis of $(E_{ij})$
under $B$ is $(E_{ji})$, so the invariant Casimir tensor is
$$\Omega=\sum_{i,j=1}^NE_{ij}\otimes E_{ji}\in U(\mathfrak g)\otimes U(\mathfrak g),$$
Its action on a tensor product of two $\mathfrak g$-modules commutes with the diagonal action, as computed in [F2]. Multiplying its two factors gives the central Casimir element of [[def-casimir-operator-relative-to-an-invariant-form]].

Let $M$ be a $\mathfrak g$-module and $V=\mathbb C^N$ the natural module
([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). On the tensor product
$M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]],
[[thm-associativity-of-balanced-tensor-products]]) label the factors
$0,1,\dots,d$, with factor $0$ equal to $M$. For $0\le a\ne b\le d$ let
$\Omega_{ab}$ denote the operator obtained by applying $\Omega$ in the two
labelled factors, and for distinct $1\le a,b\le d$ let $P_{ab}$ denote the
operator that interchanges the two labelled factors (the flip of
$V\otimes V$ on two $V$-factors). Define, for $1\le j\le d$ and
$1\le i\le d-1$,
$$x_j:=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj},\qquad s_i:=P_{i,i+1}.$$
Finally put $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}:=\Omega-\tfrac1Nz\otimes z$ and define the
Arakawa-Suzuki normalized operators
$$y_j:=x_j-\tfrac1Nz_M+\tfrac{N-1}{2},$$
where $z_M$ denotes the endomorphism of $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ given by the
action of $z$ on the factor $M$. This is a central endomorphism, and is a scalar only when $z$ acts scalarly on $M$.

The verification below records the properties of these operators used on this
page: $\Omega$ acts on $V\otimes V$ as the flip; the operators $x_j$ and
$s_i$ are natural in $M$ and commute with the $\mathfrak g$-action; the
recursion $x_{j+1}=s_jx_js_j+s_j$ holds; $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ is the Casimir
of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ relative to the restricted trace form; and the operators
$y_j$ are exactly the source operators of [AS, (2.2.2)]. For $d=0$ the family
$(x_j)$ is empty; for the trivial module $M=\mathbb C$ one has $\Omega_{0j}=0$,
so $x_j=\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $x_1=0$.

Let $M$ be a right $R$-module, let ${}_RN_S$ be an $(R,S)$-bimodule, and let $P$ be a left $S$-module. There is a canonical group isomorphism

$$\alpha_{M,N,P}:(M\otimes_RN)\otimes_SP\longrightarrow M\otimes_R(N\otimes_SP)$$

determined by

$$\alpha_{M,N,P}((m\otimes n)\otimes p)=m\otimes(n\otimes p).$$

It respects any compatible outer module actions and is natural in $M,N,P$.

Work over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]],
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Fix $N\ge1$, let
$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with its matrix units $E_{ij}$ and the
trace form $B(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, which is symmetric, nondegenerate and
invariant ([[prop-trace-forms-are-symmetric-and-invariant]]), and let
$$z:=\sum_{i=1}^NE_{ii}\in\mathfrak g$$
be the central element (the identity matrix). The dual basis of $(E_{ij})$
under $B$ is $(E_{ji})$, so the invariant Casimir tensor is
$$\Omega=\sum_{i,j=1}^NE_{ij}\otimes E_{ji}\in U(\mathfrak g)\otimes U(\mathfrak g),$$
Its action on a tensor product of two $\mathfrak g$-modules commutes with the diagonal action, as computed in [F2]. Multiplying its two factors gives the central Casimir element of [[def-casimir-operator-relative-to-an-invariant-form]].

Let $M$ be a $\mathfrak g$-module and $V=\mathbb C^N$ the natural module
([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). On the tensor product
$M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]],
[[thm-associativity-of-balanced-tensor-products]]) label the factors
$0,1,\dots,d$, with factor $0$ equal to $M$. For $0\le a\ne b\le d$ let
$\Omega_{ab}$ denote the operator obtained by applying $\Omega$ in the two
labelled factors, and for distinct $1\le a,b\le d$ let $P_{ab}$ denote the
operator that interchanges the two labelled factors (the flip of
$V\otimes V$ on two $V$-factors). Define, for $1\le j\le d$ and
$1\le i\le d-1$,
$$x_j:=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj},\qquad s_i:=P_{i,i+1}.$$
Finally put $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}:=\Omega-\tfrac1Nz\otimes z$ and define the
Arakawa-Suzuki normalized operators
$$y_j:=x_j-\tfrac1Nz_M+\tfrac{N-1}{2},$$
where $z_M$ denotes the endomorphism of $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ given by the
action of $z$ on the factor $M$. This is a central endomorphism, and is a scalar only when $z$ acts scalarly on $M$.

The verification below records the properties of these operators used on this
page: $\Omega$ acts on $V\otimes V$ as the flip; the operators $x_j$ and
$s_i$ are natural in $M$ and commute with the $\mathfrak g$-action; the
recursion $x_{j+1}=s_jx_js_j+s_j$ holds; $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ is the Casimir
of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ relative to the restricted trace form; and the operators
$y_j$ are exactly the source operators of [AS, (2.2.2)]. For $d=0$ the family
$(x_j)$ is empty; for the trivial module $M=\mathbb C$ one has $\Omega_{0j}=0$,
so $x_j=\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $x_1=0$.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are

[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Work over the field $\mathbb C$ and fix an integer $d\ge 0$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[def-commutative-ring]]). Let
$\mathcal F_d$ be the free associative unital $\mathbb C$-algebra on the
$d+\max(d-1,0)$ symbols $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ (for $d=0$ there is only
the unit; for $d=1$ only $x_1$), with its word basis and universal property
([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]), and let
$I_d\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}\mathcal F_d$ be the two-sided ideal
([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]])
generated by the following elements:

- $x_ix_j-x_jx_i$ for all $1\le i,j\le d$;
- $s_i^2-1$, $s_is_{i+1}s_i-s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}$, and $s_is_j-s_js_i$ for
  $|i-j|>1$, for $1\le i,j\le d-1$;
- $s_ix_j-x_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$, $s_ix_{i+1}-x_is_i-1$, and
  $x_{i+1}s_i-s_ix_i-1$, for $1\le i\le d-1$ and $1\le j\le d$.

The **degenerate affine Hecke algebra** is the quotient $\mathbb C$-algebra
$$H_d:=\mathcal F_d/I_d$$
with unit element written $1$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-laws]]). We keep the symbols
$x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ for their images, and for $w\in S_d$ we write
$w$ for the image in $H_d$ of any word in the $s_i$ representing $w$; this is
independent of the chosen word once the basis theorem below is proved. For
$d\ge1$ and $a\in\mathbb C$, the notation $H_d/(x_1-a)$ means the quotient by the two-sided
ideal generated by $x_1-a$.

The verification below establishes exactly the structure of $H_d$ used
throughout this page: the ordered monomials
$$x_1^{r_1}\cdots x_d^{r_d}w,\qquad r_1,\dots,r_d\ge0,\ w\in S_d,$$
form a $\mathbb C$-basis, so that
$H_d\cong\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[S_d]$ as a vector
space with polynomial and group-algebra subalgebras
([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]], [[def-group-ring]]);
$H_0=\mathbb C$ and $H_1=\mathbb C[x_1]$; for $d\ge1$ and every $a$ there is a unique
algebra isomorphism
$$H_d/(x_1-a)\cong\mathbb C[S_d],\qquad x_j\longmapsto a+\sum_{k<j}(k\ j);$$
and total polynomial degree is an algebra filtration whose associated graded is
the semidirect product $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$ in which
$s_i$ acts by swapping $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$. For $d\ge2$, the cross relation is
inhomogeneous, so it does not turn $H_d$ into a graded algebra with
$\deg x_i=1$ and $\deg s_i=0$. For $d=0$ the algebra $\mathbb C$ has its
degree-zero grading, and for $d=1$ the algebra $\mathbb C[x_1]$ has its
natural polynomial grading.

The Casimir element $\Omega_B$ is independent of the chosen dual bases and
belongs to the center of $U(\mathfrak g)$. Consequently its action on every
$\mathfrak g$-module is a $\mathfrak g$-intertwiner.

For a vector space $V$ over $k$, write

$$\mathfrak{gl}(V)=\operatorname{End}_k(V)$$

with commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Expansion of triple composites shows
that this is a Lie algebra in every characteristic.

A **representation** of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ on $V$ is a Lie-algebra
homomorphism

$$\rho:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow\mathfrak{gl}(V).$$

Writing $xv$ for $\rho(x)(v)$, this is equivalently a $k$-bilinear action
$\mathfrak g\times V\to V$ satisfying

$$[x,y]v=x(yv)-y(xv)$$

for all $x,y\in\mathfrak g$ and $v\in V$. No finite-dimensional hypothesis is
imposed on either $\mathfrak g$ or $V$. The zero vector space and the zero
action are allowed.

derivations.claim: The infinitesimal braid identities. For distinct labels $a,b,c$ one has $[\Omega_{ab},\Omega_{ac}+\Omega_{bc}]=0$: expanding $\Omega=\sum E_{uv}\otimes E_{vu}$ and using [F3], the double commutator sum splits into terms $[E_{uv},E_{xy}]\otimes E_{vu}\otimes E_{yx}$ and $E_{uv}\otimes[E_{vu},E_{xy}]\otimes E_{yx}$, and the two resulting sums cancel term by term after relabelling; equivalently, this is the identity $[\Omega_{12},\Omega_{13}+\Omega_{23}]=0$ in $U(\mathfrak g)^{\otimes3}$, which is the derivative of the invariance of $\Omega$ under the diagonal adjoint action. Consequently $[\Omega_{ab},\Omega_{ac}]=-[\Omega_{ab},\Omega_{bc}]=[\Omega_{ac},\Omega_{bc}]$. In particular, for three natural factors this is the identity $[P_{ab},P_{ac}]+[P_{ab},P_{bc}]=0$ for the flips.

The Coxeter relations for $s_i$. $s_i=P_{i,i+1}$ is an involution; $s_is_j=s_js_i$ for $|i-j|>1$ because the pairs of interchanged labels are disjoint; and $s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}$ because both sides are the permutation operator inducing the same permutation of the three labelled factors.

Cross relations. Conjugation by $s_i=P_{i,i+1}$ interchanges the labels $i$ and $i+1$ in any operator supported on those factors, so $s_i\Omega_{0,i+1}=\Omega_{0i}s_i$ and $s_iP_{k,i+1}=P_{ki}s_i$ for $k<i$. Therefore $s_ix_{i+1}=s_i\Omega_{0,i+1}+\sum_{k<i}s_iP_{k,i+1}+s_iP_{i,i+1}=\Omega_{0i}s_i+\sum_{k<i}P_{ki}s_i+1=x_is_i+1$, and symmetrically $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$. For $j<i$, all labels in $x_j$ are disjoint from $\{i,i+1\}$, so $s_i$ commutes with every summand. For $j>i+1$, $\Omega_{0j}$ and the terms $P_{kj}$ with $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$ commute with $s_i$, while conjugation by $s_i$ interchanges $P_{ij}$ and $P_{i+1,j}$. Their sum is invariant, so again $s_ix_j=x_js_i$; the two overlapping summands need not commute individually.

Polynomial commutation. Fix $i<j$. Since $x_i=\Omega_{0i}+\sum_{k<i}P_{ki}$ and $x_j=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{l<j}P_{lj}$, the commutator is $[\Omega_{0i},\Omega_{0j}]+\sum_{l<j}[\Omega_{0i},P_{lj}]+\sum_{k<i}[P_{ki},\Omega_{0j}]+\sum_{k<i}\sum_{l<j}[P_{ki},P_{lj}]$. The second sum reduces to the single term $[\Omega_{0i},P_{ij}]$ (all other $P_{lj}$ are disjoint from the labels $0,i$), and the third sum vanishes (all pairs $\{k,i\}$, $\{0,j\}$ are disjoint since $k<i<j$). In the fourth sum only the terms with $k=l$ or $l=i$ can fail to vanish, so it equals $\sum_{k<i}([P_{ki},P_{kj}]+[P_{ki},P_{ij}])$. Hence $[x_i,x_j]=([\Omega_{0i},\Omega_{0j}]+[\Omega_{0i},P_{ij}])+\sum_{k<i}([P_{ki},P_{kj}]+[P_{ki},P_{ij}])$. The first bracket vanishes by step 1.1 with $a=0$, $b=i$, $c=j$ together with $\Omega_{ij}=P_{ij}$; each summand of the second bracket vanishes by step 1.1 for the three distinct labels $k,i,j$. Therefore $[x_i,x_j]=0$.

Naturality, commutation with $\mathfrak g$, and the right action. The place permutations are natural in $M$ and commute with $\mathfrak g$; the Casimir operators are intertwiners by [F5]; hence every $x_j$ and $s_i$ is natural and $\mathfrak g$-linear. The relations established in steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2 are exactly the defining relations of $H_d$ [F4], so the assignment $x_j\mapsto x_j$, $s_i\mapsto s_i$ defines a left $H_d$-action. The generator-fixing anti-automorphism $\omega$ of $H_d$ (which preserves each defining relation because the reversed cross relation $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$ is also a defining relation) converts it into a right action by $e\cdot u:=\rho(\omega(u))e$; the anti-automorphism property gives $(e\cdot u)\cdot v=\rho(\omega(v))\rho(\omega(u))e=\rho(\omega(uv))e=e\cdot(uv)$. This proves both assertions.

For any fixed order on the family $D_i^{(r)}$ ($r\ge1$),
$E_{i,j}^{(r)}$ ($i<j$, $r>s_{i,j}$), and $F_{j,i}^{(r)}$ ($i<j$, $r>s_{j,i}$),
with each root mode included once, their ordered monomials form a $\mathbb C$-basis of $Y_n(\sigma)$. Its canonical associated graded algebra is the polynomial
algebra on the corresponding symbols, while its loop associated graded algebra
is the universal enveloping algebra of the current algebra
$\mathfrak{gl}_n[t](\sigma)$; the two graded algebras are different and
non-isomorphic in general. In the finite quotient $W(\lambda)$ the ordered
monomials in the finite Gauss range
$$s_{i,j}<r\le s_{i,j}+p_{\min(i,j)}$$
form a basis, and the commutative Kazhdan/canonical associated graded and the
noncommutative loop associated graded are distinct. Equivalently, the finite
$T$-coefficients with $s_{i,j}<r\le S_{i,j}$ form an ordered PBW basis, where
$r$ is the unshifted coefficient index of $T=FDE$, not a reindexed value.

Work over $\mathbb C$ and fix $n\ge1$ together with a shift matrix
$\sigma=(s_{i,j})_{1\le i,j\le n}$ of nonnegative integers satisfying
$s_{i,j}+s_{j,k}=s_{i,k}$ whenever $i\le j\le k$ or $i\ge j\ge k$, and
$s_{i,i}=0$. The **shifted Yangian** $Y_n(\sigma)$ is the associative unital
$\mathbb C$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) generated by the
shifted Drinfeld generators $D_i^{(r)}$ ($1\le i\le n$, $r\ge1$),
$E_i^{(r)}$ ($1\le i<n$, $r>s_{i,i+1}$), and
$F_i^{(r)}$ ($1\le i<n$, $r>s_{i+1,i}$). For $i<j$, the higher-root
coefficients $E_{i,j}^{(r)}$ have range $r>s_{i,j}$ and
$F_{j,i}^{(r)}$ have range $r>s_{j,i}$; they are defined recursively by
adjacent-root commutators, not declared as a duplicate independent family.
Put $D_i^{(0)}=1$, $D_i(u)=\sum_{r\ge0}D_i^{(r)}u^{-r}$ and $\widetilde D_i(u)=-D_i(u)^{-1}$. The defining relations are the following, for every index for which all displayed generators exist (in particular the $E$ and $F$ indices exceed their respective shifts):

$$[D_i^{(r)},D_j^{(s)}]=0,\qquad [E_i^{(r)},F_j^{(s)}]=\delta_{ij}\sum_{t=0}^{r+s-1}\widetilde D_i^{(t)}D_{i+1}^{(r+s-1-t)}.$$

$$[D_i^{(r)},E_j^{(s)}]=(\delta_{ij}-\delta_{i,j+1})\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}D_i^{(t)}E_j^{(r+s-1-t)}.$$

$$[D_i^{(r)},F_j^{(s)}]=(\delta_{i,j+1}-\delta_{ij})\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}F_j^{(r+s-1-t)}D_i^{(t)}.$$

$$[E_i^{(r)},E_i^{(s+1)}]-[E_i^{(r+1)},E_i^{(s)}]=E_i^{(r)}E_i^{(s)}+E_i^{(s)}E_i^{(r)}.$$

$$[F_i^{(r+1)},F_i^{(s)}]-[F_i^{(r)},F_i^{(s+1)}]=F_i^{(r)}F_i^{(s)}+F_i^{(s)}F_i^{(r)}.$$

$$[E_i^{(r)},E_{i+1}^{(s+1)}]-[E_i^{(r+1)},E_{i+1}^{(s)}]=-E_i^{(r)}E_{i+1}^{(s)}.$$

$$[F_i^{(r+1)},F_{i+1}^{(s)}]-[F_i^{(r)},F_{i+1}^{(s+1)}]=-F_{i+1}^{(s)}F_i^{(r)}.$$

For $|i-j|>1$, $[E_i^{(r)},E_j^{(s)}]=[F_i^{(r)},F_j^{(s)}]=0$. For $|i-j|=1$ impose

$$[E_i^{(r)},[E_i^{(s)},E_j^{(t)}]]+[E_i^{(s)},[E_i^{(r)},E_j^{(t)}]]=0,$$

$$[F_i^{(r)},[F_i^{(s)},F_j^{(t)}]]+[F_i^{(s)},[F_i^{(r)},F_j^{(t)}]]=0.$$

The higher roots are specified without new independent generators by $E_{i,i+1}^{(r)}=E_i^{(r)}$, $F_{i+1,i}^{(r)}=F_i^{(r)}$, and, for $j>i+1$,

$$E_{i,j}^{(r)}=[E_{i,j-1}^{(r-s_{j-1,j})},E_{j-1}^{(s_{j-1,j}+1)}],\qquad F_{j,i}^{(r)}=[F_{j-1}^{(s_{j,j-1}+1)},F_{j-1,i}^{(r-s_{j,j-1})}].$$

These are [BK, Section 2.1, (2.7)–(2.18), and Section 2.2, (2.21)–(2.22)], with the negative root written in matrix-row order here. Two filtrations are fixed on it: the **canonical
filtration**, in which each generator of upper index $r$ has degree $r$, and
the **loop filtration**, in which it has degree $r-1$; their associated
graded algebras are different (the canonical one is commutative polynomial,
the loop one is a current algebra).

for $i\ge j$, and the **type-A finite W-algebra** is the quotient
$$W(\lambda)=Y_n(\sigma)/\bigl(D_1^{(r)},\ r>p_1\bigr)$$
of $Y_n(\sigma)$ by the two-sided ideal generated by the higher modes of

with $T(u)=\sum_{r\ge0}T_{i,j}^{(r)}u^{-r}$, $T_{i,j}^{(0)}=\delta_{i,j}$, and
**no** additional factor $u^{s_{i,j}}$: the coefficient of $u^{-r}$ is the
mode $T_{i,j}^{(r)}$. Its modes satisfy $T_{i,j}^{(r)}=0$ for
$0<r\le s_{i,j}$, and in the finite quotient also $T_{i,j}^{(r)}=0$ for
$r>S_{i,j}:=s_{i,j}+p_{\min(i,j)}$, so the finite quotient has the PBW basis
of ordered monomials
$$T_{i,j}^{(r)},\qquad s_{i,j}<r\le S_{i,j}.$$
The auxiliary signed path polynomials used in the source to construct the
Gauss generators are not all identified with these shifted $T$-modes; the root
of $T_{i,j}^{(r)}$ is the weight $\varepsilon_i-\varepsilon_j$, and the
surviving modes have loop leading term $(-1)^{r-1}e_{i,j;r-1}$ in the
centralizer basis of the pyramid.

Work over $\mathbb C$ and fix $n\ge1$ together with a shift matrix
$\sigma=(s_{i,j})_{1\le i,j\le n}$ of nonnegative integers satisfying
$s_{i,j}+s_{j,k}=s_{i,k}$ whenever $i\le j\le k$ or $i\ge j\ge k$, and
$s_{i,i}=0$. The **shifted Yangian** $Y_n(\sigma)$ is the associative unital
$\mathbb C$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) generated by the
shifted Drinfeld generators $D_i^{(r)}$ ($1\le i\le n$, $r\ge1$),
$E_i^{(r)}$ ($1\le i<n$, $r>s_{i,i+1}$), and
$F_i^{(r)}$ ($1\le i<n$, $r>s_{i+1,i}$). For $i<j$, the higher-root
coefficients $E_{i,j}^{(r)}$ have range $r>s_{i,j}$ and
$F_{j,i}^{(r)}$ have range $r>s_{j,i}$; they are defined recursively by
adjacent-root commutators, not declared as a duplicate independent family.
Put $D_i^{(0)}=1$, $D_i(u)=\sum_{r\ge0}D_i^{(r)}u^{-r}$ and $\widetilde D_i(u)=-D_i(u)^{-1}$. The defining relations are the following, for every index for which all displayed generators exist (in particular the $E$ and $F$ indices exceed their respective shifts):

$$[D_i^{(r)},D_j^{(s)}]=0,\qquad [E_i^{(r)},F_j^{(s)}]=\delta_{ij}\sum_{t=0}^{r+s-1}\widetilde D_i^{(t)}D_{i+1}^{(r+s-1-t)}.$$

$$[D_i^{(r)},E_j^{(s)}]=(\delta_{ij}-\delta_{i,j+1})\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}D_i^{(t)}E_j^{(r+s-1-t)}.$$

$$[D_i^{(r)},F_j^{(s)}]=(\delta_{i,j+1}-\delta_{ij})\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}F_j^{(r+s-1-t)}D_i^{(t)}.$$

$$[E_i^{(r)},E_i^{(s+1)}]-[E_i^{(r+1)},E_i^{(s)}]=E_i^{(r)}E_i^{(s)}+E_i^{(s)}E_i^{(r)}.$$

$$[F_i^{(r+1)},F_i^{(s)}]-[F_i^{(r)},F_i^{(s+1)}]=F_i^{(r)}F_i^{(s)}+F_i^{(s)}F_i^{(r)}.$$

$$[E_i^{(r)},E_{i+1}^{(s+1)}]-[E_i^{(r+1)},E_{i+1}^{(s)}]=-E_i^{(r)}E_{i+1}^{(s)}.$$

$$[F_i^{(r+1)},F_{i+1}^{(s)}]-[F_i^{(r)},F_{i+1}^{(s+1)}]=-F_{i+1}^{(s)}F_i^{(r)}.$$

For $|i-j|>1$, $[E_i^{(r)},E_j^{(s)}]=[F_i^{(r)},F_j^{(s)}]=0$. For $|i-j|=1$ impose

$$[E_i^{(r)},[E_i^{(s)},E_j^{(t)}]]+[E_i^{(s)},[E_i^{(r)},E_j^{(t)}]]=0,$$

$$[F_i^{(r)},[F_i^{(s)},F_j^{(t)}]]+[F_i^{(s)},[F_i^{(r)},F_j^{(t)}]]=0.$$

The higher roots are specified without new independent generators by $E_{i,i+1}^{(r)}=E_i^{(r)}$, $F_{i+1,i}^{(r)}=F_i^{(r)}$, and, for $j>i+1$,

$$E_{i,j}^{(r)}=[E_{i,j-1}^{(r-s_{j-1,j})},E_{j-1}^{(s_{j-1,j}+1)}],\qquad F_{j,i}^{(r)}=[F_{j-1}^{(s_{j,j-1}+1)},F_{j-1,i}^{(r-s_{j,j-1})}].$$

These are [BK, Section 2.1, (2.7)–(2.18), and Section 2.2, (2.21)–(2.22)], with the negative root written in matrix-row order here. Two filtrations are fixed on it: the **canonical
filtration**, in which each generator of upper index $r$ has degree $r$, and
the **loop filtration**, in which it has degree $r-1$; their associated
graded algebras are different (the canonical one is commutative polynomial,
the loop one is a current algebra).

For the pyramid $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ with conjugate
$q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$ ([[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]])
the relevant shift matrix is $s_{i,j}=p_j-p_i$ for $i\le j$ and $s_{i,j}=0$
for $i\ge j$, and the **type-A finite W-algebra** is the quotient
$$W(\lambda)=Y_n(\sigma)/\bigl(D_1^{(r)},\ r>p_1\bigr)$$
of $Y_n(\sigma)$ by the two-sided ideal generated by the higher modes of
$D_1$ beyond $p_1$.

Write the Gauss decomposition $T(u)=F(u)D(u)E(u)$ of the generating matrix,
with $T(u)=\sum_{r\ge0}T_{i,j}^{(r)}u^{-r}$, $T_{i,j}^{(0)}=\delta_{i,j}$, and
**no** additional factor $u^{s_{i,j}}$: the coefficient of $u^{-r}$ is the
mode $T_{i,j}^{(r)}$. Its modes satisfy $T_{i,j}^{(r)}=0$ for
$0<r\le s_{i,j}$, and in the finite quotient also $T_{i,j}^{(r)}=0$ for
$r>S_{i,j}:=s_{i,j}+p_{\min(i,j)}$, so the finite quotient has the PBW basis
of ordered monomials
$$T_{i,j}^{(r)},\qquad s_{i,j}<r\le S_{i,j}.$$
The auxiliary signed path polynomials used in the source to construct the
Gauss generators are not all identified with these shifted $T$-modes; the root
of $T_{i,j}^{(r)}$ is the weight $\varepsilon_i-\varepsilon_j$, and the
surviving modes have loop leading term $(-1)^{r-1}e_{i,j;r-1}$ in the
centralizer basis of the pyramid.

Work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ be a partition
of $N\ge0$ with transpose $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, where $l=p_n$ for a
nonempty row list and $l=0$ for an empty row list. Zero-length rows have no
boxes. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with matrix units
$e_{i,j}$ in the standard basis
$v_1,\dots,v_N$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]). Number the
boxes of the diagram of $\lambda$ by $1,\dots,N$ down columns from the left,
and for a box $i$ write $\mathrm{row}(i),\mathrm{col}(i)$ for its row and
column, $L(i)$ for the box immediately to its left (or $\emptyset$ if absent),
and $R(i)$ for the box immediately to its right (or $\emptyset$ if absent).
Define the nilpotent endomorphism
$$e=\sum_{i:\ L(i)\ne\emptyset}e_{L(i),i}\in\mathfrak g,\qquad ev_i=v_{L(i)},$$
and declare $\deg e_{i,j}=\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)$ for all $i,j$, so
that $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_r$ with
$\mathfrak g_r=\operatorname{span}\{e_{i,j}:\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)=r\}$.
Put
$$\mathfrak p=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r,\qquad \mathfrak h=\mathfrak g_0,\qquad \mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r,$$
and for rows $1\le i,j\le n$ define the shift $s_{i,j}=p_j-p_i$ if $i\le j$
and $s_{i,j}=0$ if $i\ge j$, together with the centralizer elements
$$e_{i,j;r}=\sum_{\substack{\mathrm{row}(h)=i,\ \mathrm{row}(k)=j\\ \mathrm{col}(k)-\mathrm{col}(h)=r}}e_{h,k} \qquad(s_{i,j}\le r<p_j).$$
Finally let $\chi\colon\mathfrak m\to\mathbb C$ be $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$,
where the trace is the trace of the $N\times N$ matrix.

The verification below records the properties of this data that are used
throughout this page. $e\in\mathfrak g_1$ has Jordan type $\lambda$; $\mathfrak p$
is a parabolic subalgebra with Levi factor
$\mathfrak h\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{q_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{q_l}$ and
nilradical $\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$, while $\mathfrak m$ is the
nilradical of the opposite parabolic; the elements $e_{i,j;r}$ with
$s_{i,j}\le r<p_j$ form a basis of the centralizer
$\mathfrak g^e=\{X\in\mathfrak g:[X,e]=0\}$; the box set
$J=\{(a,b)\in\{1,\dots,N\}^2:\mathrm{col}(a)\le\mathrm{col}(b),\ R(b)=\emptyset\}$
is in bijection with $K=\{(i,j,r):1\le i,j\le n,\ s_{i,j}\le r<p_j\}$ via
$(a,b)\mapsto(\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b),\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a))$, and
$$\xi_{a,b}:=\sum_{t=0}^{\mathrm{col}(a)-1}e_{L^t(a),L^t(b)}=e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)};$$
and $\chi$ is a Lie algebra character, $\chi([\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m])=0$. This
grading is the type-A pyramid good grading in the degree-one convention:
$\operatorname{ad}e:\mathfrak g_r\to\mathfrak g_{r+1}$ is injective for
$r<0$ and surjective for $r\ge0$. For $e\ne0$ it differs from the standard
Dynkin grading, in which $e$ has degree $2$ rather than $1$. For $e=0$ all
boxes lie in one column or there are no boxes, and the pyramid grading and
the trivial Dynkin grading both concentrate $\mathfrak g$ in degree zero.
If $N=0$, take $\mathfrak{gl}_0=0$: the box set and both centralizer index
sets are empty, $e=0$, $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak h=\mathfrak m=0$, and
$\chi=0$. These conventions also permit an empty row list.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_r$ be an ordered basis of a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Then the monomials

$$x_1^{a_1}x_2^{a_2}\cdots x_r^{a_r} \qquad (a_i\in \mathbb N_0)$$

form a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)$. In particular, multiplication identifies $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)$ with the symmetric algebra $S(\mathfrak g)$ on the symbols of the $x_i$.

Let $A$ be a unital algebra with an increasing **multiplicative filtration**

$$0=F_{-1}A\subseteq F_0A\subseteq F_1A\subseteq\cdots,$$

where $1\in F_0A$ and $(F_mA)(F_nA)\subseteq F_{m+n}A$. Its
**associated graded algebra** is

$$\operatorname{gr}_F A=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}F_nA/F_{n-1}A,$$

with multiplication on homogeneous classes

$$ (a+F_{m-1}A)(b+F_{n-1}A)=ab+F_{m+n-1}A.$$

This product is well-defined. Indeed, if $a$ changes by
$u\in F_{m-1}A$ and $b$ by $v\in F_{n-1}A$, the product changes by
$ub+av+uv\in F_{m+n-1}A$. Associativity and the unit class descend from $A$.

For any fixed order on the family $D_i^{(r)}$ ($r\ge1$),
$E_{i,j}^{(r)}$ ($i<j$, $r>s_{i,j}$), and $F_{j,i}^{(r)}$ ($i<j$, $r>s_{j,i}$),
with each root mode included once, their ordered monomials form a $\mathbb C$-basis of $Y_n(\sigma)$. Its canonical associated graded algebra is the polynomial
algebra on the corresponding symbols, while its loop associated graded algebra
is the universal enveloping algebra of the current algebra
$\mathfrak{gl}_n[t](\sigma)$; the two graded algebras are different and
non-isomorphic in general. In the finite quotient $W(\lambda)$ the ordered
monomials in the finite Gauss range
$$s_{i,j}<r\le s_{i,j}+p_{\min(i,j)}$$
form a basis, and the commutative Kazhdan/canonical associated graded and the
noncommutative loop associated graded are distinct. Equivalently, the finite
$T$-coefficients with $s_{i,j}<r\le S_{i,j}$ form an ordered PBW basis, where
$r$ is the unshifted coefficient index of $T=FDE$, not a reindexed value.

derivations.claim: **Actual ambient leading term.** Give a matrix unit $e_{a,b}\in\mathfrak p$ its good degree $\operatorname{col}(b)-\operatorname{col}(a)$. In the explicit signed path formula a term of canonical degree $r+1$ with $k$ matrix-unit factors has good degree at most $r+1-k$; a diagonal scalar replacement only lowers that degree. Therefore only single-factor terms contribute in good degree $r$. Those terms sum to $(-1)^r\sum e_{a,b}$ over $\operatorname{row}(a)=i$, $\operatorname{row}(b)=j$, $\operatorname{col}(b)-\operatorname{col}(a)=r$, namely $(-1)^re_{i,j;r}$. Products introduced by Gauss factorization or its inverse have at least two factors and have smaller good degree. Thus the leading homogeneous component of $T_{i,j}^{(r+1)}$ in the actual graded algebra $U(\mathfrak p)$ is exactly $(-1)^re_{i,j;r}$. This proves the leading-symbol claim using the path degrees rather than a claim that Gauss inversion alone supplies its sign.

**Independence in the ambient enveloping algebra.** The elements $e_{i,j;r}$ form a homogeneous basis of the actual Lie subalgebra $\mathfrak g^e\subseteq\mathfrak p$. Extend that finite basis to a homogeneous basis of $\mathfrak p$, with an order extending the prescribed order of the centralizer basis. Enveloping PBW implies that the ordered monomials in the $e_{i,j;r}$ are linearly independent in $U(\mathfrak p)$, and that the natural homomorphism $U(\mathfrak g^e)\to U(\mathfrak p)$ is injective. Their products and brackets are the actual ambient products and brackets, including all boundary terms of the centralizer strings. No projection of a current bracket with an arbitrary out-of-range convention is needed.

**Strictness of the loop basis.** The finite $T$ monomials form a vector-space basis of $W(\lambda)$ by [F1]. For a monomial with total loop degree $d$, step 1.1 says that its degree-$d$ homogeneous component in $U(\mathfrak p)$ is, up to the product of its displayed signs, the corresponding PBW monomial in $U(\mathfrak g^e)$. In any nonzero finite linear combination of $T$ monomials, take the largest total loop degree $d$. The degree-$d$ homogeneous component is nonzero by step 1.2, even when degree-zero generators occur. Thus that combination belongs to $\bigoplus_{s\le d}U(\mathfrak p)_s$ and not to $\bigoplus_{s<d}U(\mathfrak p)_s$. Consequently the intersection filtration in the Statement is exactly the span of $T$ monomials of total loop degree at most $d$, and their degree-$d$ symbols form a basis of its associated graded. This verifies symbol independence directly, rather than inferring it from independence of filtered elements.

**The graded algebra isomorphism.** For any subalgebra of a nonnegatively graded algebra with its intersection filtration, taking highest homogeneous components embeds its associated graded into that graded algebra: if a representative's component of degree $d$ is zero it already lies in filtration $d-1$, and multiplication agrees with multiplication of homogeneous components. Apply this to $W(\lambda)\subseteq U(\mathfrak p)$. Step 2.1 identifies its image with the span of the ordered monomials in $\mathfrak g^e$, which is precisely the embedded algebra $U(\mathfrak g^e)$ from step 1.2. Hence $\operatorname{gr}^{\mathrm{loop}}W(\lambda)\cong U(\mathfrak g^e)$, and the identification sends the symbol of $T_{i,j}^{(r+1)}$ to $(-1)^re_{i,j;r}$ as asserted.

**Filtration and the second graded algebra.** Each generator has finite nonnegative good degree, and each element is a finite sum of $T$ monomials, so the loop filtration is exhaustive and bounded below with $F_{-1}=0$. The actual homogeneous decomposition in $U(\mathfrak p)$ and step 2.1 give separatedness. The finite basis is already established in [F1], and step 3.1 establishes its filtered deformation property. Independently, the Kazhdan filtration uses positive weights $\operatorname{col}(b)-\operatorname{col}(a)+1$ on $\mathfrak p$ and has associated graded $\mathbb C[S]$ by [F4]; in the doubled convention its weights are twice these. That graded algebra is commutative, whereas $U(\mathfrak g^e)$ is noncommutative whenever $\mathfrak g^e$ is nonabelian. These are the two claimed filtrations and their respective graded algebras.

citations.quote:
An endomorphism $N:V\to V$ is **nilpotent** if $N^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$. Its **nilpotency index** is the least positive integer $r$ such that $N^r=0$; this least exponent exists by the well-ordering principle ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

The unique endomorphism of the zero space is nilpotent. With the same least-positive-exponent convention, its nilpotency index is $1$ because its identity and zero endomorphisms coincide.

Every nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ has an ordered basis that is the concatenation of Jordan strings for $N$ at $0$. For $V=0$, this is the empty basis and the empty family of strings.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $e$ be a nilpotent endomorphism of a
finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$ ([[def-nilpotent-endomorphism]]),
let $X=\overline{\mathrm{GL}(V)\cdot e}$ be the closure in
$\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ of its conjugacy orbit
([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]), and let
$\partial X=X\setminus\mathrm{GL}(V)\cdot e$. Then $\mathbb C[X]$ is a reduced
irreducible normal domain and $\operatorname{codim}_X\partial X\ge2$. This
holds for every Jordan type, not only the regular nilpotent cone.

The proof uses the *chain schemes*: if the Jordan partition of $e$ has column
lengths $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_t>0$, put $n_i=q_t+\cdots+q_{t-i+1}$ and
$U_i=\mathbb C^{n_i}$ for $0\le i\le t$. Let $M=\prod_{i=1}^{t-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Hom}(U_i,U_{i+1})\times\operatorname{Hom}(U_{i+1},U_i)\bigr)$
with coordinates $(A_i,B_i)$ and let $Z\subseteq M$ be the closed subscheme
$B_1A_1=0$, $B_iA_i=A_{i-1}B_{i-1}$ $(2\le i<t)$. Then $Z$ is a complete
intersection, smooth outside a closed subset of codimension $\ge2$, reduced,
irreducible and normal, and the invariant ring $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ under
$H=\prod_{i<t}\mathrm{GL}(U_i)$ is the coordinate ring of $X$ via the end map
$\theta=A_{t-1}B_{t-1}$ when $t\ge2$. For the empty Jordan diagram ($V=0$,
$t=0$) and the single-column diagram ($e=0$, $t=1$), the chain has no
variables or equations: take $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$, $H$ trivial
and $\theta=0$; the equation list above is imposed only on existing links.
In these cases $X$ is a point, its boundary is empty, and its boundary
codimension is $+\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $e$ be a nilpotent endomorphism of a
finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$, let
$G_e=\{g\in\mathrm{GL}(V):geg^{-1}=e\}$ be its centralizer, and let $d\ge0$.

1. Every $G_e$-fixed endomorphism $B\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V^{\otimes d})$
   is the value at $e$ of a $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant polynomial map
   $\Phi\colon\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$
   (polynomial in the matrix entries of the input, with
   $\Phi(gXg^{-1})=(g^{\otimes d})\Phi(X)(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}$).
2. Every such equivariant polynomial map is a finite sum
   $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h\,\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$ with
   $h_i\ge0$, where $\sigma_h$ is a place permutation of the $d$ tensor
   factors and $c_h$ is an invariant scalar polynomial in $X$ (a polynomial
   in the traces $\operatorname{tr}(X^k)$).

The extension in (1) is proved by Hartogs lifting on the normal codimension-$\ge2$
orbit closure; the structure in (2) is proved by polarization and the
Schur-Weyl description of tensor invariants, not by importing a
first-fundamental-theorem for the full matrix algebra.

Work over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]],
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Fix $N\ge1$, let
$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with its matrix units $E_{ij}$ and the
trace form $B(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, which is symmetric, nondegenerate and
invariant ([[prop-trace-forms-are-symmetric-and-invariant]]), and let
$$z:=\sum_{i=1}^NE_{ii}\in\mathfrak g$$
be the central element (the identity matrix). The dual basis of $(E_{ij})$
under $B$ is $(E_{ji})$, so the invariant Casimir tensor is
$$\Omega=\sum_{i,j=1}^NE_{ij}\otimes E_{ji}\in U(\mathfrak g)\otimes U(\mathfrak g),$$
Its action on a tensor product of two $\mathfrak g$-modules commutes with the diagonal action, as computed in [F2]. Multiplying its two factors gives the central Casimir element of [[def-casimir-operator-relative-to-an-invariant-form]].

Let $M$ be a $\mathfrak g$-module and $V=\mathbb C^N$ the natural module
([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). On the tensor product
$M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]],
[[thm-associativity-of-balanced-tensor-products]]) label the factors
$0,1,\dots,d$, with factor $0$ equal to $M$. For $0\le a\ne b\le d$ let
$\Omega_{ab}$ denote the operator obtained by applying $\Omega$ in the two
labelled factors, and for distinct $1\le a,b\le d$ let $P_{ab}$ denote the
operator that interchanges the two labelled factors (the flip of
$V\otimes V$ on two $V$-factors). Define, for $1\le j\le d$ and
$1\le i\le d-1$,
$$x_j:=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj},\qquad s_i:=P_{i,i+1}.$$
Finally put $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}:=\Omega-\tfrac1Nz\otimes z$ and define the
Arakawa-Suzuki normalized operators
$$y_j:=x_j-\tfrac1Nz_M+\tfrac{N-1}{2},$$
where $z_M$ denotes the endomorphism of $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ given by the
action of $z$ on the factor $M$. This is a central endomorphism, and is a scalar only when $z$ acts scalarly on $M$.

page: $\Omega$ acts on $V\otimes V$ as the flip; the operators $x_j$ and
$s_i$ are natural in $M$ and commute with the $\mathfrak g$-action; the
recursion $x_{j+1}=s_jx_js_j+s_j$ holds; $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ is the Casimir
of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ relative to the restricted trace form; and the operators
$y_j$ are exactly the source operators of [AS, (2.2.2)]. For $d=0$ the family
$(x_j)$ is empty; for the trivial module $M=\mathbb C$ one has $\Omega_{0j}=0$,
so $x_j=\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $x_1=0$.

Let $N\ge1$, let $M$ be a $\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$-module, let
$V=\mathbb C^N$ be the natural module, and on $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ use the
operators $x_j=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $s_i=P_{i,i+1}$ of
[[def-arakawa-suzuki-casimir-operators-on-tensor-functors]]. Then:

1. The operators $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ commute with the
   $\mathfrak g$-action and are natural in $M$, and satisfy all the defining
   relations of the degenerate affine Hecke algebra
   [[def-degenerate-affine-hecke-algebra]]: the Coxeter relations for the
   $s_i$; $s_ix_j=x_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$; $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i+1$ and
   $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$; and the polynomial commutation $[x_i,x_j]=0$.
2. Consequently they define, via the generator-fixing anti-involution of the

   commuting with the left $\mathfrak g$-action.

The commutation of the $x_i$ is an independent check: it does not follow from
the braid relations of the $s_i$ alone.

An operator $T\in\operatorname{End}(E)$ commutes with the action of $B$ if and only if it commutes with the individual $e$-operators and with the place permutations: the first condition says $T\in A^{\otimes d}$ by [F2], and then the second says $T\in(A^{\otimes d})^{S_d}$, which is spanned by the elements $a^{\otimes d}$, $a\in A$. The image of $U(\mathfrak g^e)$ under the diagonal representation is contained in $\operatorname{End}_B(E)$: the diagonal action of $A$ commutes with the individual $e$'s and with places. Conversely, for $a\in A$ the element $a^{\otimes d}$ equals the product of its individual-position operators; For the commuting individual operators $a_i$, put $Q(t)=\prod_i(1+a_it)=\sum_r q_rt^r$ and $p_k=\sum_i a_i^k$. Formal differentiation and the geometric series for each factor give $Q'(t)=Q(t)\sum_{k\ge1}(-1)^{k-1}p_kt^{k-1}$, so $q_0=1$ and $q_r=r^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^r(-1)^{k-1}p_kq_{r-k}$. Each $p_k=\Delta_d(a^k)$ belongs to the enveloping image because $A$ is an associative algebra; here $a^k$ is the matrix power, regarded as an element of the Lie algebra $A$. The recurrence therefore puts $q_d=\prod_i a_i=a^{\otimes d}$ in that image. Hence $a^{\otimes d}\in\varphi(U(\mathfrak g^e))$ and $\varphi(U(\mathfrak g^e))=\operatorname{End}_B(E)$.

The second centralizer. An operator $T$ commutes with the diagonal $A$-action if and only if it is $G_e$-fixed, as follows. If $T$ is $G_e$-fixed, commuting with $(1+ta)^{\otimes d}$ for all but finitely many $t$ and comparing its linear coefficient gives $[T,\Delta_d(a)]=0$. Conversely, if $T$ commutes with every $\Delta_d(a)$, it commutes with $\Delta_d(a^k)$ for all $k$. Newton identities express $a^{\otimes d}$ in these power sums, so $T$ commutes with $a^{\otimes d}$, in particular for every unit $a\in G_e$. By [F3] every $G_e$-fixed operator is $\Phi(e)$ for an equivariant polynomial covariant $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h(X)\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$; evaluating at $X=e$ replaces each $X^{h_i}$ by $e^{h_i}$, which is a polynomial in the individual $e$-operators of degree less than $l$, so $\Phi(e)\in\psi(B)$ (the truncated algebra $B$ contains exactly the polynomials $e^0,\dots,e^{l-1}$ in each factor and the places). Conversely every element of $\psi(B)$ commutes with the diagonal $A$-action: for $a\in A$ put $\Delta_d(a)=\sum_{k=1}^d a^{(k)}$; each individual $e^{(j)}$ satisfies $[\Delta_d(a),e^{(j)}]=[a,e]^{(j)}=0$, and each place permutation $P_\sigma$ satisfies $P_\sigma\Delta_d(a)P_\sigma^{-1}=\Delta_d(a)$.
